en: Now begins the third chapter.
1. The Section Concerning Heaven and Earth (dyubhv-ādhikaraṇa).
In this section, he generally demonstrates the reconciliation (*samanvaya*) of words well-known in other [contexts] with Viṣṇu.
It has been stated that Viṣṇu is the object of the higher knowledge (*paravidyā*);
he now shows what is to be established in this section by saying "therein" (*tatra*).
The two words "ca" (and) signify mutual conjunction.

The term "prāyeṇa" (mostly) is used in the sense of abundance, for the purpose of excluding those cases not treated in the sections concerning deities (*devatādhikaraṇa*) and the section concerning Śūdras (*apaśūdrādhikaraṇa*), since those were not included in the section on systematic reconciliation (*samanvaya*).

And thus, for the most part, in this third quarter [of the Brahma-sūtras], there is the "harmonization" (*samanvayam*) in Viṣṇu of those words consisting of names and attributes that are well-known through direct scriptural statement (*śruti*), indicative marks (*liṅga*), and so forth, as referring to Hari— that is, to Him— and "elsewhere," namely to Rudra, Prakṛti, and others.

The meaning is that the author of the Sūtras "shows" or establishes [the conclusion] by means of the primary mode of signification and through powerful reasons based on the intended purport (*tātparya*).

Having cited the scriptural passage that serves as the subject matter (*viṣaya-vākya*)— which provides the connection with the Śruti and so forth— he demonstrates the doubt regarding the subject matter along with the prima facie arguments (*pūrvapakṣa*) supported by reasoning, beginning with the words "Of Viṣṇu."

In this regard, [it is said]: "Know that alone as the one Self, in whom heaven, earth, and the intermediate space are woven, together with the mind and all the vital breaths" (Muṇḍaka Upaniṣad 2.2.5); and:
"You are the knot of the vital breaths; enter me, O Rudra, the destroyer" (Mahānārāyaṇa Upaniṣad 35).
This is because Rudra is perceived as the substratum of the vital breath (*prāṇa*) through such passages as: "The Lord of Breath, clad in skins, the wielder of the Pināka bow" (*Ghṛtasū*).

And because of the characteristic mark of the individual soul (jīva) in the passage, "This very one moves within, being born in many ways" (Muṇḍaka Upaniṣad 2.2.6), the attainment of those two [results] follows.
The word "uktam" (it has been said) is repeated. Therein, the indeclinable "tatra" also carries the sense of "tat" (that).
The word "atra" is also repeated.
The word "ādi" (etcetera) connects with both [terms].
In the phrase "of Rudra," the genitive case is used in the sense of a remainder (*śeṣe*).
The term "of those two" is also indicative of the primary wind and [the other wind].

And likewise, in that very Atharvaṇa [Upaniṣad] where it is stated that Viṣṇu—the Imperishable characterized by qualities such as invisibility—is the object of the higher knowledge (*paravidyā*), there it is said:
"In whom heaven, earth, and the intermediate space are woven, along with the mind and all vital breaths—know Him alone as the one Self; abandon other words" (Muṇḍaka Upaniṣad 2.2.5).
In the statement "This is the bridge to immortality," one interpretation is that this was said regarding that which is the support of heaven, earth, and so forth;
therein, in the context of being the abode of heaven, earth, and so forth, [the word] "of those two" [is used].
There is the possibility that [the Self] refers to Rudra or the individual soul (jīva).
Why? Because in this passage, there is the hearing of the perception that the abode of heaven, earth, and so forth is the support of the vital breaths (prāṇa);
likewise, because there is the hearing of the marks of the individual soul in the phrase "He is this."
Nor should it be asked: "Even though there is a scriptural mention of being the support of the vital breaths (*prāṇa*), how can Rudra be understood here?
For there is the Taittirīya statement: "You are the knot of the vital breaths; O Rudra, enter me; as the consumer, nourish yourself with this food" (Mahānārāyaṇa Upaniṣad 35), and likewise—

"May that Brahmā, who brought forth Brahmā, the Lord of Prāṇa, clad in skins, the wielder of the Pināka bow, the Ruler—the God—grant us long life. (Ghṛtasūkta). By such passages from the Khila-saṃhitās, Rudra is perceived as the substratum of Prāṇa; this is another interpretation.

Alternatively, within this very same position, one may interpret the word "tayoḥ" (of those two) as being in the locative case and explain it as referring to the two properties consisting of the form of the indicator (*liṅga*) and the indicated (*liṅgin*).
In that case, the word "ādi" (and so forth) serves to include the statement: "Rudra alone is indeed the support of the worlds."

Thus, in that context, the attainment of those two [is established] through a distant connection (dūrānvaya); that is, another interpretation is that "therein" (*tatra*) refers to the state of being the object of the higher knowledge (*paravidyā*), wherein the attainment of Rudra and the individual soul (*jīva*) occurs.
Regarding this, in the first interpretation, by way of challenging the notion that the abode of heaven, earth, and so forth is other than Viṣṇu, [the text says] "him thus" (*tam evam*).

By such statements as these, there is an implication that [the object] is other than Viṣṇu, because of the previously mentioned status of being the object of supreme knowledge (*paravidyā*), which— by the force of the complementary passage "This is the bridge to immortality" (*Muṇḍaka Upaniṣad* 2.2.5)— is understood either, according to the *Tattvapradīpa*, as being the object of the knowledge that produces the knowledge generating liberation, or as being primarily knowable through non-exclusive connection (*ananya-yoga*). Thus, its being other than Viṣṇu is implied.
By means of the section on "the invisible" (*adṛśyatvādhikaraṇa*), the introductory connection (*ākṣepikī saṅgati*) of this [section] has been stated.
Likewise, the subject matter (*viṣaya*)—consisting of the state of being the abode of heaven, earth, and so forth—has been shown.
Furthermore, in the two-fold second interpretation, the prima facie argument (*pūrvapakṣa*) along with its supporting reasoning has been presented.
However, it should be understood that in the third [verse], the result of the prima facie view (*pūrvapakṣa*) is shown:

"in whom" refers to the Supreme Self (*paramātman*), in whom the two worlds and so forth reside; "mind" (*manaḥ*) refers to the presiding deity of that [mind]; and "with all the vital breaths" (*sarvaiḥ prāṇaiḥ*) refers to the vital functions.
"Know Him"— the Supreme Self who has entered along with the senses and those who identify with them— as "One," that is, as the primary principle.
"You should know" is the meaning of the Vedic text.
The word division is "rudra u mā āviśa.
The particle *u* is an indeclinable, a nipāta used to indicate the vocative case.
The word *mā* is an indeclinable (*avyaya*); it is not the pronominal substitute *mā* for the first person plural.
Alternatively, by the term *mā*, both the pronominal substitute for the first person and the indeclinable word *mā* are simultaneously included through the principle of *tantra*.
And that has the sense of negation. Thus: O Rudra, you are the "knot" (*granthi*), so called because the vital breaths—the senses—are knotted (*grathyate*) therein.
You are the "End-maker," the one who withdraws all;
as such, "enter" me.
The meaning is: "Enter [me]; establish your presence within me. Alternatively, it means: "O Rudra, you are the Ender; do not enter me.
By that "food" offered in the form of an oblation;
"Make me swell"— make me happy;
"to him who is not Brahman"—
to the four-faced one, "Brahman."
"He lifted up the Vedas"; he raised them up;
he is the "Lord of Breath";
he is the "Lord of the Senses" and the one "Clad in a Tiger Skin."
He whose garment is a skin— that is, a hide—
is *Pinākī*; "may Īśāna grant us life" means "may he nourish us," according to the meaning of another Vedic text.
In our established doctrine (siddhānta), however, words such as "Rudra" and others refer to Viṣṇu.
The meaning of the Atharvaṇa Śruti passage— "this individual soul (jīva) which is manifold"— is that it is produced through many bodies and moves within the body.
Therefore it is said: Sūtra 1.3.1: "The abode of heaven, earth, and so forth [is Brahman], because of its own word."
"Know Him alone as the one Self" (Muṇḍaka Upaniṣad 2.2.5);
because of the word "Self," the support of heaven, earth, and so forth is Viṣṇu alone.
Since words such as "Self" (Ātman) and "Brahman" cannot apply to anyone other than the imperishable Viṣṇu, therefore no one else has attained the state of being complete in all qualities.
Thus it is stated in the Brahmavaivarta Purāṇa. // 1 //
Introducing the aphorism that establishes the final conclusion, he explains it with the words "Therefore" (ataḥ).
This is because it is stated in the *Viṣṇutattvanirṇaya* that "from the word *sva* [in the Sūtra] means from the word *ātman*, which is a synonym for *sva*";

because it is stated in the *Tattvapradīpa* that by the etymology "the word *sva* is the word *svaśabda*," the word *ātman*—which is a synonym for *svaśabda*—is understood as Viṣṇu, since this word *ātman* is indeed the direct designator of Viṣṇu’s own nature (*svarūpa*);

and because, by adopting the analysis "the word *svaśabda* is the word that denotes Viṣṇu himself (*sva*)," and relying on the fact that the word *ātman* refers back to that same [Viṣṇu], the phrase "from the word *sva*" has been explained as meaning "from the word *ātman*."
And likewise, in the phrase "because of the word 'Self' (ityātmaśabdāt)," the meaning is "because of hearing the word 'Self'.
By the expression "the support of heaven, earth, and so forth," the word "support" (āyatana) is explained.
In some places, the reading is simply "āyatana" (abode).
By the phrase "Viṣṇu alone," the word "tat" (that), which recurs from the *Samanvaya* Sūtra, is explained through a change of gender in accordance with the scriptural text (*śruti*).
By this [sūtra], [the reason] "because of its own word" (*svaśabdāt*) is indicated.

The meaning of the Sūtra is thus stated: from the word *sva* which is a synonym for words denoting Viṣṇu, and from the word *sva* [in the sense of] "the abode of heaven, earth, and so forth"— meaning the support of everything including heaven and earth— "that indeed" is Viṣṇu alone.
From what [source] is it known that Viṣṇu is also denoted by the word "ātman"? To this he says: "Ātman."
Because "by them"— that is,
by the other living beings such as the four-faced Brahmā and others— perfection in qualities has "not been attained at all," meaning it has not been acquired in any way whatsoever.

Therefore, words such as "ātman" and "brahman" cannot apply to anything other than Viṣṇu— who possesses the eternal and unsurpassed grounds for their application— without Him; they do not exist [as designations] apart from Him.
The meaning is that they do not attain [the status of primary denotators] by way of being primary signifiers.
By this, it is stated that the word *ātman* also has "perfection of qualities" as its meaning.
Following the phrase "in the Brahmavaivarta," the ellipsis is to be supplied as "because it is stated elsewhere [to have] no other scope."
This connects with the phrase "because of the word 'Self'" (tasyātmaśabdāt).
Sūtra: Oṃ.
Because there is the designation of that which is to be approached by the liberated one.
"This is the bridge to immortality" (Muṇḍaka Upaniṣad 2.2.5).

Now, one might object: "Even if the word *ātman* primarily denotes Viṣṇu, could it not here have a secondary meaning due to the force of the characteristic mark (*liṅga*) of being born, which belongs to the individual soul (*jīva*)? And if so, the determination that Viṣṇu is the abode of heaven, earth, and so forth would not follow from that. Anticipating this doubt, [the author] presents the sūtra and cites the very scriptural passage it employs, beginning with the words "mukta... (the liberated...).
The grammatical connection (*anvaya*) is as follows: "because of the designation [of it] as something not to be attained by the liberated.
In the Sūtra, the phrase "of the abode of heaven, earth, etc. (*dyubhvādyāyatanasya*) is to be supplied by modification (*vipariṇāmena*).
"Attainable by the liberated" (*muktopasṛpya*) is a statement in the abstract sense (*bhāva-nirdeśa*).

In this context, "being approachable" (*upasṛpyatva*)—by virtue of the force of the scriptural term "bridge" (*setu*)—is intended to mean being an object of attainment that is devoid of any intervening space.
Now, one might argue that it is merely an object of attainment, like the path of light (*arcir-ādi*).
And so it is said: "of the immortal abode of heaven, earth, and so forth."

Thus, because of the statement that [He] is to be reached by the liberated (*muktopasṛpyatva*), there is certainty that it is Viṣṇu; therefore, one should not assume that the abode of heaven, earth, and so forth is something other than Viṣṇu by resorting to a non-primary sense for the word "Self" (*ātman*).
From the Smṛti passage, "of the liberated" (*muktānām*), it follows that "of the immortal" (*amṛtasya*) is used in the singular to denote the class.
And thus, "of the immortal" (*amṛtasya*)...
For one who has been liberated from birth, this Supreme Self is the "bridge"; the meaning is that He is the bridge, like a bridge, being the primary support.
"The knower of Brahman attains the Supreme" (Taittirīya Upaniṣad 2.1).
"Nārāyaṇa, the great object of knowledge, the soul of the universe, the ultimate refuge" (Mahānārāyaṇa Upaniṣad 11).
"The supreme goal of the liberated";
"He attains this Self consisting of bliss" (Taittirīya Upaniṣad 2.8), and so forth.
For it is precisely that [state] which is designated as "unattainable by the liberated.
What need is there for much more to be said here? As long as the yogi has not reached the White [Abode], he shall not be liberated; such is the definitive conclusion of the scriptures.
Thus, in the Āditya Purāṇa. // 2 //

Now, one might ask: "How does the fact that the abode of heaven, earth, and so forth is to be attained by the liberated serve as a determinant for its identity as Viṣṇu? Anticipating this objection, he explains the Sūtra—"brahmavid" [etc.]—as a means of resolving it.

By the phrase "by such [statements] as," and by the words "of Him" (referring to Viṣṇu) alone, it is shown that He is the goal to be attained—that is, the state of being attained while being devoid of any other goal to be attained.

By this, the Sūtra is explained through repetition: because the abode of heaven, earth, and so forth is designated as that which is approached by the liberated, and because that very same [abode] is designated as that which is approached by the liberated only for Viṣṇu.

It is indicated that the term "that" (*tat*), which recurs from the primary aphorism (*pradhānasūtra*), is to be supplied here by modification. The word *upasṛpya* has been explained by treating it as having the state (*bhāva*) as its primary meaning.
The particle *eva* serves to exclude the possibility that the gender belongs to anything else.
The meaning of the Taittirīya Śruti is that the knower of Brahman (*brahmavid*), being liberated, attains the Supreme (*param*), namely Viṣṇu.
This is heard in both the Taittirīya Upaniṣad and the Mahopaniṣad in the passage beginning with "Nārāyaṇa."
Here, the phrase "the universe depends upon that" is understood as a carryover; and thus, "that universe... [is connected].
The world is to be known as venerable, or rather, as worthy of worship and knowledge;
[it is] the Lord of the universe, the "supreme refuge."
The meaning of the scripture is that [He] subsists upon the support of the liberated;
"the supreme goal of the liberated" is one name found among the Thousand Names (Sahasranāma).
The "goal" (*gati*) is that which is reached as the supreme and primary; it is the substratum (*āśraya*).
The phrase "this one" (*etam*) has been explained in the section concerning the one consisting of bliss (*ānandamaya-vidyā*) in the Taittirīya Upaniṣad.
By the word "etcetera" (*ādi*), the passage "having approached this self consisting of bliss" (*etam ānandamayam ātmānam upasaṅkramya*) is included.
The passage beginning with "the supreme goal" (paramaṃ yaḥ parāyaṇam) is taken [as evidence].
Now, let it be granted that by the cited statements Viṣṇu is the one to be attained by the liberated; however—

Nevertheless, one might suspect that the inferential mark (liṅga) has room for another interpretation, thinking: "Since there is no exclusion of others here, why should another [deity] not be the one attained by the liberated, just as Viṣṇu is? Anticipating this, he states with scriptural authority—beginning with the words "by many"—that even if the mere state of being attainable elsewhere were possible, the specific state of being "approachable" (upasṛpyatva) mentioned in the Sūtra, or rather the state of being attainable by the individual soul endowed with the liberation intended by the word "mukta" in the Sūtra, has no scope elsewhere. Thus he says: "By many... [and so forth].

Regarding the phrase "here," concerning the subject of liberation and its means to be attained, the sense is that there is "no purpose" in using "much speech"— that is, in stating "this and that" with numerous individual words; on the contrary, it would merely result in a prolixity of expression.
To the question "In that case, how is the decision reached?", he says: "as far as Śveta.
"Śveta" refers to the abode of Viṣṇu known as Śvetadvīpa; "as long as he does not go" means as long as he has not attained it.
As long as the yogi does not perceive Viṣṇu residing therein, he—though possessing the means known as direct knowledge (aparokṣajñāna)—would not be liberated;
that is, he would not be freed from the veil consisting of the Lord’s will, and thus would not possess the fully manifested knowledge, bliss, and other attributes. This is "he" (eṣaḥ).

*Upadeśaḥ* means "the definitive determination of the scripture" (*śāstravinirṇayaḥ*); that is to say, it is the means for arriving at a definitive determination concerning the true nature of the scripture.
This is the meaning of the term *śāstravinirṇayaḥ*.
Or rather, [the definition] is "that which is the object of the determination produced by that.
However, in the *Bhāvabodha*, it is stated that in both the Sūtra and the Purāṇa, the term "liberated" (*mukta*) intends one who has undergone the dissolution of the subtle body (*liṅgabhaṅga*).
Here, by stating that the visitor of Śvetadvīpa is not liberated, it is understood that liberation belongs only to one who has reached Śvetadvīpa.
And thus, the sense is that Viṣṇu alone, who abides therein, is established as the goal to be attained by the liberated through the exclusion of all others.
The phrase "in the Āditya Purāṇa" is to be construed with the words "because of the designation of him alone as the goal to be attained by the liberated.
By this, the utility of the restrictive particle *eva* (alone) in the expression "of him alone" (*tasyaiva*) is made known.

For this reason, it should not be suspected that the inferential mark (*liṅga*) has a limited scope; this is the connection with the implied probandum (*sādhya*). Sūtra: "It is not inference, because of the absence of words denoting that."
There is no inference [of such a self], because there is no word for it. Om. 3.3.3.
Rudra, as postulated in scriptures consisting of inference, is not what is to be understood here.

Now, one might ask: "Could it not be that, according to the method previously stated, both Rudra and Prakṛti are the abode of heaven and earth? To this, the author of the Sūtras replies: "Not by inference," stating that because there is no evidence to prove it, neither of those two can be that abode.

Here, he explains the portion of the thesis stating "not [based on] inference" with the words "not consisting of inference. According to the *Tattvapradīpa*, which states: "Scripture whose authority is not established by inference is 'consisting of inference' (*anumātmaka*)," the meaning is that [the Lord] is conceived and taught as the substratum of all [scriptures], including the Pāśupata and other scriptures, which consist of inference—that is, whose authority is established through inference.
However, some have explained that *anumāna* is so called because it is "inferred as a means of valid cognition" (*pramāṇa*).
In this view, the word *ātman* is redundant;
this is stated in the *Tattvapradīpa-ṭīkā*.
The term "Rudra" is indicative of *pradhāna* and so forth.

By means of the phrase "the abode of heaven, earth, etc. (*dyubhvādyāyatana*), which is carried over from the *Pradhāna-sūtra*, he shows the counter-correlate (*pratiyogin*) of the meaning of the negative particle (*nañ*).
The word "here" (*atra*) means in the context of the section concerning the abode of heaven, earth, and so forth.
‘Vācyaḥ’ means that which is to be established; the phrase ‘as the locus of all’ is to be supplied as the remainder [of the sense],
because there is an absence of words such as ‘bhasmadhara’ (ash-bearer) or ‘ugra’ (fierce) [which would otherwise indicate a specific individual].
Having thus explained the part concerning the proposition (*pratijñā*) in the Sūtra, he explains the part concerning the reason (*hetu*): "bhasmadharā" (the bearer of ashes).
The phrase "the sound of that Rudra" (tasya rudrasya śabdaḥ) means the sound consisting of the word for him; that is, it consists of the word [Rudra] as its indicative mark (liṅga).

Thus, the meaning is that there is an absence of words such as "bhasmadhara" (ash-bearer) or "ugra" (fierce), which would denote a substratum (dharmin) qualified by attributes such as bearing ashes or being fierce.

Alternatively— regarding the statement, "Why is it said that the wearing of ashes, ferocity, and so forth possess the nature of that [word]?"— the suffix *tva* is used in its own sense (*svārthe*) with the intention of expressing the non-difference between the state (*bhāva*) and the entity (*bhavitṛ*).
Its employment, moreover, is for the purpose of including words that consist of gender (*liṅga*).
In the *Bhāvabodha*, however, it is stated: by the term "bhasmadharā" (the bearer of ashes), words consisting of names that denote Rudra are included;
by the term "ugratva" (ferocity), words consisting of signs (*liṅga*) that take the form of ferocity are included;
and by the word "etc. (*ādi*), other words consisting of both names and signs are included.
This [phrase] is an indicator for "designation" (*samākhyā*) and so forth.

Thus, it has been stated that the meaning is: because of the absence of designations and so forth that establish Rudra—such as the scriptural passages concerning Rudra wearing ashes (*bhasmadhara*), his characteristic marks (*liṅga*) such as ferocity (*ugratva*), and other such indicators.

Here, instead of saying "because of the absence of words like Rudra or Śiva," the expression "wearing ashes, ferocity, and so forth" is used [to indicate] the passage: "Rudra wears ashes and is naked."
This is because of the statement [in the scripture] made with the intention of referring to specific names.
Therefore, it should be understood that only the words "naked" (*nagna*) and so forth, as mentioned in this very statement, are to be included by the word "etc. (*ādi*).

Furthermore, the term *bhasmadhara* (the bearer of ashes) should also be explained as indicating other [meanings], since there is an absence of Vedic mantras (*śruti*), indicative marks (*liṅga*), and so forth that would establish its nature as being primarily composed of the three *guṇas* or as being *prakṛti*.

Although, if *atacchabdāt* were explained as "due to the absence of that word" (*tacchabdābhāvāt*), there would be an impossibility of forming a compound because the negative particle (*nañ*) lacks semantic capacity due to its dependence on a verb;

nevertheless, just as in the case of *nirmakṣikam* and similar examples, there is no such impossibility here, as one may resort to the *avyayībhāva* compound by the rule: "That which is an indeclinable [expressing] the absence of something."
Because it is in the fifth case (pañcamī), the suffix *ām* does not occur here.

By this sūtra, [the term] is understood as "that by which the world-creatorship is inferred," or else, according to the statement in the *Sattarkadīpāvalī*, "ānumānam" means "that which relates to inference"; thus, by resolving the word as "ānumānam," or by the word "anumāna," that which is established by the authority of the Pāśupata and other Āgamas—proving Rudra to be the supreme principle—is what is grasped.
Alternatively, *anumāna* refers to the scriptures of the Pāśupatas and others, as they are inferred to be authoritative means of knowledge (*pramāṇa*).
From that [word], by applying the suffix *ac* to the class beginning with *arśas* in the sense of possession (*matvartha*), the term denotes that which is propounded by them.
Even when the word *ānumānam* is analyzed as *eva-m-ānumānam*, another suffix *-an* must be applied after the one ending in *-an*.
In that case, the first word ending in *-an* expresses the scripture (*āgama*),
while the second expresses the state of being what is to be established (*pratipādyatva*).

And likewise, Rudra and others, who are taught in scriptures such as the Pāśupata which consist of inference, are not the abode of heaven, earth, and so forth; nor are they what is to be taught as the support of all in the context beginning with "In whom," why?
"Because of the absence of that word."

The meaning of the sūtra is thus stated: because there is an absence of scriptural authority (*śruti*), indicative mark (*liṅga*), and so forth, establishing Rudra, Pradhāna, or others [as the subject].

This is because, through such passages as "He is Antaka, he is Rudra, he is the sustainer of breath, he is the leader of breath; he who is Hari, he who is Ananta, he who is Viṣṇu, he who is the highest of the high," it is Viṣṇu alone who is declared to be the knot of the vital breath (*prāṇagranthi*) and Rudra, and so on.

Now, one might object: even though there is no explicit indicator of Rudra and others in the *Atharvaṇa*, since the name-based scripture (*samākhyā*) stating that He is the support of the vital breaths—namely, "Thou art the knot of the vital breaths, O Rudra" (*Mahānārāyaṇa Upaniṣad* 16.2)—and other such passages mention the words "Rudra" and so forth, as well as indicative marks (*liṅga*) such as being the "terminator," why could the status of being the abode of heaven, earth, and so on, mentioned therein, not belong to Rudra and the others by virtue of that? To this, he says:
"He who is the terminator, the destroyer—he alone is heard to be denoted by those words; and he is indeed Viṣṇu."
That Rudra who is celebrated in scripture is also Viṣṇu alone;
he who is denoted by the term "Prāṇagranthi," which signifies the support of the vital breaths, is [Viṣṇu].
He too is indeed Viṣṇu;
he who is the "leader of the vital breath" (prāṇanāyaka), his master, and for that very reason designated by the term "Lord of Breath" (prāṇeśa), he too is indeed Viṣṇu.
He who is celebrated as *Iśa* is also Viṣṇu alone;
he who is *Ananta*, denoted by that term, is also Viṣṇu alone because of being devoid of the three kinds of limitations (*pariccheda*), and not Śeṣa.

He who is *parovarīyān* (higher than the high) is also Hari alone and no other, because he is higher than Rudra and others, higher than Vāṇī and others, higher than Viriñca, and higher than Prakṛti—such is the meaning of the Śruti.

In this regard, according to the statement in the *Caturvedaśikhā* cited in the intermediate section (*antarādhikaraṇa*), "it is declared to be higher than the highest," one should understand that in the illustrative sentence (*vṛttivākya*), the substitution of *su*, the replacement by *u*, the *guṇa* change, and the elision of the word identical to it (the *samānaśabdalopa*) for the *su*-affix are employed to convey the four stages: the highest (*para*), the higher than the highest (*paratara*), the most excellent (*vara*), and the most excellent of the excellent (*varatama*).
The use of multiple instances of *yat* and *tat* is intended to indicate the connection of the predicate with each respective subject.

The meaning is that by such scriptural passages as "ityādinā," the characteristics of being the "knot of the vital breath" (*prāṇagranthi*) and so forth, as well as the fact of being denoted by the word *rudra*, are stated to belong to that very Viṣṇu alone.
The meaning of the word "and so forth" (*ādi*) includes being denoted by terms such as "Lord of Breath" (*prāṇeśvara*) and the characteristic of being the "terminator" (*antaka*).
This [term] is also an indicator for *prakṛti*, direct Vedic statement (*śruti*), indicative mark (*liṅga*), and so forth;
however, the meaning of the particle *eva* (only) is that it does not apply to Rudra and others.
By means of the particle *eva*, its existence elsewhere is admitted only in a secondary sense.
The phrase "because it has been stated" connects with the supplied probandum (sādhya), namely, "there is no contradiction with the Śrutis and Liṅgas concerning Rudra and others.
And in the Brahmāṇḍa Purāṇa:
Because he causes suffering to melt away, he is Rudra; because he afflicts [the world], he is Janārdana;
because he is the supreme ruler, he is Īśāna; and because of his greatness, he is Mahādeva.
Those men who drink from the celestial ocean (nāka) are liberated from the ocean of saṃsāra;
since Viṣṇu is the support for that, he is therefore remembered as Pinākī.
He is Śiva because his nature is bliss; he is Śarva because he destroys all things; and he is Hari because he wears this body composed of *kṛtyā* (magical power), setting it in motion.
Therefore, the god is called Kṛttivāsas; and Viriñca because of his act of emission (virecana);
he is named Brahmā because of his expansion (bṛṃhaṇa), and he is called Indra because of his sovereignty (aiśvarya).

But even so, there is still no certainty that Viṣṇu is the subject to be propounded in the scriptural texts containing designations (*samākhyā*) that indicate being the support of the vital breaths or being the abode of heaven, earth, and so forth;

for the words such as "Rudra" found therein are conventionally established (*rūḍha*) only in Paśupati and others, and thus do not apply to Viṣṇu, or if they did apply, there would still be no certainty.

Even though a secondary (yogic) application of the term is possible in the case of Viṣṇu, it is not determinative because that application is weaker than its primary (rūḍhi) sense; for there are no other scriptural marks (liṅgas) of Viṣṇu [in this context]. Therefore, he says: "And in the Brahmāṇḍa.
The word "and" (ca) has the sense of "also," serving as a conjunction.
The phrase "because it has been stated" (uktatvāt) is understood to carry over [from the previous context]. Thus, it connects with this [current argument].
To address the question "What was stated?", he recites the passage establishing the *mahāyoga* and *vidvadrūḍhi* [meanings] of words such as *rudra*: "rujam... and so forth.
Because he "melts away" (*drāvayate*)—that is, pacifies or turns back—"sickness" (*rujam*), such as disease and its arising, he is therefore called Rudra.
To the question "Who is he?", he states his specific nature: "Janārdana."
The etymological derivation is "he who crushes (mardayati) the birth [of beings]. Furthermore, because he causes Brahmā and the others to act, he is also Īśāna; such is the meaning.
The term "by way of greatness" (*mahattvataḥ*) is an elliptical expression; it should also be understood as including "because of illumination" (*dyotanāt*) and so forth.
Those who are "non-men" (*anarāḥ*) are people who, having been liberated from the ocean of *saṃsāra*, [attain] "the non-sky" (*anākam*).
They drink— that is, they enjoy— the supreme bliss; they are the Pinākas, for Viṣṇu is their support.
Therefore, their support is remembered as Pinākin; this is stated in the Śruti—
the word "śruta" (heard/stated) being the natural reading of the text.

The meaning of "Śarva" is: because he exists having obstructed happiness—even that which is innate to one's own nature—up until liberation; or because he exists having restrained the friend of the asuras. For this reason, he is "consisting of action" (kṛtyātmaka).
"Causing this body made of skin to function"—
that is, creating or regulating it— he "clothes" himself or the individual soul (jīva) with it; he covers them and abides within them.

Alternatively, the meaning is that he is called "Kṛttivāsas" (Clad in a Hide) because he wears or dwells upon the body. Because of "emission" (virecanāt)—that is, the creation of the world—he is Viṣṇu; because of "nourishing" (bṛṃhaṇāt) or "expanding" (vardhanāt), he is named Brahmā;
and because of his supreme sovereignty, he is called Indra.
"Thus, by various names, the one alone, Trivikrama,
the Supreme Person, is celebrated in the Vedas along with the Purāṇas.

Having thus explained the *mahāyoga* (great etymological application) of words such as Rudra and others in reference to Viṣṇu, he speaks of their conventional usage among the learned (*vidvadrūḍhi*) with the word "thus."
The word "by means of signs" (*nimittaiḥ*) is to be supplied [as the object of the verb].
And thus, in this manner— namely, by means of these various kinds of signs found in the Vedas along with the Purāṇas, and by means of these various kinds of words— Viṣṇu alone is "sung."
The meaning is that [He] is primarily denoted [by the word "all"].

How is it that this [Being], not seen elsewhere [to possess such a quality], has the status of being the primary denotation of the word "all"? To this, the justification is stated by the two [epithets]: "Puruṣottama" (the Supreme Person) and "Trivikrama" (the one who strode the three worlds).
For Trivikrama pervades the word "the purpose of the three worlds," and Puruṣottama is indeed the Lord who is the cause of the designation "the Supreme Person" (sarvapuruṣa).

Thus, by this [text], because the terms Rudra and so forth are explained in Viṣṇu through both great yogic etymology (*mahāyoga*) and the conventional usage of the learned (*vidvadrūḍhi*), it is established that Viṣṇu is the subject to be propounded even in other scriptural designations (*samākhyā-śruti*), since those two [modes of signification] possess greater force than mere conventional usage (*rūḍhimātra*).
This is the intended meaning.
The phrase ending with "Puruṣottama" [is found] in the *Brahmāṇḍa-purāṇa*.
Thus, the connection is with what precedes. And in the *Vāmana*: "But the names beginning with Nārāyaṇa cannot possibly occur elsewhere."
"Viṣṇu alone is proclaimed as the goal for those who bear other names.

Now, one might object: if it is asserted that words such as "Rudra" refer to Viṣṇu, and that scriptural passages such as "May the destroyer Rudra enter me" are therefore non-conclusive (as they do not establish a different deity), [then how can they be taken otherwise?]

In that case, since names such as Nārāyaṇa and others could refer to Rudra and other deities, the scriptural passages such as "Nārāyaṇa, the great object of knowledge" (Mahānārāyaṇa Upaniṣad 11) would lack determinative power; therefore, he says: "And in the Vāmana [Purāṇa]..."
"In whatever sense" means that since this too has already been stated, there is no contradiction; this is how it connects with the preceding [text].
To the question "What was stated?", he recites that passage: "But not... and so forth.
The word *tu* is used for emphasis.

The phrase "of Nārāyaṇa and the others" implies that the primary application (*mukhyavṛtti*) of the term "Nārāyaṇa" and so forth exists elsewhere, namely in Rudra and others; this is the sense to be supplied.
The meaning is that Viṣṇu alone is the "resort" (gati) of other names, such as the word Rudra and others; that is, he is proclaimed as their primary denotation.
The word *iti* is connected with the term *vāmana*.

Since it has been stated that names such as Nārāyaṇa and others have no other scope [for application], the intention is that the Vedic texts mentioning them do not lack determinative power; thus, it is connected with the intended probandum (*sādhya*).
And in the Skanda Purāṇa:

"Except for names such as Nārāyaṇa, the Lord Puruṣottama bestowed [other names] elsewhere, just as a king [bestows] his own city upon another. To the objection—namely, that since there is no difference in their being names of the Lord (bhagavannāmatva), why should names such as Nārāyaṇa not also apply to Rudra and others, just like the names Rudra and so forth?—he says: "And in the Skanda [Purāṇa]."
The word *ca* (also) has the sense of conjunction (*samuccaye*). Its connection with the preceding [phrase] is: "because this too has already been stated.
To the question "What was stated?", he recites that passage: "From the Real (*ṛta*)."... [and so on].
The meaning is "to lead away.
Regarding the word "elsewhere" (*anyatra*): the ellipsis is that there are names other than Rudra and the rest, distinct from Rudra and the others.
By the word "etcetera" (*ādi*), [names such as] Viṣṇu and so forth are included.
Regarding this, he states an illustration: "The king."
The meaning is that it is just as a king gives his own city to others, such as his ministers, except for [one person];
this connects with the word "iti" at the end of the passage from the *Skānda*.
And because it has been stated that those names, such as Nārāyaṇa and so forth, do not apply elsewhere, they are not equal; this connects with the supplied phrase [at the end].

By this, since the names such as Nārāyaṇa and others are stated in the *Skānda* to belong to Viṣṇu alone, it is indicated that the particle *eva* (only) used previously has another function, namely, through the method of positive concomitance (*anvaya*), that there is no equality [between them]. Furthermore, "the four-faced one," "Śatānanda," and "the lotus-born Brahmā" refer to Brahmā; and "the fierce one," "the wearer of ashes," "the naked one," and "the skull-bearer" refer to Śiva.
Keśava also bestowed his own specific names upon them.
And thus it is stated in the Brāhma [Purāṇa]. 3.
If words such as "Rudra" and so forth are thus solely devoted to Viṣṇu, then why is it said that [terms like] "wearing ashes" and "ferocity" are words for Him?

If it is argued that this is with the intention of [the attributes] being given by Viṣṇu—then words such as "Rudra" are also of that nature; how then can there be a lack of certainty on account of them? To this, he says: "The four-faced one."
Although they are his own,
nevertheless, "Keśava"—
Viṣṇu, the initiator of Brahmā and Rudra— [possesses] "his own."
The meaning is that he gave to Brahmā specifically those particular names which primarily denote him himself— namely, the specific names "Caturmukha," "Śatānanda," and "Padmabhū."
"‘Nagnaḥ’ means ‘digambaraḥ’ (clothed in the directions).
‘Śivasya’ means ‘for Śiva’. The word ‘ca’ has the sense of ‘tu’ (but/indeed)."
The phrase "because this has also been stated regarding the Brāhma [state]" connects with the preceding [argument].
Its meaning is that [qualities] such as the wearing of ashes and ferocity found in Rudra and others were obtained from Viṣṇu himself.
And the connection of that [fact] with the probandum is that what was previously stated is logical.
Sūtra—Oṃ.
And [the term] "prāṇabhṛt" [is used]. Om. 4.4.

For these very reasons, neither the individual soul (*jīva*) nor the vital air (*vāyu*) [is the subject]. [Objection: But surely, because the characteristic mark of the individual soul is heard in the text, "This one moves within, being born in many ways" (Muṇḍaka Upaniṣad 2.2.6), and because the individual soul as a general category is well known to possess the quality of breathing, [it must be the subject].

He reads and explains the Sūtra—"And [it is] the Prāṇabhṛt"—in order to dispel the following doubt: "Since it is well known from another Śruti passage—'O Gautama, by the thread of Vāyu indeed this world, the other world, and all beings are held together' (Bṛhadāraṇyaka Upaniṣad 5.7.2)—that the state of being the support for the worlds as objects resides in Vāyu, why should it not be Vāyu who is taught here in this context as the substratum of heaven, earth, and so forth? *prāṇabhṛcceti //* (And [it is] the Prāṇabhṛt). [The commentary continues: The term "Prāṇabhṛt" refers to the individual soul (jīva), because it is the bearer of the vital breaths (prāṇas). It is not Vāyu. Why? Because the attributes of being the support of heaven, earth, and so forth are impossible for the individual soul. Furthermore, the word "Prāṇabhṛt" is used in the sense of the individual soul in the passage: "Then he becomes one with that Prāṇabhṛt alone; he does not know anything else, nor does anyone else know him" (Bṛhadāraṇyaka Upaniṣad 4.1.3). "By these" means by the previously stated reasons, namely: the word "Self," the state of being approached by the liberated, the word "not-that" (atad-śabda), and the fact that the scriptural passages concerning the attainment of Rudra and others have Viṣṇu as their ultimate referent.
The meaning of the word "eva" (only/just) is that no other reason need be stated here.
By the statement "the living being is air," the term *prāṇabhṛt* (bearer of breath) is explained.
Here, the word "denoted" (*vācya*) is supplied from the context;
the particle *ca* is used for conjunction.
By this [explanation], it is stated that the word "and" (*ca*) in the Sūtra draws forward the previously mentioned reasons as well as the negative particle (*nañ*),

signifying that not only is Rudra not to be denoted here, but that the individual soul (*jīva*) and the vital air (*vāyu*) are also not to be denoted; thus, it serves the purpose of conjunction (*samuccaya*).
"Though unborn, he is born in many ways"—thus it is stated that he himself is born in manifold ways (Taittirīya Āraṇyaka 3.13.1). // 4 //

Now, one might object: "Even if the Śruti passage beginning with 'Vāyunā vai Gautama' does not establish Vāyu because it refers to Viṣṇu, why could the individual soul (jīva) not be the subject here, given the various marks such as 'being born'? To this, he says: "Ajāyamāna" (unborn).
In terms of the body, though "unborn" and "unchanging," he "is born in many ways" in forms such as Rāma, Kṛṣṇa, and others.
The meaning is that he manifests in various places.
Regarding the word "iti": it means by means of the statement contained within the *Puruṣasūkta*.

The meaning of the word "only" (eva) is that it is precisely this Viṣṇu—of whom the absence of birth was stated by the proponent [in the previous Sūtra]—and not the individual soul (jīva), for whom birth is possible.
Thus, the indicative mark (liṅga) remains applicable, and there is no contradiction with it; such is the remainder of the sentence.
Sūtra: Oṃ.
Because there is a designation of difference.

Nor can their identity be asserted, because of the designation of difference in the passage: "When he sees the other, the Lord, as the one who is worshipped, and His majesty... (Muṇḍaka Upaniṣad 3.1.2). // 5 //
Now, what is the point of the effort to demonstrate that the characteristic marks of the individual soul (jīva) pertain to Viṣṇu?
On the strength of those very marks, it would be the individual soul itself that is the abode of heaven, earth, and so forth;
nor is there any contradiction with the previously mentioned reasons, such as the word "Self" (ātman).

He reads and explains the sūtra—*bhedeti*—while refuting the objection that the word "Self" (*ātman*) and so forth can be appropriately applied even to the individual soul (*jīva*) with the intention of expressing non-difference between the individual soul and the Lord (*īśvara*).

The phrase "identity is not to be expressed" is to be understood as the conclusion; and the words "intended here [in this context] to refer to the individual soul and the Lord" are the necessary ellipsis.
Because [the word] "not" (na) does not appear in this Sūtra, the negative particle must be supplied;
and it is stated that this [negation] should be joined with the counter-correlative (*pratiyogin*) of the distinction residing in the reason (*hetu*).

The word "and" (*ca*) serves to aggregate [other points], meaning that the denotability by the word "Self" (*ātman*) resulting from the identity of the individual soul (*jīva*) and the Lord (*īśvara*), as well as being understood through this particular context, are also [excluded].
To the question "What is this designation?", he says: "juṣṭam" (enjoyed). Thus, "because of the designation of difference" means "because of the scriptural statement of difference."

By this, the meaning of the Sūtra is stated as follows: in the sentence "enjoyed by him" (*juṣṭam*), because the previously mentioned individual soul (*jīva*) is designated as the agent of seeing through the word "sees" (*paśyati*), and because a distinction from the Lord is expressed by the mention of the term "Lord" (*īśa*), it must be said that their identity is not intended here.
The scriptural authority for the doctrine that [Brahman] consists of bliss has been explained.
Sūtra: Oṃ.
From the context.
"Two sciences are to be known"; for this [passage] constitutes the context for that [two-fold knowledge]. (Muṇḍaka Upaniṣad 1.1.4) // 6 //

Now, one might raise the objection: "In this context, is it not stated that the individual soul (jīva) is distinct from some Lord (īśa), and not from the Supreme Self (paramātman); therefore, there is no difference between these two"? Anticipating this doubt, he presents and explains the sūtra: "On account of the context" (prakaraṇāt).

The word "iti" [in the original text] implies the ellipsis: "having begun with this [statement], it was studied"; and the word "hi" means "because," since "this"—the collection of sentences beginning with "juṣṭam" (enjoyed)—belongs "to that very [Self]."
The meaning of the word "only" (eva) is that the context (*prakaraṇa*) belongs to the Supreme Self alone, which is the object of higher knowledge (*paravidyā*), and not to anything else.
By this, [it is shown] from its own context that "two kinds of knowledge are to be known."

Thus, by showing the application of the sūtra, it has been demonstrated that since the subject matter here is the reality that is the scope of higher knowledge (paravidyā), this is a section concerning Viṣṇu; therefore, because the designation of difference is understood to refer to the Supreme Self alone, it must be stated that non-difference between the individual self (jīva) and the Supreme Self is not intended here. Sūtra: Oṃ.
And by means of abiding and eating.
Oṃ. 7.
"Two birds, inseparable companions, cling to the same tree;
one of them eats the sweet fruit, while the other looks on without eating. (Muṇḍaka Upaniṣad 3.1.1).
This is because it describes the abiding and the eating of the Lord (Īśa) and the individual soul (jīva). // 7 //
Thus ends the first chapter, "The Lord of Heaven and Earth."

It is understood not only from the scriptural statement of distinction, "enjoyed," that the difference between the individual soul (jīva) and the Lord (īśvara) is not intended here in this context, but also from an indicative mark (liṅga); thus the author of the Sūtras says: "In the state of abiding... (Sūtra 2.3.18).
To prevent the objection that this [reason] is unestablished, he explains by citing a scriptural passage: "Two birds...

By this, the meaning of the Sūtra is stated: that on account of the two reasons heard in the scripture—"two birds"—namely, the state of not subsisting on the fruits of action and the state of subsisting on them, the identity of the individual soul (jīva) and the Lord (īśvara) cannot be asserted here.
The word "ca" (and), however, is not explained because its function as a collector of reasons is self-evident.

Although hearing (*śruti*) is mentioned first [in the source], in both the Sūtra and the Bhāṣya, the mention of "abiding" (*sthiti*) comes first, overriding the scriptural order; this is because abiding is more venerable due to its connection with the Lord (*īśa*), and because it consists of fewer syllables.
‘Sayujā’: two joined together (sayujau), existing in a state of mutual non-exclusion by virtue of being related as the beneficiary and the benefactor; ‘sakhāyā’:
two friends (sakhāyau), staying in one place out of affection; ‘dvā’: two; ‘suparṇā’: two with beautiful wings (suparṇau).
They have the form of two *suparṇas* (birds).

Based on the natural force of the qualification "two *suparṇas* as friends," and given that this [text] concerns living beings in general, the individual soul (*jīva*) and the Lord (*īśvara*)— who are of the nature of supreme bliss— are "equal."
They both embraced the single "tree" called the body, the *aśvattha*, as they clung to it.
Between those two birds, the individual soul (jīva), which is "other" than the Lord, "eats" the pippala— the fruit of the aśvattha tree in the form of the results of actions produced by the body.
He eats only that which is indeed tasteless as if it were sweet;
while the individual soul (jīva) "eats," the Lord (īśvara), however, "does not eat."
Not consuming even the first [category] beginning with the living beings (jīva), it "shines forth" (cākaśīti)—that is, it manifests—on all sides ("abhi," meaning "abhitaḥ").
It does not, however, depend upon the fruit of karma for its own maintenance as the individual soul (jīva) does; such is the meaning of the Muṇḍaka Śruti. // 1 //
Thus concludes the section concerning Heaven and Earth (the Dyubhv-ādhikaraṇa). 1.
// 2. The Section on the Grounds //

Having stated, "Prāṇa is indeed greater than hope," [the text] says, "That which is the Plenum (bhūman) is happiness" (Chāndogya Upaniṣad 7.23); thus, the attainment of the state of being the Plenum belongs to that very [prāṇa].
In this section, the concordance of the term *bhūman* with Viṣṇu is established.

While the word *bhūman* in such passages as "like a sacrifice, from *bhūman*" (*bhūmnaḥ kratuvat*) sometimes denotes a quality (*dharma*), here it refers to the possessor of qualities (*dharmī*) in his complete form.
And it should be understood that "fullness" means excellence in qualities.

Indicating the connection with the Śruti and other sources, as well as the subject matter and so forth, he presents the prima facie view (pūrvapakṣa) along with its supporting arguments: "Prāṇa... [and so on].
In passages such as "in the Chāndogya," the term *upaskāryam* (to be explained) is to be supplied.
The phrase "having said thus" (*ity uktvā*) is an elliptical expression for "having begun with"; it should also be understood to imply "without having stated what follows that."
For this very reason, the restrictive particle *eva*—meaning "of that very [prāṇa]"—was employed to exclude others.
In the Śruti, according to the prima facie view (*pūrvapakṣa*), the word *prāṇa* refers merely to air;
however, according to the final conclusion (*siddhānta*) and the method of the Commentary (*bhāṣya*), it refers to both air and Viṣṇu.
According to the *Nyāyavivaraṇa* and the *Chāndogyabhāṣya*, however, [the term] refers to Vāyu alone.
Nor is there any contradiction between the two meanings— referring to both Vāyu and Viṣṇu, and referring to Vāyu alone—
because the *Bhāṣya* proceeds with the intention of referring to the Inner Controller (*antaryāmī*), whereas the *Vivaraṇa* and other works proceed without that intention.
Just as in the passage, "From the Self [arose] space" (Taittirīya Upaniṣad 2.1),

although the word *sambhūta* has multiple meanings, Viṣṇu, as the Inner Controller (*antaryāmin*), is also denoted by the term "space"; however, if that word were to mean only "origination," he would not be denoted by it.

Likewise, in the *Tattvapradīpa*, it is stated that the commentary proceeded by means of an "admitted argument" (*abhyupagamavāda*), beginning with the words, "because it is an admitted argument," asserting that this vital breath (*prāṇa*) is indeed Viṣṇu.
And thus, according to the first position, the vital breath [is superior] to "hope" (*āśā*).
Bhāratī is "greater" (bhūyān), meaning superior in quality;
likewise, so is Prāṇa.

The meaning is that Viṣṇu, as its inner controller (*antaryāmī*), is greater than even that [wind] and hope precisely because He is the inner controller. By this, the *ākṣepikī* (suggestive) connection with the *Ānandamayādhikaraṇa* is indicated, since here the "fullness" (*pūrṇatva*)—characterized by being superior to those of the same class as previously denoted by the term *ānandamaya*—is extended (*ākṣepa*) to the wind.
The subject matter is that which is called "the Infinite" (*bhūman*) as stated in the *Chāndogya* Śruti.
Furthermore, the doubt as to whether it is Vāyu or Viṣṇu has been indicated;
likewise, the prima facie view (pūrvapakṣa) is that it is the attainment of the state of being "much" (bhūman) for that very [Vāyu],
and therein the reasoning consisting of the introduction concerning Prāṇa and the mention of him as the highest is shown.
In the statement, "That which is the Infinite (bhūman) is bliss; there is no bliss in the finite (alpa); the Infinite alone is bliss," the word "bliss" (sukha) signifies full, absolute bliss.
"That which is bliss is the Infinite."

According to the statement of Vyāsatīrtha and because it is said that all nouns take on their respective genders in turn, even the word *sukha* (bliss) alone, when used without an adjunct, signifies complete bliss.

Therefore, there is an exchange between the subject and the predicate in the phrase: "That which is independent bliss consisting of full bliss is the *bhūman* (the Infinite); He is Nārāyaṇa, full in His attributes."

For this very reason, by qualifying bliss (*sukha*) with independence (*svātantrya*), he demonstrates that there is no lack of pervasion (*anaikāntya*) regarding liberated souls (*muktajīva*), intending to establish this with the words "not in the small" (*nālpe*).
The meaning is: "in the small," that is, in the incomplete liberated soul, there is no bliss without His grace. He concludes: "Bliss is only the Infinite" (*bhūmaiva sukham*).
Here too, there is a reversal;
for from such indicative marks as "those whose vital breaths have departed" (Chāndogya Upaniṣad 7.15.3), the word *prāṇa* refers to the wind (*vāyu*).

Now, one might object: since the word "prāṇa" used in the statement "Prāṇa is indeed greater than hope" refers to Viṣṇu according to the principle stated in "Therefore [He] is Prāṇa," it follows that Viṣṇu alone possesses the quality of being the "Great" (bhūman); how then can Vāyu be established as the Great by the force of the word "prāṇa"? To this, he says: "utkrānta... (regarding the departure).

The phrase "ityādi" (and so forth) is a reference in which the case-ending has been elided. By the word "ādi" (etcetera), one includes such passages as: "One should burn with an iron spike those whose life-breaths have departed, crushing them completely; they should not say of him, 'You are a slayer of a father.'"
A complete sentence is taken [as the subject]; and the analysis of the compound is either "that which is both that and a mark" (tat ca tat liṅgaṃ ca) or "the mark of that" (tasya liṅgam).
The word "this" (*ayam*) is to be supplied as the remainder [of the sentence]. The particle *ca* is used in the sense of restriction (*avadhāraṇe*).
And the phrase "and denoting air" (*vāyuvācī ca*) involves a shift in the order of the words (*bhinnakramaḥ*).
And thus, this word "prāṇa" denotes only air; it does not denote Viṣṇu.

Why? Because of the "mark" (liṅga) in the passage beginning with "those whose vital breaths have departed"; the construction is that this is because the mark consisting of the departure and so forth of that vital breath is heard [in scripture].
Those from whom the vital breath has departed are described as such; "them"— the mother, father, teacher, and so forth— one should "completely" (*samāsam*), that is, in their entirety, "interweave."
And even if one were to drag it along with a spear at one point and burn it, whether it be a son or a disciple, people would not say of him,
"Why is this?"— namely, "He is a patricide" or "He is a matricide.
The implication is that this is because of the absence of the presence of the principal vital breath (mukhyaprāṇa).
Such is the meaning of the scripture.
Therefore, he says:
Sūtra—Oṃ.
The Infinite [is Brahman], because it is taught as being superior to the serene faith (saṃprasāda).
Because of the teaching of "perfect serenity" (samprasāda), because of being of the nature of full bliss, and because of the teaching that [He] is above all, Viṣṇu alone is the Bhūman.
He introduces the aphorism that establishes the final conclusion with the words "ataḥ" (therefore).
"Prasāda" (serenity) is so called because by means of it people become clear; it is happiness.
"Samyak-prasāda" (perfect serenity) is "samprasāda"; such is the analysis of the compound.
One should not suspect that suffering might exist in the Lord just as happiness does;

for, by the effect of perfect bliss—namely, perfect serenity (samprasāda)—the absence of suffering is ascertained. With this intention, he restates and explains the reason "from perfect serenity" (*samprasādāt*).
With the intention that the word "and" (*ca*) from the subsequent sūtra should be drawn in here, [he states] "because of the teaching regarding [the Self]" (*adhyupadeśāt*).
Having thus restated this [sūtra] as referring to another reason, he explains it with the words: "Because of the specific instruction" (adhyupadeśāt).
The meaning is: "because of the teaching" (upadeśāt), that is, because of the statement that [the Self] is "above" all things, beginning with Name, by virtue of being superior to them.
The particle *ca* is used here in the sense of a collection of causes; in this context, each [individual factor] is indeed a cause,
but it is not a single, complete cause.
If that word "Īśvara" is intended to emphasize the state of being (bhāva-pradhāna),
then the meaning of the reason— "because he is the Lord of all"— should be understood as "because he is the Lord of the entire [universe]," as stated in the *Anuvyākhyānasudhā*.
The pursuit [of the argument] up to the point of the scriptural teaching (*upadeśa*) is for the purpose of avoiding the fallacy of the unestablished (*asiddhi*).

The sense is that, due to the context of the passage (*prāyapāṭha*), the lordship over all is established through [the mention of] the lordship over the vital breaths (*prāṇādhipatya*) within the "Abundance" (*bhūman*). He states the meaning of the term *tattvam*, which follows from the *Samanvaya* Sūtra and serves to provide the predicate: "Viṣṇu alone. The syntactical connection (*anvaya*) is: "The Abundance is Viṣṇu alone. [As it is said:
"The thousand-headed God, the all-eyed, the source of bliss for the universe..."
The universe is the divine Nārāyaṇa, the imperishable, the supreme state.
"For [He is] eternally supreme in every respect"—thus indeed says the Śruti (Mahānārāyaṇa Upaniṣad 11).
To the question, "How does the state of possessing full bliss and so forth serve as a determinant of Viṣṇu-hood?", he replies: "By the thousand... [sahasra-].
Regarding "iti hi":
because (*yasmāt*) there exists a scriptural passage (*śruti*) contained within the Nārāyaṇa-anuvāka that begins with "iti."

Therefore, the meaning is that from this state of supreme serenity (*samprasāda*), the certainty of Viṣṇu’s nature indeed arises. [The text says] "the thousand-headed god" (*sahasraśīrṣaṃ devaṃ*), meaning the deity whose heads are infinite, as indicated by the word "thousand."
"Viśvākṣam" means whose form is light and who sees everything;
"viśvaśambhuvam" means the abode of perfect bliss; and "nārāyaṇam" means existing as one who has entered into the entire world.
In the liberated community, it is clearly the "imperishable" (*akṣaram*);
that is, either devoid of destruction by its very nature, or delighting in the senses (*akṣeṣu*).
Or, it is the "supreme station" (*paramaṃ padam*), meaning that which is measured as superior to others such as Brahmā and so forth, or that whose supreme measure (*parā mā*) belongs to it.
The analysis of the compound is: "He who is supreme (para) and who eats (aś) everything (viśva) from all sides (viśvatas).
This is a case of *savarṇadīrgha* [vowel lengthening].
This word is like the word *somapa*.
Alternatively, by means of correct grammatical usage, there is a change of gender based on its being in the feminine form ending in *-ā*.
Thus, "supreme in every respect" (*viśvataḥparamām*) means that which is higher than everything;
or it refers to the Supreme Being denoted by the syllable *A*, who is eternal and supreme over all.
The "Universe" (viśvam) is that which is devoid of destruction by its very nature;
"Hari" (harim) because he accepts the oblations in sacrifices and because of his golden (hari) complexion;
and "the God" (devam).
The meaning of the Śruti is that the universe subsists upon that god named ‘Nārāyaṇa,’ whose qualities include play and so forth;
although the Drāviḍa recension reads “viśvataḥ paramam” (the Supreme beyond the universe).

Nevertheless, following the Āndhra recension, the word "supreme" (paramām) was stated; thus, there is no contradiction with the indicative marks such as departure, based on [the passage] beginning with, "As he departs, the vital breath (prāṇa) departs after him" (Bṛhadāraṇyaka Upaniṣad 6.4.2). // 8 //

If it were accepted here that the word *prāṇa* denotes Viṣṇu, there would be a contradiction with the previously mentioned marks such as "stepping across" (*kramaṇa*); therefore, he says "no," [introducing the verse] beginning with "him" (*tam*).
By the word "first" (*prathama*) and so forth, the subsequent sentences are included; by the second [word], its other indicative marks (*liṅga*) are included.
The word "also" (*api*) serves as a conjunction (*samuccaya*), and it also carries the sense of "even though... nevertheless" (*yadyapi tathāpi*).
And thus—it is not only that there is no contradiction with the introductory reference to "Prāṇa," since that [term] has Viṣṇu as its referent;
rather, "also" (api): if it is accepted here that Viṣṇu is denoted by the word "Prāṇa," there is no contradiction with the indicative marks (liṅga) such as the act of departing (utkramaṇa).

Why? The construction is as follows: "even so" (api); that is, even though Viṣṇu is omnipresent, the mark of departing and so forth is established by the Vājasaneyaka statement beginning with "him as he departs" (tam utkrāmantaṃ).
The sense is that when a matter is established by scripture, opposition from worldly perception is of no consequence.
"In the preceding passage, 'The tip of this very heart flashes forth;
by that flash, this Self departs' (Bṛhadāraṇyaka Upaniṣad 6.4.2),
the Supreme Self under discussion is referred to by the word 'this' (saḥ)."
And thus, following the Supreme Self as it "departs"— that is, goes out— from the body of one possessing direct knowledge, whose heart-tip has been thus illuminated, the "vital breath" (prāṇa),
namely the primary vital air, "departs."
The meaning of the scriptural statement is that [the soul] departs from the body.
Sūtra: Oṃ.
And because of the logical consistency of the Dharma.
Oṃ. 9.
And because properties such as omnipresence and so forth are logically established. // 9 //
Thus ends the section concerning the "Abundance" (bhūman). 2.
Having introduced another sūtra that establishes the all-pervasiveness (*bhūmatva*) of Viṣṇu by means of a different argument, he explains it with the words: "Dharma... and so forth.
By the word "etcetera" (*ādi*), independence, self-establishedness, and so forth are included.
This reason is connected with the primary probandum: that Viṣṇu alone is the *bhūman*.
Although in the Chāndogya [Upaniṣad] it says, "where one sees nothing else... (Chānd. 7.24.1).

Thus, following the statement that makes known His independence, one hears the statement "He alone is below" (Chāndogya Upaniṣad 7.25.1), which declares His omnipresence. Having grasped the attribute of independence first heard by means of the word *sva* (Self), one should grasp His omnipresence by means of the word *sarva* (all).

Nevertheless, it should be understood that in that [latter] sentence, since omnipresence is clearly perceived as being restricted to the state of being "much" (*bhūman*), that very [attribute] is grasped by its expressive term.
By this—where *ca* signifies a conjunction of reason—the word "dharma" follows immediately after [the word] "parama.
This pursuit, extending as far as logical justification (*upapatti*), is for the purpose of making known that there is no other possible ground (*niravakāśatva*) for the gender [of the term].
And thus, it is not only [the case] with *samprasāda* and so forth.
However, in the passage: "He is below, He is above, He is behind, He is in front, He is to the south, He is to the north; He indeed is all this" (Chāndogya Upaniṣad 7.25.1); likewise, in the passage:
"Where one sees nothing else, hears nothing else, understands nothing else—that is the Infinite" (Chāndogya Upaniṣad 7.24.1);
and likewise: "In what, O Venerable One, is He established? In His own majesty" (Chāndogya Upaniṣad 7.24.1).

And because attributes such as omnipresence are heard in such passages, the meaning of the Sūtra is stated to be that the "Abundant One" (bhūman) is Viṣṇu alone, since those attributes are applicable to Viṣṇu alone.
"He"— Nārāyaṇa, denoted by the word "Abundant"— exists below, above, behind, in front, to the south, to the north, and everywhere.
He states its purpose: "That alone is all this.
By that alone is this world pervaded; it is He who bestows existence upon everything, and for that very reason He abides everywhere—this is the meaning.
Regarding the word "wherein" (*yatra*): without which [He] depends on which, the qualified seeker perceives nothing else, but perceives everything as dependent upon that.
In the same way, he hears and cognizes that as "the ground" (bhūmi);
or, "wherein"— meaning, when that is seen, one does not see anything else as independent.

To Nārada’s question, "He is the Blessed One; that Blessed One is the Infinite (bhūman); in what is He established?", Sanatkumāra replies, "He is established in Himself," meaning He is supported within His own majesty or in His own glory. This is the meaning of the Śruti. // 2 //
Thus concludes the section on the "Abundance" (bhūman). 2.
3. The Section on Syllables (Akṣarādhikaraṇa)
The qualities of invisibility and so forth are attributed to Viṣṇu by such scriptural passages as:
"The unseen seer, the unheard hearer" (Bṛhadāraṇyaka Upaniṣad 3.7.23).
Since such [statements] as "I bear the mighty Soma" (Ṛgveda 10.125.2) are also possible for him, the middle syllable is thus described.

In this section, the coordination of the names of the Imperishable (akṣara) is carried out. Having cited the scriptural passage that constitutes the subject matter and indicating the relevant topics such as the subject matter itself, he presents the prima facie view (pūrvapakṣa) along with its supporting arguments, beginning with the words "adṛśyatvādi" (on account of being invisible, etc.).
The word "uktāḥ" (stated) is repeated;
"te" (they) is the ellipsis. By the word "ādi" (etcetera), qualities such as being ungraspable and so forth are included.
By the word "qualities" (guṇāḥ), the quality of being the substratum of the moon, sun, and so forth is also included.
By the phrase beginning with "second," [it is meant]: "That which is unheard is the hearer, that which is unthought is the thinker, that which is unknown is the knower;
there is no other seer than this, no other hearer than this, no other thinker than this, no other knower than this—in this very Imperishable (akṣara)."
"The ether, O Gārgī, is woven like warp and woof" (Bṛhadāraṇyaka Upaniṣad 5.8.11);
and likewise: "By the command of this Imperishable, O Gārgī, the sun and moon stand held apart" (Bṛhadāraṇyaka Upaniṣad 5.8.9).
And by the word "and so forth" (*ādi*), the sentence "I [invoke] Tvaṣṭṛ and Pūṣan and Bhaga" (Ṛgveda 10.125.2) is included; likewise, the verse:
"But those who worship the Imperishable, the Indefinable, the Unmanifest... (Gītā 12.3).
"Omnipresent, inconceivable, immutable, immovable, and eternal"—this is a statement from the *Bhagavad Gītā* (12.3).
"This was then enveloped in darkness, unperceived, and without defining characteristics. (Taittirīya Upaniṣad 2.7)
It is beyond reasoning, unknowable, and as if entirely asleep.
And the statement cited in that commentary is also included.
By the word "ca" (and), the reason indicated by the term *akṣara*—namely, that the word *akṣara* is well-known in the sense of the Śrī-tattva—is conjoined. The word *tasya* is repeated.
And it undergoes transformation;
not only Viṣṇu's alone, but "his" as well.
The word "also" (*api*) in the phrase "of the imperishable also" (*akṣarasyāpi*) has this meaning.
The term "intermediate" (*madhyamā*) is used for the purpose of excluding Viṣṇu and the insentient (*jaḍa*).
[This refers to] "the attainment of the state of being *bhūman*."
Thus, from the previous section, the word "attainment" (*prāpti*) is understood here through the intellect by way of distinction; and so it is:

those qualities of the Imperishable Viṣṇu, such as invisibility and the rest, which were stated previously in the *Adṛśyatvādhikaraṇa*, are found in the Vājasaneyaka [Bṛhadāraṇyaka Upaniṣad] in the passage: "That indeed is this Imperishable, O Gārgī, unseen yet seeing."

By means of this sentence beginning with "ityādi," one interpretation is that the [qualities] of the "middle syllable"— that is, the venerable *śrītattva*— are "spoken of" (*uktāḥ*), meaning they are being described (*ucyante*).
But another [interpretation] is: "of that"— because those qualities such as invisibility and so forth are possible and appropriate even in that middle syllable, it is "of that."
Furthermore, the mark consisting in being the substratum of the moon and so forth is applicable to that Imperishable (akṣara) from such scriptural passages as "I [drank] the exhilarating Soma";
and because the word "Imperishable" (akṣara) is well-known to refer to that middle Imperishable, [the pronoun] "of him" refers to that.
There is also the attainment of the status of being denoted by the name "Akṣara" for the middle syllable as well.

In that regard, since the first interpretation implies that the Akṣara— possessing qualities such as invisibility as stated in the *Adṛśyatvādhikaraṇa*— is other than Viṣṇu, it is said that this constitutes an "implicatory connection" (*ākṣepikī saṅgati*) with it.
Likewise, the subject designated as "the Imperishable" (akṣara) is indicated to be distinct from insentient matter by considering the subsequent sentence which designates it as a "seer" (draṣṭṛ).
Furthermore, the doubt is suggested as to whether its nature is that of primordial materiality (prakṛti) or Viṣṇu.

It should be understood that in the second interpretation, the prima facie view (*pūrvapakṣa*) has been presented along with its supporting arguments. According to the method of the established conclusion (*siddhānta*), the meaning of the passage beginning with "That, verily" (*tadvai*) is as follows:
"That" refers to the "Imperishable" (*akṣara*), which will be described as having space as its substratum.
That which does not decay is denoted by the word "akṣara" (the Imperishable), namely Brahman;
and this is well known as being characterized by these attributes.
He states that very same thing with the words beginning with "adṛṣṭam" (unseen).
Because it is not seen by others in its entirety, yet it sees for itself, it is called "the unseen seer.
The subsequent statements should also be explained in this manner.
He states a distinction regarding its nature as a seer and so forth with the word "not."
"Therefore" means that there exists nothing other than this Imperishable (akṣara) that is an independent seer, hearer, thinker, or knower.

"In this"—that is, in the Brahman denoted by the word 'Imperishable' which has been described—lies the principle of Śrī, referred to by the term 'space' as the cause of luminosity; it is "woven across and woven lengthwise," meaning it is both woven across (otu) and woven lengthwise (prota) within this.
And thus, the meaning is that everything indeed rests upon it in its entirety.
"O Gārgī" is the address to his wife by Yājñavalkya. "Of this very syllable... [and so forth].
"In the command of Viṣṇu" means "in his decree"; thus, it is a locative of cause (*nimitta-saptamī*).
And so, by his mere decree, [he established] "the sun and the moon."

According to the statement in the *Bṛhadbhāṣya*, "The two hairs are considered to be the Sun and the Moon," and according to the method of the commentary on the *Bhāṣya*, Brahmā and Rudra— and likewise the well-known Sun and Moon— are "held apart" (*vidhṛtau*),
meaning they are specifically sustained.

The proponent of the prima facie view (pūrvapakṣin), however, considers the word "akṣara" to refer to the Śrī-tattva. In that view, the word "ākāśa" refers to something other than primordial nature (prakṛti) that is to be nourished;
[and] "I am the 'āhanasam'."

Through the medium of the creeper identified with myself, I sustain "Soma"— the Moon who presides over the Soma-creeper while being pressed in sacrifices— as well as Tvaṣṭṛ, and "also Pūṣan," that is,
both Pūṣan and Bhaga.
"I bestow" is the meaning of the statement by Ambhraṇī;
Tvaṣṭṛ and the others, however, are specific manifestations of Sūrya.
But according to the Bṛhadbhāṣya, in the *Tattvapradīpa* and *Sattarkadīpāvali*, [the reading is] "soma".
It has been explained that "together with Umā" means "the slayer," the destroyer, Rudra;
and "the imperishable" (akṣaram) means not subject to destruction even by way of the body.
"Inexpressible" means beyond the range of words;
"all-pervading."
It is all-pervading in terms of space;
it is "inconceivable," being ungraspable by the mind due to the abundance of its qualities.
It is "immutable" (kūṭastha) because it remains in the peak of space through its sense of self-identity;
it is "immovable" (acala); it is "constant" (dhruva), never falling from its own state; and it is devoid of origination and destruction.
The meaning of the *Gītā* is: "those who worship the unmanifest, the principle of Śrī," which is "unbecome" (*abhūtam*)— meaning unborn— at the time of dissolution,
and "unknowable" (*aprajñātam*).
It is not cognizable through direct perception because it lacks the characteristics of being an object of cognition; for that very reason, it is "incomprehensible by reasoning" (atarkya);
it is "unknowable" (avijñeya) because it is not cognizable through inference;
and it is "uncognizable through scripture" because one identifies with beginningless ignorance.
The meaning of the Smṛti is that this reality called Lakṣmī, which is denoted by the word *tamas*, was "as if asleep"— meaning inactive— "everywhere," that is, in all places.
Therefore he says:
Sūtra—Oṃ.
The Imperishable [Brahman] is [the cause], because it supports that which extends to the limits of space.
"In this very Imperishable, O Gārgī, the ether is woven like warp and woof" (Bṛhadāraṇyaka Upaniṣad 5.8.11).
Since the entire universe, ending with the ether, is supported by it, the Imperishable is indeed Brahman.
The author introduces the aphorism that establishes this conclusion with the words "ataḥ" (therefore).

Because the meaning of the Sūtra is profound, he cites the scriptural authority (*śruti*)—namely, "In this..."—while about to explain the first part concerning the cause (*hetu*), in order to avoid the charge of unestablished proof (*asiddhi*).
The word "iti" is followed by the word "vākye" as a necessary supplement.
Showing the external referent (*anyapadārtha*), he demonstrates the grammatical analysis (*vigraha*) with the words "ambareti."

The meaning is that "ambaram" refers to space (*ākāśa*), because it is stated to be the sustainer of everything, including the earth and so forth. Although in the sentence "in this," only the support of space is mentioned; [the implication is as stated].

But that [space] is not the support of everything within it. Nevertheless, after stating the all-supporting nature of space—which is the material cause consisting of consciousness—by the passage: "O Gārgī, that which is above the heaven, that which is below the earth, and that which is between heaven and earth... in space alone is that woven, warp and woof" (Bṛhadāraṇyaka Upaniṣad 5.8.7), [the text continues] immediately with: "In this... [Bṛhadāraṇyaka Upaniṣad 5.8.8].

Since this statement declares that the Imperishable (akṣara) has such a primordial nature (prakṛti) as its substratum, it is stated here that the Imperishable is the substratum of everything up to the ether by means of that primordial nature; thus, there is no fault.
And this is indicated in the Sūtra by the use of the word "up to" (anta) in the term "up to the ether" (ambarānta).
He explains the portion of the proposition (pratijñā) in the Sūtra, which consists of the two recurring words "that" (tat) and "itself" (iti), with the words: "Brahman alone."
The grammatical connection (*anvaya*) is that the Imperishable (*akṣara*) is indeed Brahman.

By this, the meaning of the Sūtra is stated: since the scripture declares that the Imperishable is the support of everything up to space by way of its being the source (*prakṛti*)—as indicated by the phrase "in this"—the Imperishable is indeed Brahman.

Regarding the question, "How does the fact of being the support of all constitute a definitive proof of Viṣṇu-hood?", [the author] replies with the word "yaḥ" (He who), stating that this is established by scripture as a characteristic mark (*liṅga*) of Viṣṇu: "He who alone has supported the threefold earth and the sky, and all dwellings" (Ṛgveda 1.154.4).
This scripture has been explained according to the doctrine of birth:
"Being the supporter, he who is supported supports;
the one God has entered into many forms."
"When he becomes weary of bearing the burden,
his burden goes back to its setting.
"Being the bearer," so says the Taittirīya Śruti.
The "Lord" (devaḥ)—the Blessed One known as Prāṇa—being himself sustained in the heart by the world or by the individual soul (jīva), "sustains it" (bibharti); that is, He holds and nourishes it.
To the objection that this implies an equality between the Lord and the world, he says: "being the sustainer" (bhartā san).
Being the fundamental sustainer of the world, He is indeed sustained—not by His own inherent state, this is the meaning.

Now, one might ask: how can the single Blessed Lord be the object of various modes of worldly discourse, such as being the "sustainer," "being sustained," and "sustaining"? To this, he says: "One, yet manifold."
"Though one," he is "established in many ways" by virtue of being the Lord and so forth; that is to say, he is pervaded [by manifold forms].
Or [it means] "having entered therein";
the completion of the sentence is: "When one tires of bearing the burden, having cast off the burden, he goes again to his setting."
