When that Viṣṇu, having cast down that burden of the world, "becomes weary" and does not wish to bear it again, then that burden "sets."
The meaning is that it perishes.
In whom all this trembles, in whom all the gods have taken their seat. (Mahānārāyaṇa Upaniṣad 1.2)
This is according to such scriptural passages. Furthermore, there is another sentence in the Taittirīya [Upaniṣad] beginning with "In which...";
here, the word "which" (yat) refers to "that very same supreme Brahman" (Mahānārāyaṇa Upaniṣad 1.6).
Thus, there is a grammatical connection with the word "tat" (that) situated in the subsequent sentence; the particle "ca" (and) serves to aggregate the modes (*prakāra*).
And so: "In which this [world exists]..."
The entire world ‘saṃ’— completely, ‘vi’— variously, and ‘caidhi’— grew.
This is a Vedic form of the verb *edh* in the *liṅ* mood;
or rather, it means "it prospers" (*edhi vardhate*),
or its meaning is "it exists" (*asti*).
In this view, the form [of *asi*] is a Vedic usage in the second person singular of the present indicative (*laṭ*);
in reality, however, it is the form of the second person singular of the imperative (*loṭ*).
And in which [context], "all" (*viśve*)...
"All the gods sat down" means that they perceived that very [Brahman] as Brahman; this is the meaning.
The phrase "from such scriptural passages" is to be construed with the preceding term "because of the support of everything up to the ether."
The word "brahmaṇi" (in Brahman) is to be supplied as the object understood;
the ablative case is used in the sense of the instrumental.
By the word "ādi" (and so forth), [the following is included]: "By whom the sky, heaven, and earth are covered, by whose splendor and radiance the sun shines" (Mahānārāyaṇa Upaniṣad 1.3).
Passages such as these, as well as "They call him indeed death, they call him immortality; they call him the sustainer, they call him the protector" (Taittirīya Āraṇyaka 3.14), are included.
Thus, the sense is that because he is established by scripture as having the characteristics of Viṣṇu and being the support of all, there is indeed a certainty of his being Viṣṇu.
Whatever exists—past, future, and present—from the earth up to primordial nature (prakṛti), Viṣṇu alone sustains this; no other is capable of such support.
And thus it is stated in the Skanda Purāṇa.
To the objection that why another [deity] might not also possess the status of being the support of all, just like Viṣṇu, he says: "Earth and so forth."
The term *sautrānta* is explained by the phrase *prakṛtyanta*.
"Past" (*abhūta*) means what has occurred; "future" (*bhavya*) means what will occur; and "present" (*bhavat*) means what is occurring.
That which is present—
this entire universe— is supported by Viṣṇu alone; he is solitary, without a second.
Therefore, there is no one other than Viṣṇu who is ‘capable’ (akṣamaḥ) of upholding him; that is, none is competent— so it is because this has been stated in the Skanda Purāṇa.
By supplying [the word "because"], the connection with the remainder of the sentence is as follows: "therefore the indicative mark (liṅga) is not subject to any other possibility.
Sūtra: Oṃ.
And that [is established] through the authoritative teaching.
And that steadfastness is said to arise from governance:
"O Gārgī, by the governance of this Imperishable, indeed, the sun and the moon stand held apart."

By means of such passages as [Bṛhadāraṇyaka Upaniṣad 5.8.9], the author introduces and explains a sūtra which establishes that Viṣṇu alone possesses the nature of the Imperishable (akṣara) through another line of reasoning, beginning with the words: "And that... (sā ca).

And because she is also called "the sustainer of all" (*sarvadhṛti*) and so forth by virtue of her command, the syntactical connection is that for this reason also she is the imperishable Brahman (*brahmākṣara*).
By the word "and so forth" (*ādi*), various other passages within the same context of similar nature are included.
By this—when "she" [is mentioned]...
The all-sustaining power previously mentioned is itself the proof for the imperishable one's being Viṣṇu;
how much more so,
then, that which belongs to "this" [one].

Thus, the meaning of the sūtra is stated as follows: in the scriptural passage, it is declared that "all-support" (sarvadhṛti) arises from the mere fact of the Imperishable's (akṣara's) supreme command alone—a command whose scope is unrestricted and which consists solely of a preeminent knowledge independent of anything else.
Furthermore, that command belongs to Viṣṇu alone.

Now, one might ask: how is the identity of the Imperishable with Viṣṇu determined by means of this command, which is the cause of all-support? To this he says, "And that [belongs to Viṣṇu]," because that command has Viṣṇu as its agent.
The meaning is that it is the cause of all support and the governance;
the word "and" (ca) is used in a cumulative sense to indicate that it is not merely the support of all, but also the governance which is the cause thereof.
‘Of Viṣṇu alone’ means ‘having Viṣṇu as its agent’; that is, it has no other agent—this is the meaning of the particle *eva*. The function of the particle *eva* will be utilized later on.
"The seven half-embryos, the seed of the world, stand by the command of Viṣṇu in the supporting law" (Ṛgveda 1.164.36).
To the question "How is this known?", he cites scripture as the authority for the proposition stated by the words "and that": "The seven... etc.
"Filled with the womb of supernatural power" (ā-ṛddhagarbhāḥ) means "filled with the womb of supernatural power" (ārdhagarbhāḥ).

They are "filled with the womb" (samṛddhagarbhāḥ) called the cosmic egg (brahmāṇḍa). They are called "wombs" (garbhāḥ) because they are filled by being swallowed; that is to say, they serve as its covering.

The word *retaḥ* is used with a change of gender and number; it is in the singular form to convey the sense of the nominative plural. Thus, it refers to the "seed" (*retasaḥ*) of the "world" (*bhuvanasya*).
Or they are the bestowers of pleasure and the essential elements. Alternatively, because they are abundant, full, desirable, and worthy of worship, the seven—
namely Mahat, Ahaṃkāra, and the five great elements— are the gods beginning with Brahmā, who constitute the seed-form of Viṣṇu, the world-protector.

By the "command" (pradiśā)— that is, by the instruction or decree— of Viṣṇu, who is the "seed" (retaḥ) of existence and who bestows delight upon the world, [it was established] "in the law" (vidharmaṇi).
The meaning of the Ṛgveda mantra is that they abide in the support of the manifold universe. However, in the Viśveśvaratīrthīya commentary, "garbhāḥ" refers to Viṣṇu, who is the "Half."
"The seven gods are the seed (the cause) of the world";
it has been stated that these abide by the command of Viṣṇu within the cosmic order. Together with four [others], he has caused the ninety-nine names to revolve, like a turning wheel.
This is because of such scriptural passages as *Ṛgveda* 1.155.6.
As for the phrase "by four," it has been explained according to the theory of birth (*janmanaya*).
Scriptural passages of this kind constitute the meaning of the word "etcetera" (*ādi*).
By supplying the word "is known" (*jñāyate*) to this [phrase] *śruteḥ*, it connects with the preceding sentence *tac ca* as follows:
"The Teacher is one; there is no second Teacher.
Him who dwells in the heart, him I proclaim here."
One might ask: "Could the teaching that is the cause of the sustenance of all not belong to another [deity] as well, just like Viṣṇu? To this, he says: "The One."
And this statement from the *Bhārata*, occurring in the *Sabhāparvan*:
"'The Teacher' (*śāstā*) means the one who issues commands that are the cause of all sustenance;
'the One' (*ekaḥ*) means there is no second."
And the meaning is that he is indeed Viṣṇu;
"Who is the teacher of the Person lying in the womb?"— this is the statement of the learned.
The phrase "he who dwells in the heart" (*yo hṛcchayaḥ*) is another sentence which, upon consideration of the subsequent passage, is consistent with the present context;
"he who" dwells in the heart for the sake of the governance that is the cause of the support of all things.
The meaning is that I speak of Him here in this place as dwelling within the hearts of all—
not only for me and you, O King,
but He is indeed the strength of the strong and of others as well.
And so on, from this [sūtra] onwards. // 11 //
"‘Not only’ (na kevalam),” and so forth, is the speech of Prahlāda addressed to Hiraṇyakaśipu:
“O King, that Blessed Lord is not only my strength, but yours as well.”
It bestows strength and is the cause of fortitude;
however, the meaning is that it is the strength of others and of those who are strong.
Regarding the phrase "and so forth," it is understood that "that command belongs to Viṣṇu alone."
Thus is the positive concomitance (*anvaya*).
By this, the function of the restrictive particle *eva*—namely, that [the state of being the cause] belongs to Viṣṇu alone—is indicated.
Sūtra: Oṃ.
And because of the exclusion of other states.

And because of the exclusion of grossness, subtlety, and other such natures belonging to other things, as stated in passages such as "neither gross nor subtle" (Bṛhadāraṇyaka Upaniṣad 5.8.8), the Sūtra—reading and explaining it while establishing that Viṣṇu alone possesses the nature of the Imperishable (akṣara) through another reason—states: "anyā... (Sūtra 1.3.10).

By the word "etcetera" [in the compound], there is the reference to: "O Gārgī, the Brāhmaṇas declare this indeed to be that Imperishable: neither gross nor subtle, neither short nor long, neither red nor oily, neither shadow nor darkness, neither air nor ether, without contact, without taste, without smell, without eye, without ear, without speech, without mind, without radiance, without measure, without mouth, without dimension, without interior, without exterior;
it eats nothing whatsoever, and no one eats it" (Bṛhadāraṇyaka Upaniṣad 5.8.8).
Thus, the entire sentence is understood;
the expression "of the gross, the subtle, and so forth" is a designation in which the abstract state (bhāva) is the primary focus.
After the word "vyāvṛtteḥ" (from exclusion), the word "because it is so stated" is to be understood as a supplement. The particle "ca" (and) serves to aggregate reasons.
This [statement] also connects with the preceding one: "Brahman alone is the Imperishable."
By this— meaning not only by the two previously stated reasons,

but also because of the exclusion (*vyāvṛtti*) of all other things, entities, natures, and attributes such as grossness, and because the syllable "akṣara" is described in the scriptural passage beginning with "not gross" (*asthūlam*) as being devoid of dependence on anything else— it is stated that the meaning of the Sūtra is that Brahman alone is the Imperishable (*akṣara*).

The meaning of the scripture is as follows: "That" refers to the "Imperishable" (akṣara)—that which is called by the word "imperishable" because it does not decay—which will be described as having space as its substratum; this is Brahman characterized by these attributes, [which] the Brāhmaṇas [know].
The knowers indeed declare this well-known [truth].
To the question "What is its characteristic?", he says: "Not gross" (*asthūlam*).
"Gross" (*sthūlam*) means large.
But as for the other meaning [of the word] when it is self-awakened:

"this" is the imperishable (*akṣara*) which the Brahmins call "that," known as *cit-prakṛti*; they state this as the prima facie view (*pūrvapakṣa*), and they declare it to be Brahman as the final conclusion (*siddhānta*).
He states the very reason that establishes the final conclusion (siddhānta) with the words "not gross" and so forth.

By this, according to the method stated in the *Bṛhadbhāṣya*— namely, "Janārdana [is established] because of his difference from the well-known gross, subtle, and so on"— his distinction from the well-known gross and other categories is expressed.

If the words *sthūla* (gross), *aṇu* (subtle), and so forth are taken as emphasizing the abstract state (*bhāvapradhāna*), then by this it is stated that [the Self] is devoid of grossness and other qualities found in the world.

"Non-red" (*alohita*) means devoid of the general material form characterized by what is designated by the word "red," such as blood and the like. "Non-unctuous" (*asneha*) means devoid of material unctuousness.
"Shadowless"; because of the statement, "Ignorance is declared to be shadow," it is free from ignorance;
and it is also devoid of shadow, like the body of a living being [in the absence of light].
‘Without darkness’ (atamaḥ) means free from obscuration. ‘Without wind’ (avāyu) means free from breath and exhalation in the form of affliction.
Alternatively, according to the method stated by Vyāsatīrtha, it means being devoid of a body composed of those [elements], namely earth, water, fire, and ether.

For this very reason, it is stated in the *Sudhā* and *Ṭīkā* commentaries that there is a total negation [of all attributes] in the passage "without shadow, without darkness, without wind, without space.
"Unattached" (*asaṅgam*) means that although it is omnipresent, it is devoid of any stain caused by that [contact].
By the two terms "without taste" (*arasa*) and "without smell" (*agandha*), the absence of ordinary taste, smell, and so forth is indicated by way of implication.

By the phrase "without eyes," etc., the absence of ordinary sense organs such as the eye, which are distinct from [the Self], is indicated. "Without luster" (*atejaska*) means devoid of ordinary radiance.
‘Aprāṇa’ means devoid of the material organs of knowledge and action other than those already mentioned [the eyes, etc.],
or, according to the method of Vyāsatīrtha, devoid of the vital air (prāṇavāyu).
‘Amukha’ means devoid of a material body.

‘Amātram’ means devoid of measure (*parimiti-śūnyam*). According to the commentary, *mātrā* refers to the sense organs (*indriyāṇi*), because they are that by which things are measured; thus, Vyāsatīrtha’s explanation is that ‘amātram’ means being devoid of the sense organs such as the eyes and so forth.
Alternatively, it may mean being entirely devoid of the five *mātrās* that originate the body.
Since there exists neither an interior nor an exterior, it is "without interior or exterior" (*anantara-abāhya*);
the meaning is that this very [Brahman] is both the interior and the exterior of everything.
That—namely Brahman—is "neither anything at all."

Just as humans and gods are described according to whether they eat auspicious or inauspicious food, or whether they eat or do not eat; so too, Hari’s act of eating is not an eating [in the ordinary sense], for even without consuming food, he suffers no weakness.
In order to rely upon this traditional teaching (*smṛti*), [the text says] "he does not eat" (*nāśnāti*); he does not consume.
"Anything whatsoever" (*kaścana*) means anyone who is capable; "that" (*tat*) refers to Brahman; "he does not eat" (*nāśnāti*).

"He does not withdraw" refers to Viṣṇu alone, according to such passages as: "He who is neither gross nor subtle, neither middle-sized nor middling, neither all-pervasive nor non-pervasive; he who is Hari, beginningless and yet having no beginning, both the non-universal and the universal, possessing qualities and yet devoid of qualities."
Regarding those attributes:

how can the absence of worldly grossness and so forth be determinative of Viṣṇu-hood, given that they have not been ascertained as being His specific attributes? To this, he says: "Not gross" (asthūla).
"Non-gross" means devoid of worldly grossness;
"non-subtle" means devoid of worldly subtlety; "not intermediate."
He is devoid of worldly middling dimensions.
Nor should it be argued that Viṣṇu would lack an essential nature (*asvabhāvatva*) simply because he is devoid of dimensions and so forth;
for even while lacking worldly grossness and the like, there exists a transcendental (*alaukika*) dimension and so on. Thus he says with the words beginning "middling" (*madhyama*).
Nor should it be said that because [the text] does not mention grossness (*sthūlatva*) and so forth, no solution has been stated;
for since it says "the middle is pervasive" (*madhyamo vyāpakaḥ*) and so on, the terms "gross" (*sthūla*) and "subtle" (*aṇu*) are used as mere indicators (*upalakṣaka*).

Nor should it be said that Viṣṇu would incur impermanence by possessing a middling dimension; for we accept a middling dimension that does not entail impermanence. However, in the *Tattvapradīpa*, it says "not middling" (*amadhyama*).

It is devoid of a fixed intermediate magnitude, because of the statement: "The atom is [either] pervasive or likewise intermediate. It is explained as "intermediate" (madhyama) because it is measured in the middle.
In this view, the intended resolution is that there is no impermanence, since it lacks a fixed intermediate magnitude.
That which has no other pervader is "non-pervasive" (*avyāpaka*);
or, it means "a pervader distinct from worldly [conventions]. Alternatively, "non-pervasive" (*avyāpaka*) refers to that which pervades all places and times.

The beginning is the cause; being without beginning, it is "empty of that," or rather, "empty of origination. Because the full (pūrṇa) does not exist [as a separate entity], it is "not-universal" (aviśva);
because of its fullness, it is universal (viśva).
Alternatively: "non-universal" (aviśva) means not entered into worldly things;
"universal" (viśva) means entered into the heart of the world.
"Saguṇaḥ" means possessing qualities such as knowledge and bliss;
"nirguṇaḥ" means devoid of qualities such as *sattva* and so forth—this is the meaning. "Iti-ādeḥ" refers to such a statement.
By the word "etcetera" (ādi), the Kaṭha Śruti passage, "Subtler than the subtle, greater than the great" (Kaṭha Upaniṣad 2.20), is included;
"those" refers to the qualities such as non-stoutness and so forth.
The word "yataḥ" (from which) implies "decidedly so" (niścitāḥ).
This connects with the supplemented sentence: "Therefore, these [reasons] become determinative of the fact that this Imperishable is Viṣṇu.
Now, one might ask: even so, how is it that they belong to Viṣṇu alone?

Since those [qualities] exist even in the middle syllable of the non-ordinary form, this is not a fault; for they exist there only in relation to the Blessed One. Indeed, it is only those dharmas that are independent of anything else which are intended here as the cause.
He is neither gross nor subtle in form; he is both the non-universal and the universal itself.
Possessing forms of contradictory attributes, this Supreme Person is so by virtue of his sovereignty.
And thus it is said in the Brāhma [Purāṇa]. // 12 //
Thus ends the section on the syllable (Akṣarādhikaraṇa), [3].

Now, one might object: how is it appropriate for Viṣṇu to be devoid of worldly dimensions and so forth, since in the world all objects are seen to possess only material (prākṛta) dimensions? To this, he says: "Neither gross" (asthūla).
"That Supreme Person," the Blessed One, "is neither gross nor subtle in form"; that is, his body is devoid of the attributes of grossness and subtlety belonging to the material world.
Thus, he is both "non-universal" and "universal"; he exists both outside the world and within the world.
Likewise, he possesses the nature of contradictory attributes.
He is described as such because he possesses by his very nature those mutually contradictory attributes found in the world, such as grossness and subtlety.
To explain how this is so, the author provides the following justification: "On account of his sovereignty."
The meaning is: "by virtue of the power of inconceivable sovereignty.
By the phrase "precisely because of sovereignty," it is stated that no other supporting reason need be sought here.

Regarding the expression "in the *Brahmāṇḍa* [Purāṇa]," by supplying the word "are appropriate" (*yuktāḥ*), the connection with the preceding sentence is as follows: "those attributes are indeed appropriate for Viṣṇu."
Thus ends the section concerning the syllable (akṣarādhikaraṇa). 3.
// 4. The Six Subjects of Legal Dispute //
By the passage beginning with "In the beginning, my dear, this was Being alone" (Chāndogya Upaniṣad 6.2.1), the creative agency of Being (sat) is declared.
In this section, the phrase "Being alone" consists of multiple constituent passages.
Thus, the introductory section (sthāna) is connected.
Having cited the subject passage (*viṣayavākya*) which provides the connection with the scriptures and so forth, he indicates the subject matter and other elements by the word "Being" (*sat*).
By the phrase "and so forth," [it refers to] the passage from the Chāndogya Upaniṣad;
by the word "etcetera" (ādi), [it includes] "One only, without a second" (Chāndogya 6.2.1) and "That [Self] created fire" (Chāndogya 6.2.3).

The following passages are cited: "O gentle one, these [beings] have Being as their root" (Chāndogya Upaniṣad 6.8.6), and "O gentle one, at that time he becomes merged with Being" (Chāndogya Upaniṣad 6.8.1).
Etcetera.

The word "that" (tat) is drawn forward from the phrase "and that" (tac ca). Thus, by means of the word "thus" (iti) and so forth, the "creatorship" (sraṣṭṛtva) of the existent is expressed as "that" (tat) through the process of origination.
The state of having a cause that is not dependent on anything else;
this is an illustrative indication (upalakṣaṇa), and it is also said to include such qualities as being supreme over all, being the substratum of all, and being accessible through deep sleep.

The construction is: "it is being established. By this, since the causality mentioned in the section on "Origin" (janmādhikaraṇa) is challenged as belonging to Pradhāna rather than Viṣṇu, the "suggestive connection" (ākṣepikī saṅgatiḥ) between that [section] and this one is stated.
Likewise, the subject passage (viṣayavākya) is:
The object designated as "Being" has been stated;
namely, Uddālaka’s statement, "Existence alone.
O "Somya"—O Śvetaketu, who are worthy of the *soma* characterized by devotion and knowledge—"this... [is that].

"In the beginning" of this world—that is, prior to its creation, during the dissolution—Brahman alone, denoted by the word "Sat," existed independently; this is the sense. That Sat was "one only, without a second."
It is devoid of difference or non-difference from its own constituent parts and is the supreme of all.
"Having Being as their root" means those whose root is the existent Brahman alone; they are described thus.
"At that time," [the meaning of the scriptural passage] "he becomes merged with the Existent (sat) during sleep, he is asleep" is established as the sense of the Śruti according to the Siddhānta.

By employing the word "etc. (*ādi*) to include numerous passages that state the characteristics of Brahman, the objection—that there is no undesirable consequence since the Siddhānta also accepts that the Pradhāna is what is being propounded here, and thus the present section (*adhikaraṇa*) would be redundant—is refuted.

In this context, since the characteristics of Brahman mentioned here cannot possibly belong to the Pradhāna, and because it is not accepted that the Pradhāna alone is the subject to be established— Brahman also being the subject to be established— that [Pradhāna] is not Viṣṇu, because of the perception of transformation in the passage: "May I be many, may I procreate" (Chāndogya Upaniṣad 6.2.3).
He presents the prima facie argument (pūrvapakṣa) with reasoning: "And that... and so forth.
The word "ca" (and) serves to draw forward the term "pradhānam" (the primary cause) and also functions as a restriction.
The word "tad" (that), being repeated, is modified accordingly;
and thus it is "tat."
That which is heard in the Chāndogya must be the Pradhāna alone, and not Viṣṇu.
Why? Because of the word "his" (tasya).
The construction is as follows: from the subsequent sentence, "May I be many," there is the perception of a modification known as transformation (*pariṇāma*), which consists in becoming manifold.
"May I be born" (*prajāyeya*) means "may I bring forth," that is, "may I create the world."
For that purpose, "May I be many" means "May I become one who possesses many forms as a controller";
or, according to the meaning of the Śruti, "May I be many" means "May I be born."

For He is well-known as being changeless through such passages as, "The Self is forever changeless, eternally pure, and always Hari"; thus, even though there may be a perception of His being subject to modification, why should He not be Viṣṇu? To this he says: "For He... (sa hi).
For, by such authoritative means as "He is Viṣṇu, ever changeless," he is well-known to be changeless.

Therefore, because that [transformation] is impossible in Viṣṇu according to reality, while it is possible in Pradhāna, and because transformation is perceived here, the construction is as follows: "That which exists" is not Viṣṇu, but rather Pradhāna alone.
In the Śruti, the second word *sat* is connected with the phrase "the constant transformation."
But for the first [type], it is always impure;
thus he says: "it is stainless.
Therefore, he speaks:
Sūtra—Oṃ.
He is that [Brahman], because of the designation of Him as the object of the act of seeing.
"Then He thought" (*tadaikṣata*); because of this designation of the object of His seeing, it is that very Viṣṇu who is spoken of here.
Introducing and explaining the sūtra which establishes the final conclusion, [the author] says: "Therefore... (*ata iti*).
He shows the designation stated in the Sūtra with the words "taditi.

By the mention of the verbal root *īkṣati* (he sees), its meaning—the act of seeing—is indicated. The grammatical coordination (*sāmānādhikaraṇya*) in the phrase "the object of seeing" (*īkṣatikarma*) has as its primary purport the fact that [Brahman] is the agent of that [act].
And likewise, the meaning is that in the scriptural passage "It thought" (*tadaikṣata*), agency is stated with respect to the activity called "thinking.
Alternatively, by the word "action" (*karman*), the act of creation and so forth is meant.
If that were the case, there would be a lack of grammatical coreferentiality (*vaiyadhikaraṇyam*);
the meaning is that [the cause] is designated as preceded by the act of seeing and so forth regarding creation and other activities.
Although it is possible for the word "that" (*tat*) to be supplied from the *Samanvaya* Sūtra, [the text reads]: "There was only one Nārāyaṇa; having become a sage... (Mahānārāyaṇa Upaniṣad 1.1).
The word "sa" (he) was used in order to authorize such designations as well;
having restated that, it is explained as "Viṣṇu.
The grammatical connection is "Viṣṇur eva" (it is Viṣṇu alone).
The word "tu" (but) has the sense of "evam" (thus).
By this, it is indicated that from the *Samanvaya-sūtra*, only the word "tu" is to be carried over [to the subsequent sūtras].
Since the objects to be correlated are not explicitly stated in the sūtra, he says: "herein."
The meaning is: "in such passages as 'Being alone' (sadeva)"; by the word "Being" (sat), the intended meaning of the proposition is that it is the Primal Matter (pradhāna).
By this [statement], it is shown that in this passage beginning with "Being alone," that which is expressed by the word "Being" is indeed Viṣṇu.
It is not the Pradhāna. Why? "Because it is designated as the object of the act of seeing; therefore, 'it thought'.
(Bṛhadāraṇyaka Upaniṣad 1.4.7) Thus, "it thought" (tadaikṣata).

Thus, the meaning of the Sūtra is stated as follows: because the agency of the action called "seeing" (īkṣaṇa) is heard [in scripture], or because the actions of "willing to create" and so forth are heard, and because those [actions] are impossible in the case of insentient primordial matter (jaḍaprakṛti).
In the Sūtra, the word "sa" (he/that) is to be understood as repeating the word "sat" (Being), with the remainder being supplied;
according to the view that one of these is for the purpose of citing the original term (pratīka), [the Sūtra reads]: "Because of the designation of the object of seeing, 'he' (saḥ)."
It should be understood that the one taught in the context beginning with "He desired" (Taittirīya Upaniṣad 2.6) is Viṣṇu alone,
and not the Pradhāna.
"There is no other seer than this" (Bṛhadāraṇyaka Upaniṣad 5.7.23);
"There is nothing else but this that sees" (Bṛhadāraṇyaka Upaniṣad 5.8.11)— by such passages, indeed, that very [Self] is characterized by those attributes.

Now, one might ask: "Why should the agency of seeing not belong to the Pradhāna as it does to Viṣṇu? To this, with the intention of showing that even for a sentient being, primary seeing—which is intended here as the cause—is not possible, let alone for an insentient entity, he states the proof for that point: "No. (Neti).
Therefore, apart from Brahman, there is no other independent seer or knower; such is the meaning of the two statements found in the two sections of the Vājasaneyi [Brāhmaṇa].
By the word "etcetera" (ādi), similar statements of this kind are included.
‘Of him’ means of Viṣṇu alone.
The word ‘hi’ (for/indeed) indicates well-known fact.
The ellipsis is to be supplied as: “the mark characterized by being the independent agent of seeing has been stated.”
Therefore, the connection with the supplemented sentence is that one should not consider this mark (*liṅga*) to belong to anything else.
Furthermore, plurality is stated without any modification [of the singular form]: "Being unborn, he is born in many ways" (Taittirīya Āraṇyaka 3.13.1).
// Thus ends the section on the six bases // 4 //

Now, it might be argued that since Viṣṇu is established as being changeless, it is impossible for him to be connected with the modification called "becoming manifold"; therefore, the term "Iksati" (He sees) must be explained here in a figurative sense due to the indicative mark of his being devoid of change. Furthermore, since the Pradhāna is established as the material cause of knowledge based on the Smṛti statement, "From Sattva, knowledge is born," it is impossible for Viṣṇu to be its agent; thus, his [agency] therein would be secondary. To this, he says: "And manifoldness... [and so forth].
The meaning is as follows:

"without modification" (*avikāreṇa*) means precisely by way of a multiplicity of essential natures (*svarūpa*), even in the absence of any actual modification; this is the syntactical connection with what was stated in the passage beginning with those words.
And thus, since plurality has scope [in other contexts], the sense is that one should not, on the strength of that, assume that the term "seeing" (īkṣati) is used in a secondary sense.
Alternatively, "plurality" refers to [the text]:
"May I become many."
Thus, the statement regarding the state of multiplicity has been "spoken," that is,
explained.
And likewise, by such authoritative scriptural passages as "May I become many," [the meaning is established].

The construction of the phrase "iti bahubhāvavacanam 'avikāreṇa'" is as follows: it is stated that [the statement regarding becoming manifold] is appropriate precisely through the multiplicity of the nature of the controller, without any modification (vikāra), and with that very [multiplicity] as the primary subject to be established.
And thus, in the Siddhānta, [it says]: "May I become many."
Thus, it is stated that the meaning of this [passage] is the volition (*saṅkalpa*) regarding the manifoldness of the various forms that act as the controllers.
Nor should it be argued that the creation of the objects controlled is illogical immediately after the volition regarding the manifoldness of the forms that control;
for just as a teacher or a king, being dependent upon disciples or servants, brings about disciples and so forth immediately after the volition [to do so].

Since the status of being a controller (niyāmakatā) is dependent upon that which is controlled (niyamyasāpekṣatva), it is logical that after the volition for the multiplicity of controllers, there follows the creation of the objects controlled in dependence upon them; thus, the meaning of the scriptural passages "unborn" (ajāyamānaḥ) and "unchanging" (avikurvāṇaḥ) has been explained in the *Dyubhvādyadhikaraṇa*. // 4 //
// Thus ends the section on the six bases // 4 //
5. The Section on the Youthful One (Daharādhikaraṇa)
It has been stated that Viṣṇu is the substratum of the moon, the sun, and so forth. And that [is taught] in the passage:
"Now, in this city of Brahman, there is a small lotus-palace; within it is a small space... what..."
"That is found here... (Chāndogya Upaniṣad 8.1.2);
"Both heaven and earth are contained within this; both fire and wind, both sun and moon, lightning and the stars. (Chāndogya Upaniṣad 8.1.3).
By such passages as these, [the nature of] space is understood.

In this section, the reconciliation (*samanvaya*) of the mark (*liṅga*) of being located in the heart-lotus—whether directly or indirectly—is established with respect to Brahman, on account of its being the substratum of all and its being the object to be sought.

Having cited the scriptural passage that constitutes the subject matter (*viṣayavākya*) and indicating the connection with the scriptures (*śruti*) and so forth, as well as the subject matter itself, he states the prima facie view (*pūrvapakṣa*) along with its reasoning, beginning with the words "The moon... (*candra*).
The phrase "of this very syllable" (*etasya vā akṣarasya*) from Bṛhadāraṇyaka Upaniṣad 5.8.9 and so forth is understood to follow here.
By the word "and so forth" (*ādi*), heaven and earth and other such things are included.
To the question "What follows from that?", he says: "And that..."
The word "tat" (that) is repeated; the particle "ca" (and) serves both to conjoin and to emphasize.
And thus, [the phrase] is "therein."

The construction is as follows: that very status of being the support of the moon and the sun, which was stated in the *Chāndogya* Śruti by the sentence cited in the Akṣarādhikaraṇa, as well as the state of residing within the heart-lotus—which is in grammatical apposition with that [status]—is understood through the sentence beginning with "Now" (*atha*).

Although this restatement might seem inappropriate, because in the *Bṛhadāraṇyakabhāṣya* the words "sun" and "moon" found in the Bṛhadāraṇyaka Śruti cited in the Akṣarādhikaraṇa were explained as referring to Brahmā and Rudra respectively.
Nevertheless, this statement is made because it is accepted that those two [terms] refer to the well-known moon and sun.
Alternatively, even in this Bhāṣya, the words "moon" and "sun" refer to Rudra and Brahmā;
for this very reason, in the *Tattvapradīpa* on the section concerning the Imperishable (*akṣara*), [it quotes]: "I [suck] the Soma... (*Ṛgveda* 10.125.2).
In this statement, the word *soma* is explained as referring to Rudra;
thus, there is no contradiction whatsoever.

By this, since the state of being the substratum of the moon, sun, and so forth—spoken of in the method of the syllables (*akṣaranaya*)—is implicitly suggested to reside in the space situated within the heart-lotus, an "implicative connection" (*ākṣepikī saṅgati*) is thereby stated for this [text].

Thus, the object has been shown as being characterized by the common locus of being the support of all and being that which is to be sought, consisting in its presence within the heart-lotus either directly or through mediation.
And it cannot be argued that, according to the commentary stating "the moon and the sun," this support of the moon, sun, and so forth might be the small ether (daharākāśa).
Nor should it be said that there is a contradiction with the *Tattvapradīpa* regarding whether [the Lord] resides therein or not;

for while that work was composed to demonstrate that the present section’s prima facie argument (*pūrvapakṣa*) proceeds by way of challenging the *Akṣarādhikaraṇa*, it did not set out to demonstrate the specific subject matter (*viṣaya*) of this particular section.

By the term "of the ether" (*ākāśasya*), the prima facie view (*pūrvaḥ pakṣaḥ*) is presented that it is the well-known elemental ether itself which, as the support of all, resides directly within the heart-lotus.

Thus, the reasoning for the prima facie view is also demonstrated by the fact that, following a series of questions and answers, it is stated here that the ether itself resides in the heart-lotus as the support of all.

In this regard, although it is said: "Now, what is here in this city of Brahman is a small lotus-palace; within it is a small ether. That which is inside that [ether] is what one must seek, that indeed is what one must desire to understand."
And if they should say to him: "What is there in this that is to be sought after, or what is it that one should desire to understand?", he should reply:
"As vast as this external space is, so vast is this space within the heart.
Both heaven and earth are contained within it."
The entire passage beginning with "Both fire and wind, both the sun and the moon, lightning and the stars" should be cited.
However, it is not [to be taken] as a separate [topic].
Nevertheless, it should be understood that this was cited precisely for the purpose of including other scriptural passages of the same class.
In the scripture, the word "atha" (then/now) serves to introduce another subject matter.

"Brahmapura" (the city of Brahman): this should be explained in two ways—as "the city of Brahman," meaning the place of residence for Brahman, and as "Brahman itself is the city" because of its fullness.
"Within the heart."

Thus, "saptamyanta" (ending in the locative case) refers to [the word] *brahmapure*; "ākāśaḥ" (ether) is nominative (*prathamānta*). And so, in this city of Brahman—which is the body—there is a city which is Brahman; [it is] "in this."
In that Brahman, there is a "small" (*daharam*)— meaning minute or tiny— "lotus" (*puṇḍarīkam*),
which is a "dwelling" (*veśma*).
He has the form of a house; within this [house], there is the small elemental ether (*bhūtākāśa*).
What follows from this? "In that..."
"That which exists within space is to be sought"—
that is, it is to be known or searched for.
But surely, searching for it is not appropriate in the same way as one would search for a jar or similar object.
Because it is not directly perceived, he explains that very point with the words: "That indeed... (tadvāva).
The word *vāva* is used for emphasis;
and thus, that very thing is "to be desired to be known," meaning it is to be investigated.
When the Guru has spoken thus, if the disciples should say "to him" (tam) to the Guru— that is, if they should ask— [then he should reply].
"What is it?"— that which was stated as "to be sought" and "to be understood" here in the elemental ether (bhūtākāśa); that is,
what is the nature of the thing contained therein?
Regarding the phrase "of what majesty":
it should not be argued that the question is improper because the ether's identity as Brahman is already certain from the statement that it is the "abode of Brahman" in the "city of Brahman.
For even in the city of one person, the abode of another may exist, and even in the abode of one, another may reside; therefore, that statement alone is not decisive.
When the disciples have asked thus, the Guru should say:

"What [is it]? [He should reply: "In the *antarhṛd*"; for by the etymological derivation that it is that which is led (*nīyate*) within the heart (*hṛdaḥ antaḥ*), it is [located] "in the inner heart" (*antarhṛdaye*).

In that space within the heart-lotus which is understood by the word "that" (tat), there exists the Supreme Self called "Space" (ākāśa), which is the substratum of heaven, earth, and so forth. Now, one might ask: how can heaven, earth, and the rest abide in that which is atomic? To this, he states its all-pervasiveness with the words "as large as... (yāvān).
"This" refers to the "space" situated outside; that Lord known by that name, in terms of both qualities and magnitude, is exactly as much as this internal [space] is.

And thus, even though form resides in an atom, because of the presence of greatness through His divine power (*aiśa-śakti*), it is entirely logical for that all-pervading [space] to have multiple substrates—this is the intended meaning.

Since there must be a reason for this alone being the object of inquiry to the exclusion of everything else, he states its greatness—known as being the substrate of all—in the verse beginning with "Both," and so forth.
In this interval, both goddesses, Heaven and Earth— the liberated and the unliberated— remain established together;
likewise, these two gods, Agni and Vāyu, are supported by both of them.
Thus, according to the *Chāndogyopaniṣadbhāṣya*, the meaning of the Śruti is that both the released and the unreleased— the sun and the moon, as well as lightning and the stars—
are supported therein. In the *Nyāyavivaraṇa* and its commentary, the *Tadvivaraṇa-ṭīkā*,
regarding the passage "that which is within it," it is stated that Brahman residing in the space within the heart-lotus is what must be sought.
Nor is there a failure to establish that Brahman resides within the lotus;
for by the very description of the body as a lotus and [the heart] as a house in relation to Brahman, it is established that Brahman is the object to be sought.
Thus, even when it is said that Brahman is in the lotus, with the thought as to what kind of nature that Brahman possesses, [the text asks again]: "What is found there?"
When this was asked, the Guru spoke the words beginning with "as great as" (yāvān) in order to make known its specific nature.
By this, he means that within the heart, that Brahman which was stated to be sought after exists as the entire space, as vast as this well-known space [outside].

And since everything beginning with the earth is supported within that space, and it possesses qualities such as being free from sin (*apahatapāpmatva*), it is explained by way of another method that the mode [of Brahman] consisting of freedom from sin and so forth is stated because it is the support of all things, beginning with space.
But the opponent [argues]: "In the space within the heart..."

Thus, he explains that by taking the word "ākāśa" as ending in the locative case (*ākāśe*), the meaning is that the all-pervading space situated within the small space (the *daharākāśa*) is what must be sought; or, by taking "ākāśa" as ending in the nominative case (*ākāśaḥ*), the previously mentioned elemental space of the small space is referred back, and by means of the phrase "as large as," it is qualified as being equal to the external space,
after which heaven, earth, and so forth are described therein as objects of inquiry.
And that space is not Viṣṇu, for it is said:
"In its center is a subtle cavity; in that [cavity] everything is established" (Mahānārāyaṇa Upaniṣad 11).

Thus, because of the scripture [it is so]. Now, one might object: let it be that space (ākāśa) resides within the heart-lotus by virtue of being the support of all; yet, according to the principle "It is Viṣṇu, because of his characteristic marks" (Brahma Sūtra 1.1.22), that space is Viṣṇu, and thus it is established that Viṣṇu alone resides in the heart-lotus. To this, he says: "And he... (sa ca).
The word "ca" has the sense of "and," or it serves to aggregate the propositions;
and thus, that which is declared in the Śruti as being all-pervasive and residing within the heart-lotus— "that Ākāśa is not Viṣṇu."
The meaning is that it is indeed the *bhūta* (the elemental), but not Viṣṇu.
To the question "Why is it not Viṣṇu?", he says: "of its end" (*tasyānta*).
Here, the word *ca* (and), which is connected [from the previous phrase] as "and that," is mentally associated with the term *viviktasuṣira* (the distinct cavity), and it also serves for emphasis.
And this is indicative of the statement being equal to what is heard in scripture;
likewise, in the sentence "at its end," there is the mention of the word "cavity" (*suṣira*).

The meaning is: because of the hearing of the sound of a hollow space (*suṣira*), since it is the well-known space consisting of apertures that is heard; and because of its being described as residing within the heart-lotus by virtue of being the support of all; and because of its designation as such. "Of that" refers to the heart-lotus bud which was the subject of the preceding statement: "The heart is like the interior of a lotus bud and is downward-facing. "At the end" [refers to] that [bud].
In the middle, within that, there is a subtle "hollow," which is a cavity;
in that [cavity], "everything" [is contained].
"The world is established [in Him]"—this is the meaning of the Taittirīya Śruti.
Therefore, he says: Sūtra—Oṃ.
The small one [is Brahman] because of subsequent [scriptural] passages.

From the subsequent qualities mentioned in such passages as, "That Self which is free from evil, ageless, deathless, sorrowless, free from hunger and thirst, whose desires are true and whose resolves are true— that is what must be sought, that is what must be understood" (Chāndogya Upaniṣad 8.7.3), it follows that Viṣṇu alone is within the small space (dahara).
Introducing the aphorism that establishes the final conclusion, he explains it with the words "Therefore" (ataḥ).

The phrase "from such [words] as" means from those words of the form "and so forth," which are "subsequent," that is, occurring immediately after the subject-sentence (viṣayavākya), and which have been "stated"; this is the ellipsis to be supplied.
The established meaning is that this is [stated] from such subsequent statements as these;
or alternatively, "from the qualities" (guṇebhyaḥ) means "from words expressing qualities" (guṇavacanebhyaḥ).

The citation of the Śruti is for the purpose of avoiding the fallacy of the unestablished reason (*hetvasiddhi*). By the word "etcetera" (*ādi*), passages such as "He is free from sorrow, free from hunger, free from thirst, whose desires are true, whose resolves are true; He is to be sought, He is to be known" are included.
By the phrase "from the qualities" (guṇebhyaḥ), it is stated that the subsequent word indicates the various qualities denoted by the multiple terms heard later on.
By the phrase "in the small" (dahare)— meaning in the small space located within the heart-lotus— it is shown that in the Sūtra, the word "dahare" is in the locative case.
It is not stated [here] as being in the nominative case, as it is in the view of others. The ellipsis is that He is "established" as that which is to be sought after.
The meaning of the word *tat* (that), which follows from the *Samanvaya-sūtra* and functions as the predicate, is "of Viṣṇu alone."

By this— namely, the word "who" (yaḥ) [in the phrase] "that indeed" (tattu)— the meaning of the Sūtra is stated as follows: since the qualities heard in the subsequent passage following the Dahara-vidyā section are described as being "to be known" (vijijñāsyatayā) within that "small space" (dahare), it is Viṣṇu alone who is meant, and not the elemental ether (bhūtākāśa) or others.

That Supreme Self who resides in the space within the heart-lotus, and who was previously described as being incapable of being slain by the destruction of the body in the passage, "He is not slain by the slaying of this [body]" (Chāndogya Upaniṣad 8.1.5), is "free from evil" (apahatapāpman); that is to say, He is eternally and by His very nature free from evil, meaning He possesses the absolute absence of sin.
For this very reason, it is said that old age and other such effects do not belong to him— by the words "free from old age" (*vijara*) and so forth.
"Free from hunger" (*avijighatsaḥ*) means devoid of the desire to eat.

Regarding the term "apipāsaḥ," it means "devoid of the desire to drink. According to the statement in the *Jñānapāda-ṭīkā*, "the absence of affliction by hunger and so forth is expressed," this indicates the absence of the desire for food and drink.
Because it is sublated by valid means of knowledge (*pramāṇa*).
However, there is an absence of suffering therein; the reason for this is: "one whose desires are true" (*satyakāma*).
Whatever is desired by Him comes about by His own will; thus He is "one whose desires are true. The reason for this is: "one whose resolve is true," meaning one whose resolve is unimpeded.
The meaning of the scripture is that he who is of such a nature is the one to be sought:
"He who transcends hunger and thirst, sorrow, delusion, old age, and death" (Bṛhadāraṇyaka Upaniṣad 5.5);
"He has risen above all evils" (Chāndogya Upaniṣad 1.6.7).
By such statements as these, those qualities indeed belong to Viṣṇu alone.

To the objection— "How can freedom from sin (*apahatapāpmatva*) and so forth be determinative of Viṣṇu-ness, since they are not established as residing in him?"— the author replies with the words "He who" (*yaḥ*).
This is a citation from the Bṛhadāraṇyaka Upaniṣad:
"aśanāyā" means the desire for food;
"pipāsā" means the desire for drink.
"He transcends them"; that is, he exists having gone beyond. And [he transcends] "sorrow," which is suffering, and "delusion."
The meaning is that he undergoes fainting, old age, and even death;
[this refers to] the pronoun *yaḥ* occurring here [in the verse], which [is connected to] "having known that Self" (*tam ātmānaṃ viditvā*).
Thus, there is a syntactical connection with the word "tat" (that) situated in that [Chāndogya] Śruti.
"'Sa eṣaḥ' (He is this)" is the Chāndogya Śruti. "'Sa eṣaḥ' (He is this)" refers to the Supreme Self as being "from evils" (pāpmabhyaḥ).
"Risen above evils" means that he is eternally and by his very nature free from evil.
By the phrase "and so forth," the word "etc. includes other scriptural passages that indicate qualities such as having true desires and the like.
The word "hi" (for/indeed) has the sense of "yataḥ" (because/since).
The ellipsis to be supplied is: "those [qualities], such as being free from sin (*apahatapāpmatva*) and so forth, mentioned in the subsequent sentence, are established.
Therefore, this connects with the remainder of the sentence: "Consequently, there is no certainty that these are marks of Viṣṇu."

The use of the word "etc. (*ādi*) and the plural number is intended to indicate that, even if the absence of evil and so forth might somehow be possible in others, the state of having true desires and the like is in no way compatible [with them]. As it is said in the *Padma Purāṇa*: "Hari alone is eternally transcendent of hunger and other such states by his very nature; indeed, others cross over hunger and the rest only through his grace."
Nevertheless, these qualities do not belong to Viṣṇu alone, because they are also possible in the case of Ramā and others; therefore, he says: "eternal," etc.
"By Himself" (*svataḥ*): Hari alone is that by whom hunger and other such states have been eternally transcended without dependence on anything else; there is no other.

As for others than Hari, such as Ramā, Brahmā, and the rest, [they are subject to] "hunger and so forth"—that is, defects such as the desire for food and drink, sorrow, and the like—[only] by His grace (*tatprasādāt*).
The meaning is that they "cross over" or transcend [suffering] solely through the grace of that Hari, and not by their own power;
the word *hi* indicates well-known fact.
"In the *Pādme*"; the word "it is said" (*uktam*) is to be understood as the ellipsis.
Therefore, the sense is that because independent qualities do not exist elsewhere, it is stated that [these qualities belong] to Viṣṇu alone.
And between that which is dependent and that which is independent, the independent must be accepted.

Now, one might object: "Even though qualities such as being free from sin (*apahatapāpmatva*) are absent in Ramā and others, since they exist there in some sense or another, how can Viṣṇu be definitively established as the Supreme by means of those qualities residing in others? To this he says:
*sāpekṣa*—meaning dependent on others; *nirapekṣa*—meaning not dependent on others. The meaning is: "between these two."
The word "eva" (only) is used for emphasis;
it is connected with the phrase "entirely independent.
The term "freedom from evil and so forth" is understood as the subject (*viśeṣya*) because it is the topic under discussion.
"It must be accepted"; the word "as a gender-indicative" (liṅgatvena) is to be supplied.
Thus, the sense is that since the intended gender-indicative does not exist elsewhere, the determination of Viṣṇuhood indeed occurs by means of it.

"There is nothing superior to Viṣṇu, the immutable, who possesses true desires; for others to have 'true desire' would merely mean the desire for desired objects. Thus it is stated in the Skanda Purāṇa. 14.

Furthermore, although qualities such as being free from sin (*apahatapāpmatva*), which are characterized by dependence or independence and are negative in nature, may somehow exist elsewhere— in ether (*ākāśa*) and so forth—

either directly or through a presiding deity (*abhimānin*), qualities such as having true desires (*satyakāmatva*) do not exist anywhere else in any way whatsoever; therefore, he states "having true desires" (*satyakāma*) to justify the determination that [the subject] is Viṣṇu.
‘Avyayam’: Viṣṇu, whose desires are undiminished, whose desires are unfailing, and whose desires are true; ‘ṛte’: without; ‘aparaḥ’: another;
there is no one other than Viṣṇu who possesses true desires and true resolve.
This is a *vakrokti* (indirect expression) intended to demonstrate that the state of being [the Supreme] exists in Viṣṇu, while its absence exists in others;

for although the quality of having true desires (*satyakāmatva*) is perceived in some scriptural passages regarding Viṣṇu and others such as Lakṣmī, it is merely the state of possessing a desire directed toward the object of Viṣṇu’s desire, and not primary. This is the meaning.
And just as "freedom from sin" (apahatapāpmatva) is twofold— being inherent and being dependent on another—
it is not so with "having true desires" (satyakāmatva), which is of only one kind; and that [true desire] exists primarily in Viṣṇu alone.
The sense is that elsewhere, however, [the term] is technical.
The phrase "it is stated in the Skanda" is to be supplied as the ellipsis.
Therefore, the sense is that it is logical to state that those qualities belong to Viṣṇu alone, with the intention of expressing his possession of true desires and so forth.
Sūtra—Oṃ.
For it is thus seen from both movement and words, as well as from the inferential mark.
"Day after day they go to this world of Brahman, yet they do not find it" (Chāndogya Upaniṣad 8.3.2).
Thus, the movement of one who is asleep and the word "Brahman" are mentioned.

Having introduced the sūtra which establishes Viṣṇu’s residence in the heart-lotus by means of another argument, [the author] explains it, preceded by the citation of scripture, in order to remove the charge of lack of proof: "The movement... etc.
"These creatures," while asleep, "day after day"— that is, every single day— "approaching this"— meaning, reaching this— [attain it].

The meaning of the Vedic text is: they "do not find" (na vindanti)—that is, they do not know—the Brahmaloka, which is the heart-lotus serving as the abode of Brahmā and Viṣṇu, or through that [lotus], the direct support residing therein called Brahman, which is designated by the word "world" (loka);
for it is stated in scripture, "This very Self is in the heart."
Regarding the word "iti": in the statement of the Chandogas, "of the one who is not asleep" refers to the conscious self, and "its movement" refers to that [movement].
"Day by day, the going toward—the reaching of—the world of Brahman residing within the heart is said";
that is to say, it is designated. "The word Brahman" [is used here].
In this case as well, the word "that" (tat) is mentally separated and connected by way of transposition;
and thus, when that [world] located in the heart— the world of Brahman— is being reached, the term "non-Brahman" (abrahma-śabda) is used.
The meaning is "it is heard";
the word "and" (ca) is also connected with "it is said," and it serves as a conjunction for inclusion.
The word "yataḥ" (from which) is to be supplied as the remainder.
Therefore, even from this [scriptural passage], Viṣṇu alone is within the small [space]; thus is the connection with the probandum, which is the primary subject. [As it is said:
"Then, my dear, he becomes united with Being" (Chāndogya Upaniṣad 6.8.1).
Because of this scriptural statement, one indeed goes to Him while asleep.
To the question, "How does being reached during sleep establish His identity as Viṣṇu?", he says: "satā" (with the Existent).
"O gentle one, O Śvetaketu worthy of devotion and knowledge, at that time,
during the state of deep sleep,
you were united with the non-existent Brahman."
The meaning is that he becomes united.
This is the statement of Uddālaka.
"From the Śruti" is in the ablative case (pañcamī).
‘Taṃ’ means Viṣṇu.
The word ‘hi’ indicates well-known fact.
‘Gacchati’ means he attains.
The phrase "it is thus known" is to be understood as the ellipsis [of the sentence].

And so, since being attainable by one who has fallen asleep is well-known in scripture as a characteristic mark (*liṅga*) of Viṣṇu, the meaning is that the certainty of it being Viṣṇu arises from that.
[As stated in Chāndogya Upaniṣad 8.5.3: "And indeed, Ara and Ṇya, the two oceans, are in the world of Brahman."
Thus the indicative mark (*liṅga*) has been seen;
he explains the remainder of the sūtra, "And the indicative mark has likewise been seen," as being intended to provide another reason, with the words "and the spokes" (*araśca*).
The word "ca" (and) serves to aggregate the reasons;
for example, the state of being approachable by one who is asleep is seen in the Vedic revelation [Śruti] regarding the phrase "day after day" with respect to that which resides in the heart-lotus.

Likewise, the characteristic (liṅga) consisting in the state of being like the world which rests upon the two oceans of nectar named Araṇya is also seen and heard in the heart-lotus in the Śruti text, "Ara and...
The word "tathā" (likewise) is used for the purpose of comparison.
By this, the charge of being unestablished (*asiddhi*) has been refuted.

Nor should it be argued that the charge of non-establishment persists because the one residing in the heart-lotus is not mentioned in proximity to the "going" and the "word," as is the case with [the mention of] the destination and the word;
for the heart-lotus is designated as "this world of Brahman" (*etaṃ brahmalokam*) by reason of its being the abode of the Brahman residing in the heart-lotus.

Thus, since the word "Brahmaloka," when employed [in scripture], is used even for a world that is merely a locus (*āśraya*), it follows by way of that usage that the mark (*liṅga*)—consisting in the possession of such a world—is established as residing in the Brahman situated within the heart-lotus; therefore, after the word "seen" (*dṛṣṭam*), the word "because" (*yataḥ*) is to be supplied as a supplement.
This connects with the thesis-statement (*pratijñāvākya*) "Therefore, for this reason also, Viṣṇu alone is in the small [space]."
In the Śruti, the two particles *ha* and *vā* indicate well-known tradition (*prasiddhi*),
while the word *ca* denotes the mutual conjunction of the two oceans.

Thus, the meaning of the scripture is that in the world of Viṣṇu, within the White Island (*Śvetadvīpa*), there exist two oceans known as the Forest (*Araṇya*), which are oceans of nectar (*sudhā*) comparable to the ocean, or rather, two lakes of nectar resembling the ocean.
"Ara and Vaiṇya are the two oceans of nectar that bestow all desired objects right there"—by such statements, he is indeed described as having those very characteristics. (15)
Now, one might ask: even though there is scriptural mention of the signs of being situated in the heart-lotus and having the forest as its abode, how is it known that this is Viṣṇu?

To this, with the intention of showing that the state of having the forest as an abode is established by Smṛti as a unique sign of Viṣṇu’s world, he presents the Smṛti intended by the word "hi" (for) in the Sūtra: "araśca... (and the spokes).
The word *vai* signifies well-known renown;
the two words *ca* denote mutual conjunction.
"In that very place" means precisely in the world of Viṣṇu situated in the midst of the Ocean of Milk; "bestowing all desired objects" [refers to the two].
The meaning is that both [the forest-dwelling and the worldliness] are desired characteristics.
The particle *eva* (only) excludes their existence elsewhere.
By this, the non-deviation of the mark consisting of the forest-habitat and the state of being worldly from Viṣṇu is established.
For this very reason, the particle *eva* (only) is used in the Bhāṣya in the phrase "of that alone" (*tasyaiva*).
By the statement regarding the wheel of meditation on Puruṣottama beginning with "by [the mantra] beginning with," it is shown that "of that alone"— that is,
of Viṣṇu alone— "that" [is the result].
The state of having worlds that take refuge in the two oceans of nectar is "stated" as a "characteristic"; that is to say, it is presented as a logical mark (*liṅga*).
The word "hi" has the sense of "because.
Therefore, the completion of the sentence is: "Hence, by the force of this indicative mark (liṅga), it is logical to determine that [the one within] is Viṣṇu.
Alternatively, since the heart-lotus is stated to be the world of Viṣṇu in the phrase "the world of Brahman," it is thereby stated that Viṣṇu resides within it.
To the question of how the term "brahmaloka" can denote the world of Viṣṇu, he says: "And the spoke.
Because the term "brahmaloka" is used in the sense of the world of Viṣṇu in the passage "the spoke," it is employed here in the heart-lotus as "this brahmaloka."
Thus, even the word "pada" refers exclusively to the world of Viṣṇu.
Nor should it be asked why, in the Śruti passage beginning with "araśca," the term "brahmaloka-pada" also refers exclusively to the world of Viṣṇu.
The meaning is that the mark (*liṅga*) of residing in the forest is heard there [in the scripture].
Now, as to why residing in the forest is a mark of the world of the Blessed One (*bhagavalloka*), he says: "And the spokes... and so forth.

In this view, the word *liṅga* in the Sūtra is mentioned separately because it lacks the status of being a probans (*hetu*) for the accomplishment of the nature of Brahman residing in the heart-lotus; thus, it is stated as a distinct category in the Sūtra.

Even in the previous interpretation, since this *liṅga*, like the words *gati* and *śabda*, requires further justification to establish its residence in Viṣṇu, it lacks clarity; therefore, instead of saying "by the *gati*, *śabda*, and *liṅgas*," the author says "and the *liṅga*"—implying that it is not only on account of the subsequent qualities, but also on account of this *liṅga*.

However, by virtue of the two terms "going" and "sound" in the phrase "day after day," and by the terms "Brahman" and "attained during sleep" heard as residing within the lotus of the heart, it is known that Viṣṇu alone is the one within the small space (dahara).
It is not known from these alone; [there are other reasons as well].
But because, as in the scriptural passage "And without spokes," there is [the word] "thus" (tathā), just as in the case of the words "motion" and "sound," and [the word] "for" (hi).

The characteristic (*liṅga*) consisting of being a refuge for forest-dwellers, which is established by tradition (*smṛti*) as a mark of Viṣṇu, is "seen" because the term *brahmaloka*, used here for the world of Viṣṇu residing in the lotus of the heart, is applied to that very lotus of the heart; therefore, Viṣṇu alone is within the small space (*dahara*). Alternatively, why should the term *brahmaloka* used here refer to the world of Viṣṇu?
Because in the sentence "araśca," the term "brahmaloka" is used for the world of Viṣṇu,
and here too, in the phrase "this brahmaloka," it is that very same [world] which is being referred to.
Nor does that [passage] refer to the world of Viṣṇu; why? Because the indicative mark (liṅga) of "resorting to the forest" is seen there;
thus the meaning of the Sūtra—"because it is heard"—is explained.
Sūtra—Oṃ.
And because its greatness, consisting of steadfastness, is perceived in this [Self].

Having introduced the sūtra which establishes Viṣṇu’s residence in the heart-lotus by means of another reason—namely, "support" (dhṛti)—as in the passage, "This is the bridge, the support" (Chāndogya Upaniṣad 8.4.1), he explains it with the words: "Because of support. (dhṛteḥ).

Regarding the phrase "iti dhṛteḥ," by following the word "asya" from the preceding phrase "asminnasya," the meaning of this sentence is: because of the scriptural statement that He who resides in the heart-lotus is the support of all, as expressed by the term *dhṛti*.
This connects with the thesis-statement: "In this [small space], Viṣṇu alone [resides]."
In the Śruti, the connection is that "vidhṛti" (the support) is the "setu" (the bridge). Therein, the term "vidhṛti" is the reason for its being a bridge.
And thus, that very Self which was described as residing within the heart-lotus is this [Self] "of these."
"Vidhṛtiḥ" means for the non-confusion, the non-intermixture, or the non-disruption of the worlds beginning with Bhūḥ;
or, according to the method stated by Vyāsatīrtha, it means for the absence of intermixture among the castes (varṇa) and stages of life (āśrama).
Because it is capable of supporting and nourishing, it is therefore called a "bridge" (*setu*);
the meaning is that it is a support. Furthermore, its nature as a supporter does not consist in being external to that which is supported.
However, because He has internalized the entire universe within Himself—
as stated in the passage, "Since the entire world rests in Him, He is called the Setu (the Bridge)"— the word *setu* may indeed be used here in its primary sense.
Although the reading of the Chāndogya Śruti is "He is the bridge, the support," this statement is nevertheless made in this way in order to include other Vedic branches as well.
"Thus it is also in other cases," say those who know the tradition;
for the greatness of this [Ātman]— as expressed in such passages as "He is the lord of beings, he is the protector of beings" (Bṛhadāraṇyaka Upaniṣad 6.4.21)— is perceived in this [individual self].

Having thus explained the portion beginning with "and because of holding" (*dhṛteś ca*) by taking the word *sautra* in the sūtra as "that which collects the bridge" (*setu-samuccāyaka*), according to its literal syntactical connection and as referring to the statement of the indicative mark (*liṅga*), he now explains the entire sūtra as referring to the designation (*samākhyā*) consisting of a common mention—
namely, "this" (*eṣa*).
The word "dhṛteḥ" (because of support) is to be supplied here. In this view, the word "ca" (and) from the Sūtra connects with "upalabdheśca" (and because of perception).
Thus, it is not only on account of the inferential mark of support, but also...

But [the word] "of steadfastness" (dhṛteḥ) refers to the perception associated with steadfastness that makes Him known; for in the Vājasaneyaka, after stating, "He who sleeps in that space within the heart, the controller of all" (Bṛhadāraṇyaka Upaniṣad 6.4.21), it is further recorded:
"He is the Lord of all, He is the sovereign of beings, He is the protector of beings, He is the bridge and the support so that these worlds may not be confounded."
The construction is as follows: because of the statement "thus" (ityukteḥ) and because of the identical description (samānokteḥ), Viṣṇu alone is within the small space (dahara).
To the question, "From where does this designation (samākhyā) have Viṣṇu as its referent? he says: "This" (eṣa iti).
The expression "and so forth" (ityādi) is a reference where the third case ending has been elided.
By the word "etcetera" (*ādi*), the preceding passage, "He is the controller of all, He is the lord of all, He is the sovereign of all" (Bṛhadāraṇyaka Upaniṣad 6.4.22),
and the subsequent passage, "He is the bridge, the support, so that these worlds may not be confounded," are included.
For this very reason, the phrase "the words of a neutral person" has been employed.
In the expression "of this greatness," two genitives are used with different referents (*vyadhikaraṇa*).
The word "perception" (*upalabdhi*) is understood here to be repeated and thus connects [with both].
And likewise,
in this Vājasaneyaka, by the passage beginning with "He is the lord of beings," [it refers to] "of this."

The construction is as follows: because the greatness of Viṣṇu, such as his being the lord of all beings, has been stated in the passage "in this," referring to the reality situated within the small ether (daharākāśa).
He who is the sovereign lord of all, he who is the master of all,
and he who is renowned as the lord of the unmanifest;
The Lord is indeed real; His lordship is not something that has a beginning.
He who is this very protector, and for the sake of the non-confusion of these worlds, beginning with the earth—
For the non-melting of these, he is the "sustainer" (*vidharaṇa*),
meaning capable of sustaining;
it is not merely a matter of capacity alone.
However, the meaning of the Vedic text is that "the Brāhmaṇas desire to know this Blessed One, who is the bridge and the support of these worlds.
By this, it is shown that [He is to be known] not only for the reasons previously stated, but also for this further reason.

However, because of the mention of "support" (*vidhṛti*) in this context—specifically from the scriptural indication of being the support of all, namely, "He is the bridge, the support"—the one residing within the small lotus is indeed Viṣṇu.
Nor should it be asked: "How is it that He resides in the heart-lotus?"
"Of this"— of the greatness characterized by freedom from sin and so forth, residing in the heart-lotus—
"in this," the support of all, "all evils turn away" (Chāndogya Upaniṣad 8.4.1).
By this, because it has been stated [in the sūtra] "from perception" (upalabdheḥ);
not merely from the mark of support (dhṛti), but because of the statement of perception characterized by support (dhṛti).
Furthermore, because of the designation in the Vājasaneyaka—"He who lies within that space (ākāśa) inside the heart... he is the bridge, the sustainer"—Viṣṇu alone is the one in the small [space].
But how is it that even this designation has Viṣṇu as its object?
The meaning of the sūtra is thus stated: because in this Vājasaneyaka [text], the greatness of this Viṣṇu— consisting of his lordship over all beings and so forth— is declared.

Although the portion beginning with "of this greatness" (*asya mahimnaḥ*) is not syntactically connected when the commentary interprets the phrase "and because of support" (*dhṛteśca*) as referring to an inferential mark (*liṅga*),
nevertheless, in the *Ṭīkā* [it says]: "all evils [depart] from here."

Since it has been stated, "because its characteristics have been thus described," this [scriptural passage] should also be applied as establishing the property of the subject (*pakṣadharma*), namely that the *liṅga* resides in the heart-lotus. [As it says:
"In this very Imperishable, O Gārgī, is the ether woven, like warp and woof" (Bṛhadāraṇyaka Upaniṣad 5.8.11); and "By the command of this very Imperishable, O Gārgī" (Bṛhadāraṇyaka Upaniṣad 5.8.9).
Regarding the statement that Viṣṇu resides in the heart-lotus because of the scriptural hearing of his being the support of all, one might ask:
how does being the support of all determine that it is Viṣṇu, since that [support-ness] is not established as being co-referential with him? To this, he says: "In this... (etasmin).

By taking up the introductory phrase, "Under the governance of this Imperishable," [the text refers to] "O Gārgī, under the governance of this Imperishable, the sun and the moon stand held apart; O Gārgī, under the governance of this Imperishable, heaven and earth [stand held apart]."
This indicates many such statements;
these have been explained according to the method of the syllables:
"For he is the sovereign of all, he is the protector of all, he is the lord."
"Viṣṇu"; "the Lord of the universe, the Master of the Self" (Mahānārāyaṇa Upaniṣad 11), and so forth—from such scriptural passages, this is indeed His majesty.

Now, one might ask: from what source is the majesty consisting of universal lordship and so on, as declared by the scripture of the name (*samākhyā-śruti*), understood to belong to Viṣṇu? To this he says: "For He... (*sa hi*).
The passage beginning with "He indeed" and ending with "He is Viṣṇu" constitutes a single sentence found in another Śruti text. "He" refers to the subject under discussion.
"Hiḥ" signifies well-knownness;
"patiṃ viśvasya" is a statement from the Nārāyaṇa-anuvāka.
The meaning is that [the world] depends upon Nārāyaṇa, the Lord of the universe— the Lord of the insentient phenomenal world— and the Lord of sentient beings, the Self-Lord;
thus it is said in such passages.
The meaning is "from such scriptural statements as these. By the word "etc. (ādi), other passages of this kind are included.
The ablative case is used in the sense of the instrumental.
Of that Viṣṇu; "hi" indicates well-known fact or reason;
"He is the Lord of all" (Bṛhadāraṇyaka Upaniṣad 6.4.22).
Such is their greatness;
the word "understood" is to be supplied as the ellipsis.
Therefore, there is no lack of establishment of the co-occurrence (sāmānādhikaraṇya) of these with the probandum, which is the nature of Viṣṇu—this is the remainder of the sentence.
"Viṣṇu alone is the Lord of all; there is no other lord of the world," so it is said in the Skanda Purāṇa. 16.
Now, one might ask: "Could lordship over all and so forth not belong to another as well, just as it does to Viṣṇu? To this he says: "The Lord of All."
In this context, the two words "all" (*sarva*) and "world" (*jagat*) refer to the manifold of sentient and insentient beings.
Alternatively, they are a restatement of that which was already mentioned as the counter-correlative in the phrase "lord of the world" (*jagataḥ patiḥ*).
Or else, "lord" (*patiḥ*) means a protector.
And thus, the meaning is that Viṣṇu alone is the Lord of all and the Protector of all, and there is no other.
Regarding the phrase "iti skānde," by supplying the word indicated by the particle *eva* (alone), it connects with the preceding clause: "for this is indeed His greatness.
Therefore, the remainder of the sentence is: one should not suspect that these indicative marks (*liṅga*) have scope elsewhere.
Sūtra—Oṃ.
And because it is well-known.
And because it is well known from [the Mahānārāyaṇa Upaniṣad]: "Therein is a small space free from sorrow; that which is within it is to be meditated upon" (Mahānārāyaṇa 10.7).

Having recited and explained the sūtra which establishes that Viṣṇu resides in the space within the heart-lotus by means of another scriptural designation and another logical argument, he says: "And because of common renown" (prasiddheś ca).
The word "iti" implies that the phrase "in the Śruti" is to be understood as the ellipsis immediately following.
The term "of him" (tasya) is carried over [from the previous context];
"of him" refers to Viṣṇu.
The meaning of that [phrase] is "of him who resides in the heart-lotus.
By this [it is shown that] in this sūtra, the two words "asya" (of him) and "asmin" (in this) are to be carried over from the preceding sūtra.
And thus, it is not only on account of the designation "Vājasaneyi" [that this is established].

However, because of the phrase "in this" in that Taittirīya scriptural passage, and because of the well-known status of "this one"— who resides within the heart-lotus— as Viṣṇu, it is established by that very designation as well that the one residing in the small lotus is indeed Viṣṇu; such is the meaning of the Sūtra stated.
"And this Self is firmly established in the divine city of Brahman, in the ether" (Muṇḍaka Upaniṣad 2.2.7); and as it is well known in the Atharvaṇa:
"This person who is within the ether of the heart" (Taittirīya Upaniṣad 1.2.1).

Regarding the alternative interpretation of the *sūtra* "iti taittirīyavākyāntare prasiddheśca" which is indicated in the *Ṭīkā*, it should be understood that this is based on taking the word "iti" in the *Bhāṣya* to have the sense of "and so forth" (*ādi*).
In the *Śruti*: "The small, stainless lotus, the abode of the Supreme, situated in the middle of the city" (Mahānārāyaṇa Upaniṣad 10.7).

In this statement, the word "dahara" (small) refers to that which has been introduced as the lotus of the heart— situated within the city of Brahman known as the body, and therefore free from evil— which serves as the abode of the supreme Brahman; it is this very thing that is being referred to here by the pronoun "tat."
And likewise, "even there"— that is,
even within that small space (*dahara*) which is the sky (*gagana*)— there is "within" (*antaḥ*).
"In the interval, the sorrowless" (antare 'viśokaḥ):
the meaning is that Brahman—which is characterized by the state of being sorrowless and is devoid of old age and so forth—should be meditated upon.
The change of gender in the word "viśokaḥ" is a Vedic anomaly.
In the *Tattvapradīpa*, however, the purpose of the change in gender is stated to be twofold: first, to indicate that [the Self] is the Puruṣa;

and second, to draw forward (anukarṣaṇa) the qualities previously mentioned in passages such as "The Self which is free from evil, free from old age, free from death, free from sorrow," by virtue of their being brought into proximity through the identity of the substratum.
Because it depends on its being situated within that [ether], there is no contradiction with the scriptural mention of a cavity.
Now, if it is accepted that Viṣṇu is directly within the lotus, there is a contradiction with the scriptural passage concerning the "cavity" (suṣira).

Likewise, even if it is accepted that Viṣṇu is the very space (ākāśa) within the lotus, there is still a contradiction with the scriptural passage concerning the "cavity," because the word "cavity" denotes space.

Even if one abandons this [view] and accepts that the small lotus possesses the nature of space, while Viṣṇu resides within that space and is its universal substratum, there remains a contradiction with the scriptural texts concerning the "hollow" (suṣira).
In that regard, because it is stated that the cavity is the direct support of everything, he says: "That which exists within it."
By means of the intellect (*buddhi*), the word "suṣira" (hollow) ending in the sixth case is here to be construed with the word "śruti" (hearing).
And thus, in the phrase "of the hearing of the hollow" (*suṣiraśruteḥ*),
it is because [the term] depends on that which stands within the hollow.

The meaning is that there is no contradiction with the scriptural mention of a "cavity" (suṣira) in our position, because [the Supreme Self] exists within the cavity situated inside the lotus, and because He is the support of all.
The point is that just as an object located inside a chest within a temple is still said to be "in the temple," so it is here as well.
