Regarding the reading *tadantassthatvāt*, the meaning is that the scripture proceeds by taking into account the Supreme Self’s abiding within the cavity (of the heart). Sūtra: Oṃ.
If it is argued that "He" [refers to the individual soul] because of the reference to the other, we say no, because of impossibility.

If it is argued that this refers to the individual soul (jīva) because of the reference to the soul in such passages as, "Having attained the highest light, he appears in his own form" (Chāndogya Upaniṣad 8.12.3),
and "He said, 'This is the Self'" (Chāndogya Upaniṣad 4.15.1);

Having raised the objection regarding the Blessed One’s abiding within the heart-lotus and having introduced the sūtra that resolves it, he first explains the portion containing the objection, beginning with the words "itara... (the others).
The word "is produced" (*niṣpadyate*) is to be understood as referring to what was stated immediately before;
furthermore, it is syntactically connected with the word "living being" (*jīva*) which has entered into the compound.
By this, there is the recurrence of the words "in this" and "of this" within the present Sūtra.

The other term refers to the individual soul (jīva), which serves as the counter-correlate to Brahman as intended by the proponent of the final view. For this very reason, the word "this" (eṣa) in the Śruti constitutes a reference to the individual soul.
In our final doctrine, the meaning of the scriptural passage will be explained later;
[it does not refer to Brahman] because it is impossible for that [Brahman] to possess qualities such as being "freed from evil" by its own nature. // 18 //
Intending the recurrence of the phrase "because of its perception in this" from the *Dhṛti-sūtra*, he explains the part of the refutation, saying: "No."
The meaning is that the individual soul (jīva) does not reside within the heart-lotus.
Why not? To this, [the author] replies by means of the phrase "in this" which recurs in that context:
"of this."

Because the reason "on account of the perception of being free from evil" and so forth is obtained, he explains the portion beginning with "of that" (*tasya*), which intends to show that the stated reason has no scope regarding the individual soul (*jīva*) by not presenting that [other] reason.

The meaning is "of the living being" (jīva). The term "by itself" (svataḥ) is used to exclude the possibility of [the property] existing in the living being by taking on the state of liberation (muktabhāva), which would otherwise render the reason unestablished (asiddhi).
The meaning is "independently.
The phrase "and so forth" refers to qualities such as having true desires (*satyakāmatva*).
By this [word], [it is meant] "in this";

In the sentence "the supreme light," the word "this" (*eṣaḥ*) is used to enjoin that this very soul— which was previously mentioned as the agent of manifestation— is the Self (*ātman*) of the Brahman that serves as the object of attainment,
in accordance with the injunction "He who is the Self" regarding the Self residing in the heart-lotus.
"Because of the non-reflection by this word"; that is to say,
because of its presentation [of the subject],
specifically because of hearing this word "this" which reflects upon the individual soul (jīva).
If it is argued that in the case of the "small one" (dahara), he is indeed the individual soul (jīva) and not Viṣṇu—[we reply: the one residing in the heart-lotus is not the individual soul.
Why? Because in this context, qualities such as his being free from sin (apahatapāpmatva) and so forth are perceived through scriptural revelation.
And thus, the meaning of the Sūtra—"because this [creation] is impossible from itself in this living being"—has been stated.
Sūtra: Oṃ.
If it be argued that [the soul] comes from the north, [we reply: its true nature, however, has already been manifested.

If it be argued that [the one described] is indeed the individual soul (jīva), based on the subsequent statement, "He moves about there, laughing, playing, and rejoicing" (Chāndogya Upaniṣad 8.12.3) and so forth—

[the author] introduces the sūtra which resolves the impossibility of the individual soul possessing such qualities as being free from sin (apahatapāpmatva), and first explains the portion concerning the objection: "On account of what follows" (uttarāt).

The phrase "from such subsequent statements" (ityādyuttaravacanāt) means from a statement that follows either the passage concerning the small [ether] (*dahara-vākya*) or the passage concerning the reflection (*parāmarśa-vākya*).
Immediately after the word "from a statement," the words "because of its perception in this" (*asyāsminn upalabdheḥ*) are to be supplied.
The word "because of its occurrence" is to be supplied as the remainder [of the sentence].

"Of this"— namely, of the state of having true desires— "in this"— namely, in the individual soul (jīva)— because it is perceived, for that very reason there is the perception of freedom from sorrow and so forth.
The meaning of that [statement] is: "because of the possibility of the aforementioned qualities being established.
By the word *jīva*, the recurrence (*anuvṛtti*) of the term *sa* from the preceding sūtra is indicated.
The word *eva* has the sense of "not the Lord" (*neśvarāḥ*).
The phrase "residing in the heart-lotus" continues [from the previous context].
No; for it is there that one whose true nature has become manifest through the grace of the Supreme Lord is called "liberated.
He explains the portion concerning the refutation by continuing the negation—namely, "no."

The meaning is that one should not, on the strength of this statement, assume that the individual soul (jīva) possesses qualities such as having true desires and so forth, and thus declare its residence within the heart-lotus.

Why not? To this he replies with the portion "But [it is] one whose nature has become manifest," explaining the word "there" by supplying the word "in that case" (tatra). Thus: "In that case... [he says].
The meaning is that this refers to the subsequent sentence, "sa tatra" (he there).
The connection is with the statement: "there, he whose true nature has become manifest" is so described.
The explanation of the phrase "one whose true nature has become manifest" is "liberated.
The word *hi* means "because";
it is also connected with the subsequent statement [beginning with] "from the later declaration."
And likewise, from the statement "by his own nature" (*svena rūpeṇa*),
there is the scriptural teaching of the manifestation of one's true nature occurring after the abandonment of the inert body.

The point here is that since this refers to one who is liberated (*mukta*), and since it is impossible for the lotus of the heart to be liberated by virtue of residing within another body, this cannot be the individual soul (*jīva*).

Now, even if this passage concerns the liberated state, if the liberated one is still a *jīva*, then the possibility of being "free from sin" (*apahatapāpmatva*) and so forth does not exist in a *jīva*.
Nor is it impossible for such a one to reside in the lotus of the heart.

Since the individual soul (jīva), possessing qualities such as freedom from sin through its future state, is now described as residing within the heart-lotus, he says: "By the grace of the Supreme Lord.
The word "eva" (indeed) is understood to carry over [from the previous context].
By this, however, the word "tu" (but/however) is explained.
By the phrase "by the grace of the Supreme Lord," the terms *uttarāt* and *uttamāt* are also explained.
Here, the word "liberated" (*mukta*) is not merely an explanation of a term from the Sūtra; rather, it also serves to provide the subject of the statement.
By this, the repetition of the word "tu" (but) and its connection according to the literal hearing of the text are indicated.

And thus, he who is here called "liberated" is indeed one whose true nature has become manifest solely through the grace of the Supreme Lord; that is to say, he is so described because his own essential attribute—consisting of freedom from sin and so forth—has become manifest, i.e., revealed.

Therefore, the construction is as follows: since [the Self] does not possess qualities such as being free from evil by its own nature, it is not the individual soul (jīva) residing within the small space;
rather, that by whose grace one becomes liberated is the Blessed Lord mentioned previously. // 19 //

Now, one might object: in the passage, "Having reached the highest light, he emerges in his own true form" (Chāndogya Upaniṣad 8.3.4), it is stated that the liberated soul possesses manifest qualities such as freedom from sin and so forth,
but it is not stated that those qualities are dependent upon the Supreme Lord.
Therefore, [the author] says "that which" (yad) in order to show that it arises from itself alone.
The word "this" (asya) is connected with the second occurrence of the word "that" (tat).
What is called "grace" (prasāda) is a particular kind of will.
"He" refers to the individual soul (jīva).
Furthermore, by the repetition of the word "sa" (he), the recurrence of the word "sa" which follows in the sūtra is indicated.

By the phrase "pūrvokta" (previously mentioned), it is stated that the term "pūrvatras" (in the preceding case) should be supplied as the correlative to "uttaratras" (in the subsequent case) found in the sūtra. The word "tathā" (likewise) is to be understood as an ellipsis.
And thus: "by whose grace"; by whose favor, "he"—the individual soul—is "liberated."
He becomes possessed of qualities such as being free from evil;
"he" refers to the Blessed Lord, the bestower of these qualities, who was mentioned previously, having attained the supreme light.
The construction is as follows: in the preceding sentence, [the Lord] is described by the word "tathā" (thus) as being the bestower of qualities;
otherwise, the word ending in the suffix -lyap would be redundant—this is the intended meaning.
The word "stated" (*ukta*) is followed by the ellipsis "since" (*yataḥ*).
This connects with the supplemented sentence: "Therefore, there is no absence of a statement here that the attainment of the qualities of liberation is dependent upon the Supreme Lord.

Alternatively: [An objection is raised]—"But since the collection of qualities belonging to the individual soul (*jīva*) is dependent on another, let that very soul be the one described as being free from sin and so forth, and let it be the one residing in the heart-lotus"; to this he says: "That which... (*yad iti*).

The interpretation, however, is as follows: "That previously mentioned Blessed One" is He by whose grace that individual soul (jīva) becomes liberated from the inert body, and having become liberated, possesses qualities such as being free from sin.

The Self described in the preceding passage, "This Self is free from evil" (Chāndogya Upaniṣad 8.1.5) and so forth, by such qualities as being free from evil, is not the individual soul (jīva). This is because,
between the giver and the recipient, the giver alone is primary, and between the primary and the secondary, the primary alone is to be accepted [as the referent].

By this— namely, by the subsequent [text] "He goes around there" (*sa tatra paryeti*), which follows either the *dahara* passage or the referential passage concerning the individual soul (*jīva*) described in the words, "This serene being, having risen up from this body" (*eṣa samprasādo 'smāccharīrātsamutthāya*; Chāndogya Upaniṣad 8.3.4).

From such statements as these, [it follows that] "in this"— that is, in the individual soul (jīva) under discussion— there is the "perception," or apprehension, of "this," namely, the quality of having true desires.

If it is argued that, because freedom from sorrow and so forth is established for him [the one in the heart] precisely for that reason, and because there is thus no absence of the aforementioned qualities, he who resides in the lotus of the heart is merely the *jīva* and not the Lord—[we reply: no, because in that context [it says] "by his own... [and so on].
Thus, by the force of the subsequent statement, one whose true nature has been manifested is called "liberated.
And the sense is that, because he is no longer contained within a body, he does not reside in the heart-lotus.

Nor should it be argued that even for the liberated soul, since it remains a *jīva*, there is a possibility of its returning to that state—given that the attributes of being free from sin (*apahatapāpmatva*) and residing in the heart-lotus belong to different times—even though grammatical coreferentiality (*sāmānādhikaraṇya*) is possible.

For in this statement, he who is called "liberated" has manifested his true nature solely through the supreme grace of the Supreme Lord, not by himself. Nor should it be argued that what is stated here is merely that the liberated one possesses those qualities,
rather than that the entire collection of those qualities is dependent upon the Supreme Lord.
For, in the preceding passage, "the supreme light," that by whose grace he becomes liberated is the Supreme Self, who is thus described as the bestower of qualities.

Nor should it be argued that there is a re-attainment [of that state] because the individual soul (jīva) possesses qualities such as being free from sin (*apahatapāpmatva*) and so forth in some manner.

Because of that—that is, through the grace of the Blessed One, who is higher than the high—he was liberated; his true nature having become manifest (*āvirbhūtasvarūpaḥ*), meaning his qualities such as freedom from sin and so forth were fully revealed. Indeed, it was that very Blessed One who was previously mentioned in the preceding passage: "This Self is free from sin" (Chāndogya Upaniṣad 8.1.5).
Thus, the meaning of the Sūtra is stated as "the released soul" (muktajīva).
As for the meaning of the Śruti: "this" refers to the soul (jīva), because it is "serene" (samprasāda).
"Endowed with the perfect grace of Viṣṇu, having risen from this final body," [he becomes] liberated "that which is supreme."
"Having attained" (upasampadya) Brahman as "light" (jyotis),
he "manifests" (abhiniṣpadyate) in his own true nature.
"That Supreme Person" is manifested as the one known as the "Highest Light.
Regarding the manner in which the liberated one moves among sense objects, he says: "He... [sa].

"He," the liberated one who has manifested the innate bliss of attainment, "there" in the place of liberation, solely through the grace of the Supreme Self, "eating"— consuming what he desires— or "laughing," and "playing" with both his kinsmen who are liberated and those who were not his kinsmen but were liberated in previous kalpas.
"Delighting with women" means experiencing pleasure; "wanders about" means moving everywhere while experiencing the worldly happiness derived from objects such as women.
Sūtra—Oṃ.
And the reflection has another purpose.
"That which, having reached, the individual soul (jīva) manifests in its own true form—that is this Self"—this reflection refers to the Supreme Self. // 20 //

Now, one might raise the objection: "Since the word 'this' (eṣaḥ) refers to the individual soul (jīva), and then the word 'Self' (ātmā) designates that [soul] as being the Self residing in the heart-lotus, why could the individual soul—even though its qualities such as being free from sin are not primary—be the Self residing in the heart-lotus by virtue of the reference made by the word 'this'? Anticipating this doubt, the Sūtra is presented: "If it be said that it is so because of the reference to the other, we say no. (1.1.17)

Thus, since the required [subject] is obtained from the preceding sentence that follows on and because the formal proposition of the established conclusion (*siddhāntapratijñā*) is also attained, he explains the Sūtra as the reason for the probandum stated by "no" (*na*): "anyā... etc.

In the Śruti, the reference by the masculine pronoun "yam" to that which is indicated by the neuter term "paraṃjyotiḥ" is appropriate either because gender is not intended to be significant (aliṅgavivakṣā) or because the intention is to refer to the substantive noun itself.
By this, it is shown that in the Śruti, "paraṃjyotiḥ" constitutes a single word.

As he will state, "By the term 'supreme light' (paraṃjyotiḥ), the Supreme Self alone is denoted," and that, by the conventional usage of the Purāṇas, it is said to signify Viṣṇu, as in "the supreme light is the Supreme Brahman."
Some maintain that "light" (*jyotiḥ*) and "the supreme Brahman" (*paraṃ brahma*) are two distinct words.
In this view, there is a contradiction with the aforementioned commentary.
Furthermore, [it refers to] "the Blessed One known as the Supreme Light."
Thus, there is a contradiction with the commentary (*ṭīkā*) which is intent on explaining the word *yat*;
and there is also a contradiction with the commentary on the *Viṣṇutattvanirṇaya*, which states: "The supreme light is the Supreme Self."
The meaning of "having attained" (*upasampadya*) in the scripture is "having reached.
He explains the other term from the Sūtra as the Supreme Self (*paramātman*), in contrast to the individual soul (*jīva*) favored by the opponent.
That whose meaning or denotable object is the Supreme Self alone is described as such;
"parāmarśa" refers to this word.
Alternatively, it means that its purpose or aim is the teaching of the very Supreme Self as the Self; thus it is so described.
In that case, "non-consideration" (*aparāmarśaḥ*) means the inclusion [of the Supreme Self] by means of this word (*etac-chabdena*).

In the *Sūtra-bhāṣya*, the word "but" (*tu*) signifies either a conjunction—meaning that there is not only the existence of a subverting argument against the position of the individual soul (*jīva*), namely the impossibility of being free from sin (*apahatapāpmatva*), but also the absence of a supporting argument known as "reference" (*parāmarśa*)—or it expresses the meaning of the particle "indeed.
In the *Candrikā*, however, it is stated: "Not only is there an absence of subversion regarding the reference (*parāmarśa*) in the case of the Lord (*īśvara*..."

However, because it has been stated that there is an absence of proof for the position that [the subject] is the individual soul (jīva), the reference (parāmarśa) is explained as being intended to determine that it refers exclusively to the Lord,
who is other than the individual soul. By this [sūtra], "because of the reference to the other"— the "other" being the individual soul— "this" [subject]...

If it is argued that, because the text refers to him in this way and prescribes his abiding within the heart-lotus, that Self residing in the heart-lotus is merely the individual soul (*jīva*) and not the Lord (*īśvara*)—we say no. Why?
Because the reference "this one" (*eṣaḥ*) has another purpose; it refers specifically to the Lord who is distinct from the individual soul.
It is not for the sake of the individual soul; therefore.
Or rather—it is not only because of impossibility, but also because the reflection has another purpose.
Alternatively—the individual soul (jīva) does not reside in the heart-lotus because that is impossible;
rather, it is the Lord (Īśvara) himself.
And in this case, there is no inconsistency with the reference [to the soul].
Since the word "parāmarśaḥ" [is used],
and because this word has another meaning, the meaning of the sūtra is thus stated in three ways:
"'yaṃ prāpya' means having reached the vicinity of that."

By this [process], the individual soul (jīva), having approached the Supreme Self known as the Supreme Light and having known It through direct perception, then—having reached Its proximity—becomes manifest in its own nature consisting of bliss and so forth by the shaking off of ignorance;
that is to say, it becomes one whose own qualities have become manifest.
That which the soul reaches and thereby becomes manifest in its true form—

This very Self, which was previously described as the "Self," is the Supreme Self; thus he spoke to Brahmā and the others, saying "Rama"—this is the meaning of the Śruti according to the established conclusion (siddhānta). Sūtra: Oṃ.
If it be argued that this is because [the scripture] contains little to hear, that has already been answered.

If it be argued that [the Self] is not [the object of knowledge] because of the word "daharaḥ" (small) in Chāndogya Upaniṣad 8.1.1, the Sūtra refutes this objection and provides a resolution; setting forth the Sūtra and citing the scriptural passage, the author first explains the part concerning the objection with the words "alpa" and so on.

By taking up the term "daharaḥ" (the small), the sentence "In this [city of Brahman] there is a small inner space; what is within that" is understood. Furthermore, the word "small" (alpa) refers to its abiding in a small location.
Immediately after "from scripture" (śruteḥ), the word "because of impossibility" (asambhavāt) is understood to carry over;
and the word "in this" (asmin) is also present.
And thus [it refers to] "the small" (daharaḥ).

The syntactical connection (*anvaya*) in this passage is as follows: because there is a scriptural indication (*liṅgaśruti*) in this sentence regarding the object situated within the small space (*dahara*)— namely, its abiding in a limited location— and because that [indication] is "impossible" (*asambhavāt*), i.e., untenable, with respect to this Supreme Self (*paramātman*).
For this reason, Viṣṇu is not the one within the small space;
rather, he is indeed the individual soul (jīva)—this is the connection with the proposition that continues from the subsequent sūtras.
No, because it has been stated: "On account of its being perceived as such, and like space.
Intending the repetition of the negative particle (*nañ*) that recurs in the Sūtra, he explains the portion of the refutation with the word "no" (*na*).
The meaning is that it is not untenable for Viṣṇu to be heard of as abiding in a small place.

To the question "Why not?", the portion beginning with "tad uktam" (that has been said) is explained as a reason by supplying the word "yataḥ" (since), [as in]: "nicāyyatvāt" (because He is to be perceived).
The words "here too" (atrāpi) are to be supplied as the remainder of the sentence.

And likewise, in the passage "because He is to be perceived" (*nicāyyatvāt*), the meaning is that although Viṣṇu is omnipresent, His abiding in a small location is stated to be like that of space (*vyoma*); as it says:
"This is my Self within the heart, greater [than all]" (Chāndogya Upaniṣad 3.14.3).
And because it is so stated in the Śruti. // 21 //
Thus concludes the section concerning the "Small One" (daharādhikaraṇa).
Now, it might be argued that it is appropriate for space (*vyoman*) to have small abodes in its parts because a part is incomplete;
but since even a part of Brahman is complete, how can it have small abodes in its parts? To this, he explains the remainder of the Sūtra by way of another method: "This is my... (*eṣa ma*).
The word "ca" (and) serves to combine logical arguments,
or to combine the scriptural statements of the Sūtra author;
[it refers to] "the qualities that have been heard."
This is either in the sense of a collection of Śrutis,
or in the sense of a collection of Smṛtis, as indicated by the word "yasmin" (in which).
By this [it is meant] "because of the limited scope of the Śruti."

In the sentence "the small one" (*dahara*), because it is heard that the omnipresent reality resides in a limited space, and because such [limited residence] is impossible and therefore untenable in the case of Viṣṇu, Viṣṇu is not the "small one."
If it is argued that "but he is indeed the individual soul (jīva)," we say no; for it has been stated there [in the previous Sūtra],
"because of being perceived therein," that although Viṣṇu is omnipresent, He resides in a small place like the ether.
Therefore, it has been stated that [the meditation] is appropriate for the purpose of worship.
Nor is there any inconsistency in that regard even from the perspective of being a partial aspect, because of its omnipresence;
for in that [passage], it says: "This is my Self" (Chāndogya Upaniṣad 3.14.3).

Thus, in the *Chandoga-śruti*, by way of being the most excellent (*sarvajyāyastva*), the oldest (*vṛddhatamatva*), and all-pervading (*vyāptatva*), it is stated that Viṣṇu resides within that heart; and since this is also stated in the *Smṛti*, the meaning of the Sūtra has been explained.
Nor is it the case that even what is stated in Śruti and Smṛti is unworthy of acceptance.
It should not be said that this contradicts reason,
for it is logically consistent because Brahman possesses inconceivable power; thus,
"the qualities are heard [in scripture]."
And from the statement in the *Sauparṇa-śruti*: "In whom [the rivers] with contrary courses... and so forth.
The "Self" that exists within my heart is the Supreme Self;
this is an illustrative indication.

And he who dwells in the heart of all—this Blessed One, whose form consists of the portions situated within the hearts—is "the greater," meaning the most ancient and full in terms of space, time, and qualities; such is the meaning of the Śruti.
This is a statement by a seer who perceived the Upaniṣads.
"Even those with contradictory movements":
even qualities such as minuteness and magnitude, which elsewhere have different substrata, "fall upon" or "reside in" that [substratum].
He says "without interruption" (aniśam) to indicate that there is no distinction of time.
Anticipating the doubt that this might be common to liberated souls as well, he says "knowledge and so forth" (vidyādayaḥ),
because qualities such as the various powers of minuteness, magnitude, and so on belong to Viṣṇu alone and not elsewhere.

Those for whom knowledge (*vidyā*) is the cause of cognition are so described; that is to say, they are the "knowers and the objects of knowledge. He states the means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) regarding Hari, who possesses contradictory attributes, with the words "in succession" (*ānupūrvyā*).
The meaning is that they are established by Śruti, because of the definition: "The sequence, the revelation (śruti), the Veda, and the triple knowledge are called the sacred tradition (āmnāya).
As for the word "yat" [in the mantra], it refers to "that Brahman I take refuge in."
Thus, there is a syntactic connection with the word "tat" (that) occurring in the subsequent sentence. // 5 //
// Thus ends the section concerning the "small" [space] (daharādhikaraṇa) // 5 //
6. The Section on Imitation (Anukṛtyadhikaraṇa)
The qualities of invisibility and so forth have been stated as belonging to the Supreme Lord;
"their happiness is eternal, not that of others."
Thus, by such passages as "This they consider to be the supreme, ineffable bliss" (Kaṭha Upaniṣad 5.12,
14), it is stated that even the bliss of the knower is ineffable and unknowable.

In this section, the characteristic of being apprehended in a favorable manner—either as the state of being the object of a prayer for the knowledge of the knowable, expressed in the sentence "How indeed may I understand that? for the sake of knowledge, or as the state of being the object of a prayer for manifestation known as "shining forth" (bhāna) which is conducive to the knowledge of Brahman, expressed in "How indeed may I understand that? How does it shine?"—is shown to be consistently applicable to Brahman.

Indicating the connection with the scriptures and so forth, as well as the subject matter and other elements, he presents the prima facie view (pūrvapakṣa) along with its reasoning: "Because of being invisible" (*adṛśyatvāt*).
The sense is that they were "stated" in the passage concerning the "invisible" (*adṛśya*) cited in the section on the one consisting of bliss (*ānandamaya-adhikaraṇa*).
After the word "stated," the phrase "entered therein" is to be supplied as the ellipsis.
By the first word, "prathama" and so forth, there is the inclusion of [the attributes] such as being unmanifested (*anirukta*);

by the second, there is the inclusion of the latter half of the verse which indicates the characteristic to be connected, namely: "How indeed may I know that—does it shine or does it not shine? (Kaṭha Upaniṣad 5.14).
The meaning of *api* is that this applies not only to Viṣṇu, but also to the bliss of the knower (*jñānin*);
or, the word *api* may have the sense of *eva*, as in the word *api* found in the *Ānumānika-sūtra*.
"Incognizability" (*ajñeyatva*) means being entirely incognizable, that is to say, being difficult to know;
the word "and" (*ca*) serves to conjoin these qualities mutually.
Or, it may be a collection of marks (*liṅga*) to be connected [with Brahman] in the form of being apprehended in accordance [with the qualities];

thus, following the previous scriptural passage, there is "unseen-ness" (*adṛśyatva*) and so forth, while following this [present] scriptural passage, there is "indescribability" (*anirdeśyatva*), resulting in an inversion of order.
Although "this very [thing]" (*etad eva*) should have been cited [as the example],
nevertheless, in order to demonstrate the meaning of the word "that" (*tat*) in the prima facie argument (*pūrvapakṣa*), [the text uses] "of them" (*teṣām*).
Thus is the citation of a portion of the preceding statement.
For this very reason, it is stated in the *Tattvapradīpa* that the introduction with the words "of them" (*teṣām*) serves to raise the prima facie argument (*pūrvapakṣa*).

Accordingly, the construction is as follows: previously, in the section concerning the one consisting of bliss (*ānandamaya-adhikaraṇa*), those qualities such as invisibility (*adṛśyatva*) and so forth were predicated of the Supreme Lord.

In that regard, the state of being indefinable and unknowable when they have entered into those [senses]— referring even to "the happiness of the knower" (jñānisukha) which is indicated by the proximate pronoun *tat* in the Kāṭhaka passage beginning with "That this... (*tad etat*) as recited in the context of the primary subject (*prakṛta*)— "their happiness"— is [to be understood] according to the view of the opponent (*pūrvapakṣin*).

The meaning is that this is stated specifically regarding the bliss of the knower (*jñānisukha*); for by the first half [of the verse], its ineffability is expressed, and by the second half— through the phrase "Does it shine or not shine?"— its unknowability, which culminates in being difficult to know, is effectively stated.

There is no contradiction with that [commentary], because in the *Ṭīkā* the word "invisibility" (*adṛśyatva*) is intended to mean "indescribability," or because the reading "indescribability" (*anirdeśyatva*) is accepted there. The statement regarding the result here—that "indescribability and unknowability are being asserted"—is merely a summary; for what is actually under investigation here is precisely the state of being apprehended in a favorable manner.
It should be understood that this [point] has been indicated by the sentence containing the word "second" and so forth, or by the word "ca" (and).
Since this is so, the meaning is that what was stated previously is incorrect.

By this, [the arguments regarding] the nature of being invisible and unknowable, as well as the nature of being indefinable and inexpressible, as discussed in the *Anandamaya-Adhikaraṇa* [are addressed].

In this regard, because there is an objection that [the definition] over-extends (*ativyāpti*) to the happiness of the wise in other states of existence, and because there is an objection that it is impossible for it to reside in anything else alone, it follows that its "contextual connection" (*saṅgati*) is said to be "suggestive" (*ākṣepikī*).
And thus, as indicated by the word "and" (*ca*), the object [of the definition] is being perceived in a manner that is favorable [to the self].
There is a doubt as to whether [this bliss] belongs to Viṣṇu or to someone else.
The prima facie view (pūrvapakṣa) is that it belongs to the bliss of the knower alone.
The conclusion (siddhānta) is that because of its indescribability and its being unknowable, it belongs to that [bliss of the knower] alone.
The hearing of the blissful [teaching] and the logical reasoning consisting of its topical relevance and so forth are thus indicated;
therefore, he says:
Sūtra—Oṃ.
And because of the imitation of that [Brahman].
"Everything shines only after Him as He shines"; this is because of the imitation [expressed] in the phrase, "By His light all this is illumined" (Kaṭha Upaniṣad 5.15).
And because of this statement, the Supreme Self alone is of the nature of indefinable bliss.
Introducing and explaining the sūtra which establishes this conclusion, [the author] says: "Therefore... (ataḥ).

‘Because of imitation’ (ity-anukṛteḥ) means ‘because of the scriptural statement regarding resonance’ (anubhāna-śruti). Resonance (anubhāna) is a specific action consisting of appearing in accordance with His will.

In the Sūtra, because of the connection with the word "of that" (*tasya*) by means of the phrase "due to imitation" (*anukṛteḥ*), there is the attainment of both the agent of that [imitation]—who is grasped as being favorable toward the object of imitation—and the light of the sun and so forth.
Since this is self-evident, neither of those two is explicitly mentioned.

Alternatively, the intention is that because the word *tat* from the preceding Sūtra is carried over here in a modified form, there is the attainment of both; it is for this reason that neither of the two is mentioned.

The phrase "not only of that" is intended to show that it refers not only to the subject characterized by the mark known as being perceived in accordance with what is to be connected [with the probandum]—namely, the light of the sun and so forth—but also to the representative form of the Vedic revelation (śruti) which signifies the illumination of the entire world; with this intention, he explains it as having another reason for its application, saying: "of that."
By the phrase "from this statement," the ellipsis "because it is stated thus in the Sūtra" is indicated;
for although [the word] "it shines after" occurs in both the Sūtra and the Bhāṣya...
It must be stated that this is according to scripture (*śruti*) or because it is experienced (*anubhava*).
Nevertheless, [it is said]: "O King, the power that heats, cooks, dries, and illuminates does not belong to the sun; that power belongs to Nārāyaṇa."

Thus, based on the statement from the *Padma Purāṇa* cited in the *Aitareya Bhāṣya*, it is stated in the Sūtra that "because of imitation" (*anukṛteḥ*) in order to show that even the heating and so forth performed by the sun and other luminaries is dependent upon the Supreme Self.

In the Sūtra and in the corresponding Bhāṣya, the word "and" (*ca*) should be understood either as a conjunction of the previously stated reason— namely, the nature of being the illuminator of the entire universe— as explained through the different interpretations to be presented for the second Sūtra, or as a conjunction of an unstated reason— namely, the nature of not being illuminated by the sun and other luminaries.
In the Sūtra, he explains the meaning of the word "that" (*tat*), which follows from the *Samanvaya-sūtra* and refers to that which is to be enjoined, stating: "the Supreme Self alone.
The force of the word "alone" (*eva*) is to exclude the happiness of the knower (*jñānin*).
He demonstrates the fruit of your position through the concordance of the marks (*liṅga-samanvaya*), stating: "indescribable," and so forth.
The analysis of the compound is either "this [state] is inexpressible and its nature is bliss," or "its nature is that bliss which is inexpressible.
In this context, the word *rūpa* (nature/form) is displaced [from its expected position].
And thus, the grammatical connection is as follows: "the supreme bliss, which is of the nature of the Supreme Self, is indefinable.
In the passage beginning with "one" (*eka*), the word *rūpa* (form) is employed so that what was introduced in the masculine gender may be grasped here in the neuter gender by the pronoun *etad*.
This [use of the word *rūpa*] is an illustrative indication (*upalakṣaṇa*).
It should also be understood that "the object to be favored" (*anugrāhya*) is likewise to be seen.

In reality, however, it should be noted that because of the word "and" (*ca*) in the phrase "and from the statement," there is also a connection with "having the nature of happiness" (*sukharūpa*); thus, by that very same favorability, the subject of the thesis (*sādhyadharmin*) known as "that which is apprehended" is indicated.
Although both [the properties] "inexpressibility" (*anirdeśyatva*) and "unknowability" (*ajñeyatva*) are to be grasped due to the opening statement, [the former is intended here].
However, it is not "one," nor is there the addition of "having the nature of bliss.
Nevertheless, the phrase "that very [Brahman]" is used to indicate that the scriptural mention of bliss cited by the opponent finds its scope within Brahman as having the nature of bliss.
Thus, by the statement of the *itivākya*, only the nature of indefinable bliss (*anirdeśyasukharūpatva*) is grasped;
its unknowability (*ajñeyatva*) should also be understood.

Although in this commentary, the two marks (*liṅga*) appear to function as direct reasons for establishing that [the object] is Viṣṇu—whether as that which is grasped in accordance with the two marks or as that whose nature is indefinable bliss.

In the *Ṭīkā*, however, regarding the phrase "this very [one]" (*tad etat*) in the Śruti, it is argued that by setting aside the happiness of the knower mentioned in immediate proximity, the two indicators (*liṅga*) are joined as the reason for accepting the previously introduced Supreme Self (*paramātman*)— as in the verse "The conscious one among the conscious" (Kaṭha Upaniṣad 5.13)— despite its intervening position.

Nevertheless, since by means of these two reasons and the word "that" (tat), it is established that the Supreme Self alone is to be understood— by virtue of the abandonment of the happiness of the wise—
the intended meaning is that the nature of the Supreme Self, as grasped by the word "that," results in being of the form of indefinable bliss; thus,
there is no contradiction in the Commentary’s statement that the two marks serve as the reasons for the probandum under discussion.

However, some [hold that] the Bhāṣya statement, "The Supreme Self alone is of the nature of indefinable bliss," in the *Anukṛti* Sūtra, is not stated as a reason for the subject matter's being Viṣṇu— just as in cases such as "The one consisting of bliss [is Brahman], because of repetition"— but rather as a reason for the words and so forth to be construed as referring to Viṣṇu.

However, they say that regarding the phrase "but [it is] an indescribable bliss," the reason for abandoning the bliss of the wise mentioned immediately before is stated here as the indicator (*jñāpaka*),
and the *Ṭīkā* follows that interpretation.
And thus, this is the meaning of the Śruti according to the established doctrine (*siddhānta*):
The one controller, the inner self of all beings, who makes his single form manifold—those wise ones behold him abiding within themselves. (Kaṭha Upaniṣad 5.12)

Thus, in the preceding statement, "He who is one" refers to Him who is non-different from knowledge, bliss, and so forth, or who is devoid of any equal or superior; "the controller of all" means He under whose control everything exists;
and "the inner Self of all beings."

The one who is the internal regulator of all living beings, "the One," who makes his own nature manifold due to the infinity of those to be regulated— "Him," the subject under discussion, "abiding in the self."

Those who are steadfast— the wise— behold that which resides in the heart of the living being; for those very wise ones who are under discussion, there is "eternal happiness," meaning a bliss that is eternally manifest, and not for others.
By this, the power of Brahman is expressed.
Likewise, the statement "the eternal among eternals" should also be interpreted as being devoted to the majesty of Brahman.
By the words "That very [reality]" (*tad etat*) and so forth, the very nature of the Lord under discussion is specifically elucidated.
The verb "they consider" (*manyante*) connects with what follows later.
And thus: "From whence words turn back" (*Taittirīya Upaniṣad* 2.4.1).

In passages such as "This is his supreme bliss" (Bṛhadāraṇyaka Upaniṣad 6.3.32), they think, "How indeed may I know that supreme, indescribable happiness which is well-known? and thus they grasp it with favor;
or they pray for its manifestation for the sake of knowledge.
The wise declare its inscrutability, saying, "Does it shine or does it not shine?
They consider this bliss—which is the very nature of Brahman—to be its single form that it makes manifold; thus, the wise regard it as non-different from the forms of both Prakṛti and Īśvara.
Even if this word refers to Īśvara, its neuter gender is justified by its grammatical coordination with the word *rūpa* (form).
As it is stated in the *Nyāyavivaraṇa*: "That Brahman which they call indescribable bliss, they consider to be this very nature (*svarūpa*).
However, in the *Kāṭhakabhāṣya*, it says: "That secret, eternal Brahman."
Thus it was introduced:
"He became the counterpart of every form" (Kaṭha Upaniṣad 5.9),
whereby the state of the individual soul as a reflection is stated.

By the word "form" (rūpa), this subject at hand is referred to; and in the phrase "one form," the subject at hand is the form of the Blessed One, which is "indescribable"—meaning it cannot be fully defined as being "thus. This has been explained as being intended to enjoin that its nature is bliss, for the wise consider it to be supreme happiness.

In the Bhāṣya as well, by the mere mention of "having the nature of inexpressible bliss," it is indicated that the state of having the nature of bliss is the predicate to be enjoined in the Śruti. Regarding that form of the Lord, which consists of that inexpressible supreme bliss, the meaning of the remaining portion of the sentence—as stated in that very [text]—is: "Without His supreme grace, does it shine or does it not shine? It shines perfectly; how indeed may I know this? This has been explained in the Vyāsatīrthīya: "'That'..."
"Without the grace of that Blessed One, whose nature is the supreme bliss that is ineffable, how indeed could his form shine forth correctly?
Does it not shine?"—this question and its answer constitute a single statement of definitive meaning: "How may I come to know [him]?"

"In no way whatsoever"—here the word *iti* connects with both [the preceding and following clauses]. Thus, the construction is as follows: the meaning expressed by the single sentence "it does not appear," which serves as the answer to the question "What appears?", is the nature of being unknowable.

But some [hold] that the optative suffix (*liṅ*) is used here in the sense of a prayer (*prārthanā*), as in: "Since Brahman is thus [described], how may I know it without its grace?"— this being the request made at present.
The meaning is "not in any way whatsoever.
This is an imitation of the words of a knower (jñānin).
Naciketas asks Yama whether that knowledge arises in its entirety even through the grace of the Blessed One, saying: "Does it shine forth? (kim u bhāti).
The word *u* means "correctly" (*samyak*).
Or, it may mean "one";
in that case, the word "correctly" is to be supplied as the remainder of the sense.
Yama states the answer: "It does not shine.
The particle *vā* is used for emphasis;
he explains it as "it certainly does not shine."
For the bliss of the knower does not illuminate everything, nor is there illumination by it;
yet [the scripture says], "It shines only as that which shines."

Since the statement "iti vākya" [the passage beginning with *iti*] hears that the luminosity of the sun and other lights has its agency for illumination dependent upon the Supreme Self, and the statement "tasya bhāsā" [the passage beginning with *tasya*] hears that the entire world is illuminated by His light, how can the charge of being unestablished (*asiddhi*) be avoided? For if those two were not invariably concomitant (*avyabhicarita*) with the probandum—namely, being Viṣṇu—then on the strength of those two marks (*liṅga*), why should there be a rejection of the previously mentioned happiness of the knower? To this, he says: "For not... (*na hi*).
The word "all" (sarvam) is connected to both [the preceding and following clauses];
"appears" (bhāti) is the ellipsis.
And thus, for this reason, "all."
Following the bliss of the Knower, the splendor of the sun and other luminaries "does not shine," that is,
it does not manifest; likewise, by "its light."
By the manifestation of that bliss of the knower, "everything"— that is, the entire world— "does not shine";
the meaning is that it does not appear.
The intended meaning is that this would contradict the proofs to be stated later.
The word "ca" (and) functions as a conjunction.
Therefore, the remainder of the sentence is: "Thus, the two marks do not have scope elsewhere."
"I am the radiance and rays of that [light]"; for indeed, everything shines by the light of Nārāyaṇa. // 22 //
Granted that both of these [objections] are untenable with respect to the bliss of the knower (*jñānin*);

nevertheless, how can this [scriptural passage] be taken to refer to the Supreme Self (*paramātman*), since there is no certainty regarding its grammatical coreferentiality (*sāmānādhikaraṇya*) with the property to be proven—that it is the Supreme Self? To this, he cites the scriptural authority indicated by the word "also" (*api*) in the second Sūtra: "I... (*aham iti*).
Immediately after "I am," the word "from the Śruti" is to be supplied as an ellipsis.
The word "iti" has the sense of "and so forth. By this, [the following is included]: "Everything shines only after Him who shines; by His light all this is illumined" (Kaṭha Upaniṣad 5.15).
Thus, the Atharvaṇa Śruti is also cited;
"Nārāyaṇa" means that which appears dependent upon Nārāyaṇa.
The word *hi* means "since" and also indicates well-known fact. "All"— that is, the light of the sun and so forth— "shines," meaning it is illuminated.
Alternatively: "By the light of Nārāyaṇa" means by the light pertaining to Nārāyaṇa, "everything"— that is,
the entire world— "shines."
The meaning is "of light";
the words "it is known" are to be supplied as the ellipsis;
[this is] from the Śruti: "the rays."
The meaning is that by this [passage], the fact that the sun and other luminaries possess the agency of illumination dependent upon Nārāyaṇa is stated;
and by the word "light" (*tejaḥ*), the fact that the entire world is illuminated by the light belonging to Nārāyaṇa is also stated.
As for the word "I" (*aham*), the Śruti has been explained according to the internal method (*antaryāya*).
By this—since it is said "it has been stated"—the word *tat* from the sūtra is carried over (*anuvartate*).
The word *tasya* is both repeated (*āvartate*) and modified (*vipariṇamyate*).
And the phrase *asambhavāt* is also carried over. And thus:
"This is that," they consider it to be the supreme, ineffable bliss;
how indeed may I come to know it? (Kaṭha Upaniṣad 5.14)

This very bliss, which is apprehended as being thus favorable and referred to by the word "this," is the indescribable bliss; that indeed is the very form of Viṣṇu, and not the bliss of the knower mentioned immediately prior.
Why? Because of the word "his" (tasya).

Because of the "conformity" expressed in the passage "He shines following Him who shines," the pleasure that is perceived in accordance with the splendor of the sun and other luminaries belongs to that [Brahman].

This means: because of the hearing of its manifestation (*anubhāna*); because of the hearing that it is the agent of illumination dependent upon that [Brahman]; and because of the hearing that it controls other lights—such is the sense.

Likewise, because it is stated in the scripture, "By his light" (*tasya bhāsā*, Kaṭha 5.15), that this entire world is illuminated by its light—that is to say, because of the statement that it is the illuminator of the whole universe.

Furthermore, because those two marks are established with certainty in Viṣṇu alone by such scriptural and traditional texts as "I am that light" (Caturvedaśikhā), and because they are impossible in the happiness of the knowers;
Because it is impossible [otherwise];

likewise, because in that concluding passage, when it is perceived in accordance with that [Brahman], the statement "the sun does not shine there" declares its quality of not being illuminated by the sun and other luminaries— thus the meaning of the Sūtra has been explained.
Sūtra—Oṃ.
It is also recorded in the Smṛti:
"That splendor residing in the sun which illuminates the entire world,
and that which is in the moon and in fire— know that splendor to be mine" (Gītā 15.12).
This [verse] establishes that these two marks reside in Viṣṇu, as indicated by the word "I."
Thus it has been established by scripture. Now, establishing the same point through Smṛti as well, the Sūtra cites that Smṛti after reciting it, beginning with "api."
The grammatical connection is "it is thus remembered.
That light which resides in the sun and other luminaries is "mine"— dependent upon me and belonging to me.
That very [consciousness], existing as the impeller within the sun and other luminaries,
"illuminates"— that is, makes manifest— the entire world; such is the meaning of the Gītā Smṛti.
"Neither the sun, nor the moon, nor fire illumines that, reaching which they do not return—that is my supreme abode" (Gītā 15.6). Thus [it is said]. // 23 //
Thus concludes the section on imitation (anukṛtyadhikaraṇa). 6.

Furthermore, in the scriptural passage, "There the sun does not shine, nor the moon and stars; these lightnings do not shine, much less this fire," the fact that bliss—which is apprehended in accordance with such texts—is not illuminated by the sun and other luminaries is stated.
And that [bliss] is remembered as belonging to Viṣṇu alone.

Therefore, Viṣṇu alone is what is to be established by the phrase "this very [thing]" (tad etat), and not the bliss of the knower; with this in mind—and intending that the word "api" in the Sūtra has the sense of a conjunction of arguments—he cites that Smṛti: "Not that... (na tad...).
Here too, the word "iti" is to be construed with "is remembered. Regarding the knower, [it is said] that having gone to "that," having reached which they do not return from it again.
That is my supreme abode;
that very abode the sun does not illumine, nor does it manifest.
Thus, "Śaśāṅka" means the moon. And since this is so, how could this fire be inferior? This is the meaning of the *Gītā*’s traditional teaching (*smṛti*).
By this—namely, in the previous explanation—it is shown that it is not merely by imitation and so forth that [the fire says], "I am your splendor."
Thus, in another Śruti passage, such as the Atharva-veda, it is heard that "it shines following Him who shines," being described as an attribute of Viṣṇu;
however, the word "api" (also) is used for the purpose of combining the Śruti with the Smṛti, as in the verse beginning "That which [belongs] to the sun."

In the second explanation, however, the word "api" (also/even) serves to conjoin both the reason stated in the subsequent sentence— namely, the fact of following after that which shines— as expressed in "tameva bhāntamanubhāti," and the reason stated in the preceding sentence— namely, the fact of not being illumined by the sun and other luminaries— as expressed in "na tatra sūryo bhāti."

And likewise, not only is imitation and so forth— serving as the reason for the primary probandum, which is the nature of Viṣṇu in that which is grasped in accordance with what was stated in the passage "This is that"— heard in such texts as "I am your light and ray," etc.; [but it is also heard elsewhere].
But [the word] "also" (api) is used in the sense that it is also recorded in the Smṛti in the passage beginning with "But when the sun...
Furthermore—since there are not only the two marks mentioned in the first sūtra, but also another [mark] beyond them, namely, "There, [he does not see... etc.

Thus, in the Kāṭhaka passage, the characteristic mark (liṅga) consisting of the state of not being illumined by the sun and other luminaries— which was stated with reference to that [Self] being grasped as favorable— is recorded in the Smṛti as belonging specifically to Viṣṇu in the words "not that.
Therefore, this very [Self] is referred to in the phrase "How indeed may I know That?"
Thus, in this context, two meanings of the Sūtra are stated: that Viṣṇu alone is the subject to be established;
and the meaning of the passage beginning with "Not there" is as follows:
previously, it was stated that Brahman is difficult to know because it does not manifest clearly.
Why is that? To this, the following is said: for him whose very nature is such bliss, "the sun does not shine there"—that is to say, it does not illuminate that Brahman.
The term "candratārakam" is a dvandva compound in the singular;
likewise, regarding lightning as well, the phrase "na bhānti" means that they do not shine.

Regarding the subsequent phrase, "tameva bhāntam," although Vyāsatīrtha, in his commentary on the *Atharvaṇa-śikhā*, states: "'This is the statement from the Atharvaṇa consisting of this specific title';
[and] 'bhāntam'..."
It has been explained that "it shines" means that the sun and other luminaries shine only by following the Supreme Self (paramātman) who illumines them;
nevertheless, according to the *Ṭīkā*, the word "all" (*sarvam*) [is used].
The splendor of the sun and other luminaries "shines"—
that is, it shines— only by following the Blessed One who is himself shining; [it shines] by the light of that Blessed One.
It should be explained that by means of light, "all this" shines— that is, it is manifested— in the world.
However, since the commentary of Vyāsatīrtha will likely represent an alternative interpretation intended by the author of the Ṭīkā, there is no contradiction with that. // 6 //
Thus ends the section concerning imitation (anukṛtyadhikaraṇa). // 6 //
// 7. The Section on the Dwarf //
It has been stated that Viṣṇu alone is the object of inquiry.
Regarding this, [the scripture says]: "He draws the prāṇa upward and casts the apāna downward;
the All-Gods worship Him, the dwarf, seated in the middle" (Kaṭha Upaniṣad 5.3).
Thus, someone who is the object of worship for all the gods is perceived.
In this section (*adhikaraṇa*), the coordination of the name *Īśāna* is established.
He indicates the connection with the scriptures (*śruti*) and so forth, as well as the subject matter and the doubt, by stating: "It is Viṣṇu alone."
The meaning is that in the *Jijñāsā-sūtra*, it is stated that Viṣṇu alone is the object of inquiry for all those seeking liberation for the sake of attaining mokṣa.
Nor should it be argued that in that context, only the exclusion of non-inquiry (*ayoga-vyavaccheda*) was intended, and not the exclusion of inquiry into anything else (*anya-yoga-vyavaccheda*).

If anything else were also to be desired to be known, that too would entail the consequence of being the giver of liberation; consequently, explanations such as "without the grace of Nārāyaṇa" would be untenable, because the exclusion of connection with anything else (*anyayogavyavaccheda*) is also intended there.
Therefore, the particle *eva* (only) in this context should be explained as conjoining both [the object and the verb].
To the question "What follows from that?", he says: "Therein" (*tatra*).
And this [word *tatra*] recurs; furthermore, the indeclinable *tatra* can also mean "that" (*tat*).

And likewise, regarding that which was previously stated as the object of inquiry for Viṣṇu in the sūtra "Then, therefore, the desire to know Brahman," [it is said] "therein" (tatra) with respect to that state of being the object of inquiry.
Having stated "the ruler of what has been and what is to be," there is the word "someone" (*kaścit*) in the Kāṭhaka passage that records [the word] "upwards."

Īśāna is perceived as the substratum (dharmin). How so? Because he is perceived as "one to be worshipped by all the gods" and as "one to be sought after by them"; such is the construction of the sentence.
Nor should it be argued that even though Vāyu is worshipped by all the gods, this does not entail a loss of Viṣṇu’s status as being worshipped by all the gods;
for even on that basis, the restrictive rule that Viṣṇu alone is to be sought after (jijñāsya) by all those desiring liberation remains unestablished.

Nor should it be argued that the statement "He is worshipped by all the gods" is untenable because the word *viśvedeva* occurring in the Śruti refers specifically to a particular class [of deities]; [for that would be a mere partial application].

Since, if that [word "Īśāna"] were intended to refer to a particular class [of deities], its status as the Supreme Deity would necessarily follow from the fact that no greater excellence of qualities could be established for it;

by this, through the manner of refuting that the word "Īśāna" resides in another, the result is that the state of being the object of inquiry for one seeking liberation (*mumukṣu*) is also refuted as residing in another. Thus, the "contextual connection by way of implication" (*ākṣepikī saṅgatiḥ*) between this [section] and the *Jijñāsā* section is stated.
Likewise, the object known as Īśāna has been indicated; and that is [shown] in the passages:
"In this very way, this prāṇa establishes the other prāṇas, each separately" (Praśna Upaniṣad 3.4) and "This which is the middle prāṇa" (Bṛhadāraṇyaka Upaniṣad 3.5.21).

From the passage beginning with "kuvidaṅga" (Ṛgveda 7.91.1), it is understood that [the deity] is indeed Vāyu, because he is the sustainer of the vital breaths, occupies the middle position, and is the object of worship for all the gods.
Therefore, he said:
Sūtra—Oṃ.
He is known from the Word alone.
Viṣṇu is established as such from the word "Vāmana" itself;
he states the prima facie argument (pūrvapakṣa) along with its reasoning, beginning with "And he... (sa ca).
The construction here is as follows: "And he"—the Lord (Īśāna) who is worshipped by all the gods—must be Vāyu alone, and not Viṣṇu.
Why? Because of the scriptural statement here regarding his being the regulator of the vital breaths (prāṇa).
This is because it is described as being "intermediate" and because it is stated to be worshipped by all the deities.
Nor is it unestablished that these [qualities] reside solely in Vāyu;
for this Vāyu is [described as] "even so is this Prāṇa" (Praśna Upaniṣad 3.4).
By the statement beginning with "He who is this middle one" and "kuvidaṅga" (Ṛgveda 7.91.1), he is understood as possessing the quality of being the regulator of the vital breaths (*prāṇa*).

Regarding the word "ataḥ" (therefore): for it is said in the Kaṭhaka— "A person the size of a thumb resides in the middle of the self, the ruler of what has been and what is to be. (Kaṭha Upaniṣad 4.12).

By this [verse], having described the Lord's majesty— such as His thumb-sized dimension, His possession of the six perfections in their entirety, His abiding in the center of the body, and His sovereignty over the past, future, and present—
the further greatness of that very one denoted by the word "Īśāna" is stated by means of the passage beginning with "ūrdhvam" (above).

In this context, according to our established doctrine (*siddhānta*), the word "middle" (*madhya*)—due to its association with the words "above" (*ūrdhva*) and "behind" (*pratyak*)—denotes a specific location;
it does not signify a state of mediocrity such as being an intermediate deity (*avāntareśvara*). Thus, [the one] who exists in the form called *prāṇa* is "prāṇa."
He "leads upward" the wind called *prāṇa*;
that is, he causes it to rise and impels it with an upward motion.
And in the form of *apāna*, he [leads] the wind called *apāna* "backward."
Because it serves as the cause for the downward expulsion of feces, urine, and so forth,
it "casts out" (asyati)— that is to say, it ejects or impels them—
within that "middle of the body."
"Sitting in the heart" means seated; "Vāmana" refers to Viṣṇu, the leader, for women— being beautiful— are called *vāmāḥ*, and they [the *viśve devāḥ*] lead him.
According to the established conclusion (*siddhānta*), the meaning of the scripture is that "all the gods worship" means they "desire to know.
However, the proponent of the prima facie view (*pūrvapakṣin*), considering this to refer to Vāyu, [interprets] the word "middle" as "this which is the middle one."

Thus, because of the designation in another Vedic text (*śrutyantara*), he states that the term "Lord of the Middle" (*madhyameśvara*) refers to the Lord and not to a specific location. Furthermore, the statement of the six questions, namely "Just as a sovereign (*samrāṭ*) appoints his officials, saying, 'Preside over these villages,'" is to be explained together with this illustrative sentence.
The manner of that is as follows: just as a sovereign emperor, having addressed his appointed officials, issues commands;
how so? "You [should do] these."
"Preside over villages such as Pāṭaliputra";
that is, remain there by virtue of your sovereignty.
"It is exactly so."

"The vital breath (prāṇa) is born from the Self" (Praśna Upaniṣad 3.3); thus, the primary vital breath, described as being born from the Self, "places the others"— the other vital breaths (vāyus), which are distinct and metaphorically designated as divisions of the Self because they are produced by it— in their respective locations, such as the heart and so forth.
The passage from the Bṛhadāraṇyaka Upaniṣad beginning with "He who is this... refers to this very point.

For therein, after first stating that speech and the other [senses] were seized by death, and then declaring the preeminence of the principal vital breath (mukhyaprāṇa) over them because it was not seized—by means of the phrase "Now he did not reach him"—it continues with "He who is this... [and so forth].

By this [statement], among the three sentient beings denoted by the word *prāṇa*— namely Viṣṇu, Vāyu, and others than those two— because Viṣṇu is the highest, the others are inferior, and Vāyu is intermediate; or because of these reasons,

or because of being a secondary lord (*avāntareśvara*), it is stated that the primary vital breath (*mukhyaprāṇa*) possesses a state of neutrality that is not contradictory to its status as the ultimate pinnacle (*kāṣṭhā*) of all-excellence,
but not that it resides in the middle region.

Likewise, in that very same work, in the fourth chapter, in the passage cited in the *Candrikā*: "This indeed is the infant, which is this middle vital breath" (*Bṛhadāraṇyaka Upaniṣad* 4.2.1), Vāyu—in the form of a calf—is said to be the "middle" one, bound by a rope in the form of food, which is Śrī, to a pillar in the form of Viṣṇu; [this occurs] within the house consisting of the subtle body (*liṅgaśarīra*) located in the expanded region known as the gross body (*sthūladeha*). [The verse continues:
"O, how indeed were those blameless gods in ancient times, who grew through our reverence? (*Ṛgveda* 8.72.3).
They caused the Dawn to dwell with the Sun for Vāyu and for Manu when he was oppressed.
Thus, in the Ṛgvedic mantra, "aṅga" is an affectionate form of address;
likewise, those gods who [are addressed] with "namasā" to Vāyu.

Through service and other acts characterized by salutation, they have grown; "the aged" (vṛddhāsaḥ) means those filled with qualities such as knowledge; "the blameless ones" (anavadyāsaḥ) means those free from the blemishes of ignorance, passion, and so forth; and in ancient times, they were accompanied by the sun.
They [the gods] did not [grant it] anywhere; in a secret place, together with the Sun, they [gave it] to the "Manu"—
to the wise one,
to the "unoppressed," who had sought refuge from those afflicted by the sufferings of saṃsāra— to the "Vāyu."
Aiming at the wind, [he says] "the dawn"; *uṣ* means to shine,
[and] *asun*.
"He caused the intellect to dwell [there]";
the meaning of the Vedic text is that he made it have that as its object.
Introducing the aphorism which establishes the final conclusion, he explains it with the words "Therefore" (ataḥ).
"From the word 'Vāmana'";
that is, from the Vedic revelation (śruti) concerning Vāmana.

The particle "eva" (only/just) is used to state the superiority of the revelation over the indicative marks (liṅga), in order to resolve the objection: "Since the marks of Vāyu are present, why should Vāyu alone not be the Lord (Īśāna)?"
As it is stated in the *Sudhā*: "The explanation of the word 'eva' (only) is powerful," as in the phrase "He is known from the word alone" (*śabdādeva pramitaḥ*).
The meaning of the word "tat" (He), which is carried over from the *Samanvaya* Sūtra, is Viṣṇu.
The word *iti* is employed to indicate the subject (*uddeśya*) that is fit for connection with the predicate (*vidheya*)—namely, the state of being Viṣṇu. This word recurs;
moreover, the word *eva* should be applied even after the word *iti*.
The word "anu" has been explained as meaning "followed by. Likewise, because of the Śruti text, "The Ruler of what has been and what is to be" (Kaṭha Upaniṣad 4.12),
the Ruler must indeed be Viṣṇu.

Why? The construction is as follows: from that very word "Vāmana" which is established there with respect to Viṣṇu alone through the two means of great yogic usage (*mahāyoga*) and the usage of the learned (*vidvad-ruḍhi*), and which is heard in the scripture [as] "the dwarf in the middle.
The term "established" (*pramita*) indicates that the scriptural statement is of unimpeded authority (*niravakāśatva*).
By this, it is indicated that the word "iti" (thus) is to be supplied in the Sūtra;
for likewise, in the Śruti passage "the Ruler of what has been and what is to be," the Ruler is [identified with] "that" (tat).

It must be Viṣṇu alone. Why? Because the word *vāmana*, which is well-known in relation to Viṣṇu through both great yogic power (*mahāyoga*) and the conventional usage of the learned (*vidvad-ruḍhi*), has no other application; and because the scriptural passage "In the middle, [he saw] Vāmana sitting" (Kaṭha Upaniṣad 5.3) is more powerful due to its indicative mark (*liṅga*); therefore, the meaning of the Sūtra is that it is Viṣṇu because of that direct scriptural statement (*śruti*).

For the indicative mark (liṅga) is not stronger than the direct statement (śruti). By the use of the particle "eva" in the Sūtra, the superiority of the direct statement is indicated; this is shown by way of negating the superiority of the indicative mark with the words "na hi" (for it is not).
The word "śruteḥ" is in the ablative case.
The particle "hi" indicates the reason, namely, the contradiction with the means of knowledge that will be stated hereafter.
And thus, "hi"; because the indicative mark (liṅga) is not stronger than direct scriptural statement (śruti).
But [the former] is indeed weak.
Therefore, by virtue of this stronger indicative mark (*liṅga*), the meaning is that Viṣṇu alone is Īśāna, based on the word "Vāmana" itself.
[The traditional order of interpretive criteria is: scripture (*śruti*), indicative mark (*liṅga*), name (*samākhyā*), syntactical connection (*vākya*), and context (*prakaraṇa*).

"Each preceding one is stronger; thus is the determination regarding their application," so it is stated in the Skanda Purāṇa. [The author] cites that statement with the intention of addressing the question, "Why is the indicative mark (liṅga) not stronger than the direct assertion (śruti)?"—for if that were the case, it would contradict the statement that the direct assertion is more powerful than the indicative mark: "The direct assertion... and so forth.
In the phrase "iti skānde," the word "because of the subsequent statement" is to be understood as the ellipsis (*śeṣaḥ*).
This connects with the preceding "na hi.
The term *vācaka-śabda* refers to the Vedic revelation (*śruti*).
Alternatively, the unique property (*asādhāraṇadharma*) or the word that makes it known is the inferential mark (*liṅga*).
Appellation (*samākhyā*) is the designation by a common name of something already determined in another context.
It is of two kinds: by way of meaning and also by way of words.

A sentence (*vākya*) consists of words that are independent of other words, sufficient in themselves to fulfill expectancy (*ākāṅkṣā*) through the very words uttered together, for the purpose of pacifying that expectancy.
A topical section (*prakaraṇa*) consists of multiple sentences that establish a single object of knowledge (*ekaprameya*).
The word *tathā* (likewise) serves to include unstated instances of "place" (*sthāna*).
A "place" is a statement that establishes multiple objects of knowledge while being endowed with a single intended meaning.
In this context, it is said: "The sentence, the section, the place, and the designation are likewise [authoritative]."

Accordingly, following the *Anuvyākhyāna*, the sequence of position (*sthāna*) and immediate proximity (*ānantarya*) alone should be accepted as the basis for the designation (*samākhyā*), and not primacy based on the order mentioned here with respect to the sentence (*vākya*) and so forth;
for the order mentioned here is not intended to be significant.

For it is stated in the *Pramāṇalakṣaṇa-ṭīkā*: "The mention [of the means of proof] as beginning with 'designation' (*samākhyā*) follows the statement ‘Direct assertion (*śruti*), indicative mark (*liṅga*), and designation (*samākhyā*)’, which does not intend a specific order.

For this very reason, Jaimini states: "In the case of a conflict between direct assertion, indicative mark, sentence, context, position, and designation, each subsequent one is weaker than the preceding because of its remoteness from the purpose."
He states a sequence different from that mentioned in the Smṛti with the words "each preceding" (*pūrvapūrvam*).
The meaning is "that which was previously indicated.
The ellipsis to be supplied is "contradictory when co-inherent in a single locus" (*ekatra samavetam viruddham*).

"Stronger" (*balīyaḥ*) means exceedingly powerful by its very nature; as in this very section, the *vāmana* śruti mentioned previously is inherently stronger than the *liṅga* mentioned immediately after it.
*Liṅga* is stronger than *vākya*;

for example, in the *Dahara-adhikaraṇa*, [the *liṅga*] which establishes that the small ether (*daharākāśa*) is the direct support of all is stronger than [the *vākya*]: "What is there within it... both heaven and earth are contained within it" (Chāndogya Upaniṣad 8.1.2, 3).
Thus, from the perspective of the statement (*vākya*), the indicative mark (*liṅga*) of Viṣṇu—such as His being "free from sin" (*apahatapāpmatva*) which establishes Him—is more powerful.
A statement is more powerful than context (*prakaraṇa*).

As in the section [of the Brahma-sūtras] beginning with "Because of the vision of light" (*jyotirdarśanāt*), regarding the individual soul (*jīva*): "The light within the heart" (*hṛdyantarjyotiḥ*; Bṛhadāraṇyaka Upaniṣad 6.3.7).

The interrogative statement, "Which is the Self? (Bṛhadāraṇyaka Upaniṣad 6.3.7), which establishes Viṣṇu’s status as light, is more powerful than the context of the individual soul (*jīva*), which serves as the proof for [the soul's] status as light based on the aforementioned statements.
Context (*prakaraṇa*) is stronger than location (*sthāna*).

For example, the section beginning with "From the Self this vital breath is born" (Praśna Upaniṣad 3.3)— which constitutes the primary context concerning the principal vital breath— is more powerful than the entire preceding portion consisting of six questions that establishes the supremacy of Īśvara.

For this very reason, in this particular adhikaraṇa, the sublation by scripture is stated by accepting the characteristics of the principal vital breath, such as its being the regulator of the vital breaths mentioned in the six questions.

Position (*sthāna*) is more powerful than name (*samākhyā*). For example, although the name "Nārāyaṇa-anuvāka" in the passage "May my self consisting of food, vital breath, mind, consciousness, and bliss be purified" (Yājñikī 66) establishes that words such as "consisting of food" refer to the sheaths (*kośa*), the position— consisting of a collection of several contexts devoted to Brahman— is more powerful in establishing their identity with Viṣṇu.
These are precisely the grounds for determining the meaning through scripture and other means.
That which is to be determined by the first type of designation (*samākhyā*) is as follows: the identity of Vaiśvānara with Viṣṇu, based on the designation "Puruṣasūkta.
By the second type, as for example, the identity of Aja, who is mentioned in the Viśvakarman Sūkta, with Viṣṇu, based on the designation "Ambhraṇīsūkta."
To the question "Let it be so; what follows from that?", he says: "In this way" (*evam*).

When there is a conflict among these [means of knowledge] and the earlier one is sublated by the stronger subsequent one, there is "determination through scripture" (*āgamanirṇaya*); the meaning is that the determination of the disputed object of scripture occurs by means of these [subsequent ones].
And that mark belongs to Viṣṇu alone, because he alone is declared to be the vital breath (prāṇa) in the passage: "Thou indeed becamest the vital breath. // 24 //

Granted that the Śruti possesses inherent strength; nevertheless, because the numerous marks (liṅga) cited by the proponent of the prima facie view (pūrvapakṣin) also possess strength, there would be no definitive conclusion due to their equality. To this, he says: "And that... (tacceti).
The meaning is "cast" (thrown).
The word "liṅga" is a singular collective term.
And thus, "that" [refers to it].
The meaning is that the collection of marks (liṅga) cited by the proponent of the prima facie view belongs to Viṣṇu alone, and not to Vāyu.

Thus, even though the marks are numerous, they are all susceptible of other interpretations (sāvakāśa); whereas even a single scriptural passage (śruti) is unambiguous (niravakāśa). Therefore, because of the superior authority of the latter over the former, there is no lack of a definitive conclusion—this is the intended sense.

[Objection: But surely the inferential mark (*liṅga*) has no scope regarding Viṣṇu, because it has been stated by another scriptural text in the form of a name (*samākhyā*) cited by the proponent of the prima facie view (*pūrvapakṣin*) that it resides in Prāṇa alone; to this he says: "Of that very [one]"—namely, "That indeed you... (*tadvai tvam*).

The meaning is that this is because it has been stated in the Śruti that "of Him"— that is, of Viṣṇu— there is the state of being the vital breath (prāṇatva), which is to say, His being denoted by the word "prāṇa.
Thus, [it is said] "for this very reason."

This should also be explained as follows: by stating the application of the term "entirely internal" (*adhyātmika*) here, and by the author of the Sūtras—who, in the phrase "by the vision of the scripture" (*śāstradṛṣṭyā*), asserts that [the Self] refers to the Inner Ruler (*antaryāmin*)—establishing through the exclusion of others that He alone possesses the nature of Prāṇa;
thus, even though a characteristic mark is stated in another Śruti as residing in Prāṇa, there is no contradiction with this.
The intended meaning is that this is because that vital breath (prāṇa) is accepted as being Viṣṇu.

Now, one might object: "Even so, there is a contradiction with the statement of the indicative mark (liṅga) in the Ṛgvedic verse beginning with 'kuvidaṅga,' which refers to Vāyu. To this, too, the same answer applies.

In this view, the term "being the vital breath" (prāṇatva) indicates the nature of air (vāyutva). Thus, in the Antaryāmī section, the author of the Sūtras, while declaring the concordance of all terms pertaining to the divine realm, states that it is Viṣṇu alone who is designated as "the vital breath."
The meaning is that it has been stated that air possesses the nature of being denotable by the word "air.
Thus, the intention is that there is no contradiction with that [scriptural statement] either.
Nor can it be argued that even in the Siddhānta, because the context (*prakaraṇa*) is stronger than the location (*sthāna*), [the conclusion must be] "in this very way"; for...
Thus, regarding the word *prāṇa* occurring in another scriptural passage,
as well as [the passage] "He who is the middle one" (*Bṛhadāraṇyaka Upaniṣad* 3.5.21), and likewise "O, how indeed! (*Ṛgveda Saṃhitā* 1.84.10).

Since it has been stated that the word *vāyu* occurring in the mantra refers primarily to the elemental air, and that even the indicative marks (*liṅga*) mentioned therein refer to that same air—thereby being sublated by direct scriptural statement (*śruti*)—how can there be a resolution by accepting that the words *prāṇa* and *vāyu* found in other scriptural passages refer to Viṣṇu?
For this very reason, the *Candrikā* states: "The middle [term] is also the word *prāṇa*, as in: 'The *prāṇa* goes upward' (Kaṭha 2.2.3)."

Thus, because of the specification of another location for the vital breath (*prāṇa*), it is stated that [the term] refers to Brahman situated in the middle place by means of abandoning that [vital breath], and not to the vital breath denoted by the word "middle" in another scriptural passage.
Therefore: "In this very way, he... (Praśna Upaniṣad 3.4).
It should be stated that this statement was cited as an example of the superior authority of context over position (*sthāna*).

According to the reasoning already explained, since the word "prāṇa" and other such terms occurring in another scriptural passage primarily refer to Brahman, even though the various indicative marks (*liṅga*) reside in their respective inner rulers (*antaryāmin*), it is accepted—by the principle of "drawing together" (*samākarṣa*)—that they may also have another as their primary referent;
thus, there is no inconsistency even if the marks mentioned in another scripture reside in something else.
Nor does it follow that, because the indicative marks mentioned in the *Kāṭhaka* would likewise apply to another [deity], other deities would consequently possess lordship (*īśānatva*) and so forth;
for it is logical to determine that those marks mentioned in the *Kāṭhaka* reside in Viṣṇu by means of a scriptural statement (*śruti*) that admits of no other application.
Now, one might object: even so, how can Īśāna be Viṣṇu, given that the scripture describes Īśāna as being measured by the size of a thumb?
And because that [atomicity] is incompatible with Hari, who is omnipresent;
nor should it be argued that atomicity is untenable for one who is omnipresent like space, as this has already been established—
nevertheless, [the text says] "thumb-sized" (*aṅguṣṭhamātraḥ*).
Thus, because it is illogical to say that [the soul] has only that much measurement,
and because the suffix *mātra* heard in the phrase "thumb-sized" (*aṅguṣṭhamātraḥ*) does not necessarily denote measurement alone;
However, the word *mātra* does not have the sense of restriction (*avadhāraṇa*),
