because in the Smṛti passage, "The body is measured by the thumb in the body; the individual soul (jīva) is measured by the thumb in the heart," the word "measured" (*mita*) expresses only a specific dimension (*parimāṇa*).
And thus, it should not be said that there is no inconsistency;
for if that were the case, then in the scriptural passage "thumb-sized" (*aṅguṣṭhamātraḥ*) from the Kaṭha Upaniṣad (4.12), which speaks of being thumb-sized,
[the phrase] "in the middle of the self" (*madhya ātmani*) [would be contradicted].
Otherwise, the words "in this" (*ityasya*) and "in the heart" (*hṛdi*) would become redundant.

For the mention of the subtle location in the form of the heart there is intended to indicate that [the mind] is limited to that alone. Therefore, this word *mātra* must be accepted as having the sense of restriction (*avadhāraṇa*). As it is said in the *Candrikā*: "Because the word *mātra* has the sense of restriction."
Sūtra—Oṃ.
But with respect to the heart, [the Veda is authoritative] because it has humans as its qualified recipients.
Even though He is omnipresent, His being the size of a thumb is appropriate with respect to the space within the heart.

Thus, the objection that the description of Hara as being "the size of a thumb" is untenable because He is omnipresent—and therefore that Īśāna here cannot be Viṣṇu—is refuted by introducing and explaining the words of the Sūtra: "In the heart...
By the phrase "even though He is omnipresent," the word *tu* (but) is explained as having the sense of "although... nevertheless."

By the phrase "with reference to the heart" (*hṛdyapekṣayā*), he shows the probandum (*sādhya*) which is compatible with the reason (*hetu*) indicated [by that phrase]. He does so by saying "of him" (*tasya*).
The construction is as follows: although Viṣṇu is omnipresent, nevertheless, "his being the size of a thumb"—that is, the statement that he is the size of a thumb—is appropriate.

How so? Because [the text says] "in comparison with the space existing in the heart" (*hṛdi vidyamānāvakāśāpekṣayā*). In comparison with that space existing in the heart—a region measured by the size of a thumb—and in comparison with that particular form of the Lord manifested therein which is likewise measured [by a thumb], that Viṣṇu possesses the state of being "thumb-sized.
Thus it exists.
Alternatively: "In view of the space within the heart";

that is, with reference to the space existing in the heart, the statement that He is the size of a thumb is appropriate due to its connection with that [space]. This is the interpretation without repetition (*āvṛtti*).

In the first position, although the Blessed One is unlimited in power, the description of Him as being the size of a thumb is made through metaphorical usage (*upacāra*) based on His connection with the Brahman who resides in the specific form (*mūrtiviśeṣa*) as the individual (*vyakti*), which serves as the locus; this is the distinction.

In this commentary (*ṭīkā*), having treated the *bhāṣya*— which states "with reference to the space within the heart"— as being restrictive, the word *tu* in the Sūtra is explained as serving the purpose of restriction.
By this, it is stated that Viṣṇu’s being the size of a thumb is only with reference to the heart, and not because he is limited in size like worldly objects.

Or, by way of metaphorical designation (*upacāra*), based on the specific manifested forms (*vyaktamūrti-viśeṣa*) in their respective locations, there is the statement of having those respective dimensions, as in the Chāndogya Upaniṣad: "But he who [knows] this very one as the size of a span (*prādeśamātra*)," (Chānd. 5.18.1), and elsewhere, "the Person of the size of a span," and "the Supreme Person is the span."

Furthermore, because Viṣṇu residing in the heart is described as being limited to the span of a span (*prādeśa*) elsewhere; and because in another Śruti text it is said, "The Person is thumb-sized, and he rests upon the thumb" (Mahānārāyaṇa Upaniṣad 16.3), and also, "The Person is thumb-sized."

Thus, the objection regarding the contradiction— arising from the statement in the Kaṭhavallī, "The Person is the size of a thumb," and from another passage stating the measurement as "the size of the tip of a thumb"— is thereby resolved.

For within the body, in the space of the heart— that is, in the space located at the base of the pericarp of the lotus situated in the heart— there is the possibility of the manifestation of a specific form measuring a span (prādeśa), and in the space at the tip of the pericarp, there is the possibility of the manifestation of another form measuring the size of a thumb-tip; furthermore, it is possible for the attributes of those respective locations to be metaphorically attributed to that which occupies them.

As it is stated in the Bṛhadāraṇyaka-bhāṣya: "The Supreme Person (Puruṣottama), who is all-pervading within the heart and is eternal in every respect, is designated as the abode of all living beings."
Situated at the base of the pericarp of the heart and measuring the size of a thumb-tip, he is named Mūleśa; in him all living beings are established.
"When Hari, the person the size of a thumb, resides at the tip of the pericarp, they enter [into him] during deep sleep, and likewise awaken from him. Thus it is said.

In this context, one must distinguish that the state of being the size of a thumb exists between Mūlādhāra and Vyāpinī; within the body, it is measured by the thumb of the body, and within the heart of the individual soul (jīva), it is measured by the thumb of the soul. Furthermore, it should be understood that the statement in the *Prameyadīpa*, "And he rests upon the thumb," expresses that [the Self] is the presiding deity over the organs of action (*karmendriya*).

Now, from such statements as, "Viśva is in the right eye and the mouth; Taijasa, however, is within the mind," it is established that Viśva, Taijasa, and Prājña—the impellers of the states of waking and so forth—exist in the right eye and other locations respectively.
If this is so, then the individual soul (jīva) likewise resides in the right eye during the waking state, in the region of the throat during dreaming, and in the heart during deep sleep.
Because of the statement: "The individual soul (jīva), though situated far away from the Supreme who resides in the heart, comes to the state of waking";
the meaning of this is that while situated far away—namely, residing in the eye—it experiences the state of waking.
Thus, how could the form of the Lord, which is the size of a span and pervades the heart, always be the locus of the individual soul?
And how is it that the individual soul (jīva) is always established in the form of the Blessed Lord located at the base of the pericarp of the heart?
If it is argued that there is a scriptural statement that during deep sleep the soul enters Hari who has gone to the tip of the pericarp of the heart—that is not so;

because it is accepted that the very nature of the soul, while always situated in the heart, is present in a specific manner even in the eyes and other organs during the waking state and so forth, like the light of a lamp.
As stated in the Aitareya Bhāṣya: "The very form of that [Self], though residing in the heart, becomes specifically present in the eyes and other organs even during the waking state.

This is because the divine forms (mūrtis) of the Lord—which, although omnipresent through their power, reside in various places as individual manifestations—exist in manifold ways within a single body due to the difference in their purposes, namely, the functions known as establishing, supporting, and inducing sleep for the one and only living soul (jīva).
And since it is logical that [the thumb] possesses various small dimensions, there is no inconsistency whatsoever.
Furthermore, although other living beings lack a thumb, there is no contradiction because the [Vedic injunctions] pertain specifically to human beings. // 25 //
Thus ends the section concerning the dwarf incarnation (Vāmanādhikaraṇa). // 7 //
But even so, it is not logical that Viṣṇu possesses the size of a thumb.
For instance, does that "thumb-sizedness" mean being the size of that specific thumb [of a particular animal], or being the size of some thumb or other?
It cannot be the first, because since animals such as cattle lack thumbs, it would be impossible for Viṣṇu residing within them to be measured by a thumb.
The second [alternative] is not tenable;

for the statement that [the soul] is "the size of a thumb" is intended for the purpose of meditating upon it as such by various [practitioners], and since this would be impossible without determining a specific individual thumb, the statement of being "thumb-sized" would be meaningless.
Furthermore, even the commonality of being "thumb-sized" could not possibly apply to one residing in the heart of an ant or similar creature. Thus, he [the author] dispels this doubt.

Regarding the remainder of the sūtra, "Because [the scripture] has humans as its qualified subjects," he explains it by first demonstrating its connection, intending that the word "but" (tu) follows here according to the maxim of the crow’s eye (kākākṣinyāya), and that it also possesses the sense of "also" (api). He does so with the words: "Itareti... (The others...).
The meaning is "of cattle and so forth. The word "api" (also/even) recurs. This term "the size of a thumb" follows after the word "vipariṇāma" (transformation).
The word "no contradiction" (*na virodhaḥ*) is drawn from the aphorism on contradiction;
and likewise, [the word] "even" (*api*).

Even if it is accepted that [the Lord] is measured by the thumb of each respective being, there is no impossibility in the statement that Viṣṇu is "thumb-sized," for this does not contradict His thumb-sized nature even in the absence of thumbs in other living beings.
Why? Because the statement regarding His thumb-sized nature pertains to this specific meditation (vidyā), as it is directed toward human beings;
that is, it has proceeded with reference to humans.
Why is that so?
Because the study and practice of Vedic knowledge has "human beings as its qualification";
the construction of the phrase is: because it has human beings in general as its qualification.

In the Sūtra and the Bhāṣya, "human qualification" (*manuṣyādhikāra*) refers to that in which humans have the qualification; or, alternatively, it is called *adhikāra* because one is qualified therein—meaning either meditative practice (*upāsana*) or the scripture (*śāstra*). The analysis of the compound is: "the state of having human qualification" (*manuṣyādhikāra*), and [the reason] is "because of that state," i.e., "because of having humans as the qualified subjects" (*manuṣyādhikāritvāt*).
In this reading, that [scripture] in which humans are the qualified [practitioners] is described as such;
thus, the meaning is "because it has humans as its qualified practitioners.
Furthermore, by the logic to be stated later, the word "human" (manuṣya) refers to sentient beings whose nature consists of reflection (*manana*) and so forth.
Therefore, by the logic to be explained hereafter, the qualification for this knowledge is established for the gods, Jaritāri and others, who are eligible for Vedic learning.

In that regard, since Jaritāri and the others are each the size of their own thumb, it is possible for them to perform the worship of the Lord; thus, their qualification consists solely in the knowledge of the meaning of the sentences produced by this specific branch of knowledge (*vidyā*).
Nor is this the case even in the context of *upāsanā* (meditative worship).
For this very reason, the *Ṭīkā* states that "humanity" (*manuṣyatva*) is mentioned as a pervading condition, because only humans possess the qualification for the practice of Vedic knowledge.

Furthermore, it should not be argued that for non-qualified beings such as animals, the Lord residing within the body would lack the measurement of a thumb-sized dimension, and since no other measurement is mentioned, He would consequently fall into the state of being a non-substance (*adravyatva*).
Because the Supreme Self, when residing in bodies such as those of animals, possesses the dimensions corresponding to those respective forms;
as it is stated in the *Aitareya-bhāṣya*: "Saṅkarṣaṇa and Pradyumna, possessing those [human] forms, reside among men;
Nārāyaṇa and Aniruddha, however, possessing the forms of animals, reside in animals."
By this [statement]: in the Sūtra, the word *tu* has the senses of "also" (*api*) and "restriction" (*avadhāraṇa*). In that case, the sense of "also" connects with both [parts].
The ellipsis is to be supplied as: "it is logical that [the Lord] is the size of a thumb."

The word "tat" (that) is connected here by modification with what has been carried over from the principal sūtra; there is no contradiction, as the term "na" (not) is drawn forward [from that context]. [This refers to the statement:
"Because that [Veda] has humans as its qualified subjects."
Thus it recurs. And likewise, even though He is all-pervading, the statement that "that Viṣṇu is the size of a thumb" is appropriate.
And there is no contradiction;
for in this context,
it is stated that the size of a thumb is spoken of solely with reference to the space within the heart, as indicated by the phrase "but with reference to the heart."
But it is not so because of being limited;
and that [limitation] is appropriate either metaphorically or because the state of being of that measure exists in a particular form.
Furthermore, the state of being thumb-sized is not appropriate for Viṣṇu.

It should not be argued that because the statement "being the size of a thumb" (aṅguṣṭhamātratva) would otherwise be rendered meaningless or impossible, Viṣṇu must be described as being the size of the thumb of each respective being; and since animals and the like lack thumbs, it would be inappropriate for Viṣṇu to reside within them.
For [the word] "tu" means "even," and thus there is no contradiction in Viṣṇu’s being the size of the thumb of each respective being, even in the absence of thumbs in other living beings.
It is impossible.

Why? Because the statement regarding the size of the thumb-sized [Self] pertains to the knowledge that makes it known, since that [knowledge] is "for the sake of human beings" (manuṣyādhikāratvāt), meaning it proceeds by authorizing only human beings.
Why is that so?
Because "of that"—namely, the study and meditation on Vedic knowledge—"there is eligibility for humans";
that is, because there is eligibility for all human beings—thus the meaning of the Sūtra has been stated.
Thus ends the section on Vāmana. // 7 //
// 8. The Section on Deities //
It has been stated that the qualification for the knowledge of the Vedas belongs to humans alone.
In this section, the qualification of the gods for the knowledge of Brahman is established.
Since this is incidental, no need is felt to seek its connection with the chapter or the section.
He shows the connection with the scriptures and so forth, the subject matter, the doubt, and its seed, by saying: "Of human beings."
It was stated in the preceding sūtra.

With the intention that the restriction expressed by the word *tu* (but/however) also applies to the word *manuṣya* (human) which has entered into the compound, there is the restatement "of humans alone. The meaning of the word *eva* (alone/exclusively) is "not of others."
"Entitlement to the knowledge of the Veda" means entitlement to the practice (*upāsanā*) of the knowledge of the Veda.
By this— by way of the absence of entitlement to [the worship of] deities— it is shown that "all the gods worship [it]."

Because the validity of all the scriptures—exemplified by the previously cited scriptural passages such as these—is challenged [by the previous argument], there is an "introductory connection" (*ākṣepikī saṅgati*) between this section and the preceding one; furthermore, the subject matter known as "the eligibility for Vedic knowledge" has thus been stated.
[The phrase] "of humans alone" is based on the scriptural passage: "thumb-sized."

Because of the statement "thus they say" and the Śruti text "all the gods worship [it]" (Kaṭha Upaniṣad 2.2.3), which present two opposing sides and thus serve as the seed of doubt, the doubt as to whether or not the gods possess the qualification [for knowledge] is indicated by that very statement, as is the prima facie view (pūrvapakṣa) that they do not possess it.
The qualification "humanity" is stated specifically with reference to animals and the like, and not with reference to gods and so forth.
To this he says: "Then what [follows]? Thereupon, in order to resolve the seed of doubt and establish the final conclusion, he introduces the aphorism: "Animals and the like..."
The meaning is that it is for the purpose of excluding animals and others who lack distinguished cognition and so forth.
The qualification "humanity" (manuṣyatva) is intended with an exclusive emphasis.
The word "human" (manuṣya) is "stated," that is, employed.
In this context, the remainder [of the sūtra] is as follows;
its meaning is "in the preceding sūtra. He shows that which is excluded by the particle *eva* used in its own [sūtra], stating: "but not... (*na tu*).
"‘In comparison with gods and so forth’ means for the purpose of excluding gods and the like. The word ‘tu’ (but/however) serves to indicate a distinction."
Or rather, the meaning of the word "also" (api) is that [the qualification] does not apply even for the sake of the gods and so forth.
"'Thus he says' means that, with this intention, the author of the Sūtras states that the gods possess the status of being qualified.
Sūtra: Oṃ.
Bādarāyaṇa [maintains] that there is [the possibility of such knowledge] even beyond that, because it is possible. Om. 1.3.26.
"Beyond that" means beyond the attainment of the state of gods and so forth by those who are human beings;
for it is possible for them [to attain it] because they possess distinguished intelligence and other such qualities.
He recites that sūtra: "Beyond that."

Here, having restated the word "tadupari" (upon that), which indicates the subject of the thesis (*sādhyadharmin*), he explains it by relying on the analysis (*vigraha*) "teṣām tasmāt tasyāḥ" (of them, from that, of her)—that is, "tadupari."
The phrase "the author of Vedic knowledge" is to be supplied [to the end of the sentence].
The meaning of the particle *api* is that this applies not only to those who are human beings, but also to those above them.

And likewise, "of them"— meaning of those living beings who, while being human, are worthy of the state of divinity— before they attain that status, while they have yet attained the human body, "from that," i.e., from their human condition, "above."

The construction is as follows: even at a later time "after the departure from the human body"—that is, after attaining the status of a god, a celestial deity, and so forth—those who have attained the state of a god still possess the eligibility for the knowledge of the Vedas.
To the question "Why?", he explains the reason by stating: "because it is possible on account of that being the cause."
The word ‘hi’ [means] ‘because’;
it is also connected here with the phrase ‘the qualification for Vedic knowledge.’
Regarding the phrase "of them," that is, of those gods:

since one might ask from where their capacity for authority arises, he applies the very same expression "because of the possibility here as well" as the reason, by repeating it, in the words "by the distinguished... etc.
The word "of them" (teṣām) is also to be construed here. And thus, "of them"— that is,
of those fit human beings who have attained the state of gods and so forth through knowledge and ritual action— "because of the possibility" (sambhavāt).

The meaning is: "Because of the existence of distinguished cognition and so forth," that is to say, because of the existence of specific states of cognition such as the apprehension of objects and the application of them.
By the word "and so forth" (*ādi*), "desire" (*arthitva*) and "capacity" (*sāmarthya*) are to be included.
Furthermore, regarding the statement "nor is there an absence of desire," the reason remains the same: "for those [qualities] are indeed possible."
The meaning of that is: "Indeed, the attainment of liberation for them is possible through knowledge.
By this, the word "that" (tat) is repeated in the sutra;
it refers both to human beings and to what is present in the mind.
The word *api* is used in the sense of conjunction (*samuccaye*). The term "subject matter" (*adhikāra*) is mentally extracted and connected here [to the word *anadhikāra*].
The mention of the name Bādarāyaṇa is intended to indicate the disagreement between Jaimini and Bādarāyaṇa regarding the expression of what is not a subject matter and what is a subject matter.

Or rather, it may be said that Bādarāyaṇa himself speaks thus in order to make known the intended meaning according to the *Tattvapradīpa*, and for the sake of strengthening the understanding of the additional qualification;
and the word "sambhavāt" (because of the possibility) is repeated.

And so, since it is not only for those souls capable of attaining the status of gods and others that there is eligibility [for the path] while they exist as humans on earth for some time prior to attaining that station, but rather even in that very state...

But "even beyond that": therefore, even beyond the state of humanity— that is, after transcending it— by means of those two, namely knowledge and action, even for those who have attained the status of gods and so forth at a time subsequent to that attainment of the state of divinity, there certainly exists eligibility for Vedic knowledge.

Nor is there an absence of the causes for that [qualification], because they "are possible"; for specific intellect (*viśiṣṭabuddhi*) and other such qualities conducive to qualification are possible in them.
Nor should it be said that even though gods and others possess the capacity for specific intellect, they lack qualification due to an absence of desire (*arthitva*).
Why? "Because of the possibility" (*sambhavāt*);

that is, because the possibility of desiring both knowledge—which is to be accomplished through *vidyā*—and liberation exists [in humans]. This is the meaning of the sūtra as intended by the venerable Bādarāyaṇa. For animals and others, however, there is an absence [of such desire] due to the absence of those two.
Even for them, there is no contradiction in those cases where there is the presence of distinguished intellect and so forth.
Now, one might object: "The gods are not eligible for Vedic knowledge;

for if that were so, the use of the word *manuṣya* (human) in the Sūtra—which serves to exclude non-humans—would imply an inference that the gods are ineligible for Vedic knowledge because they are non-human (*amanuṣyatva*), just like animals and the like, and this would lead to a contradiction. To this [the author replies]:
He said: "Of animals and so forth."
By the word "etcetera" (ādipadena), immobile beings or dull-witted humans are included.
"Due to the absence of that" means due to the absence of specific cognition and so forth; "absence" [refers to the lack of such qualities].
Regarding that qualification for the knowledge of the Vedas:

by stating here that the absence of such qualification is caused by the lack of specific intelligence and so forth, it is shown that the reason "non-humanity" as asserted by the opponent is *sopādhika* (vitiated by a limiting condition); that is, it is seized by the counter-argument known as the "absence of the upādhi," which establishes the absence of the probandum (*sādhya*).

The meaning is that the word *manuṣya* (human) in the Sūtra, being intended to denote a nature characterized by thinking (*manana*) and so forth, excludes only that conscious entity which is devoid of specific intellect (*buddhi*) and the like, but not merely that which is different from a mortal; thus, there is no contradiction.
[Objection: But surely, the absence of specific intellect and the like is a limiting adjunct (*upādhi*).
Because [the reason] lacks the status of being a pervader of the probandum (sādhya) in the form of the absence of entitlement among animals;
for this very reason, even the absence of that [reason] is not a reason for the exclusion of the probandum (sādhyavyatireka-hetu). Therefore, he says: "Of those too... (teṣām api iti).
The word "api" (also/even) connects with both [cases].
Therein, the first [usage] is in the sense of conjunction; the word "adhikāra" (heading/section) is to be supplied as the remainder.

And thus, there is no contradiction not only in the case of the gods, but also in the case of "them"—that is, even for animals—having the qualification [for Vedic study]. Now, one might ask: how can there be no contradiction regarding animals, since it would result in a conflict with the Manu-smṛti if there were universal qualification for the Vedas among animals? To this, he says: "teṣām api" (even of them).
The meaning is "even among animals.

"Where" means in those [beings] where there exists the state of passion and so forth, characterized by specific intelligence and desire; in that very existence, regarding their eligibility, there is "no contradiction," meaning no contradiction with authoritative scripture (*māna*).
The meaning is that there is no sublation (bādha) everywhere.
By this "api" (also), it is indicated that the word "api" from the Sūtra also includes [the views of] Jaritāri and others.
As the author of the *Tattvapradīpikā* said: "'Teṣām api' etc. is the explanation of the word 'api'."
Ānandamālākāra also says: "Even certain animals are included by the word 'even'";
and thus, since there is indeed eligibility even among animals distinct from humans, non-humanity is not the reason for the absence of eligibility because it is subject to deviation (*vyabhicāra*).
Rather, the lack of specific intellect and so forth alone is the reason, as it is free from deviation.
Therefore, that qualification (upādhi) indeed exists;
for this very reason, it is logical that there should also be a restriction of the excluded scope (vyāvartyasaṅkoca) for the word "human" in the Sūtra.
This is because there is no prohibition [to the contrary].
For Jaritārya and others are indeed seen [to have attained such states]. // 26 //

Now, one might object: "How can there be no contradiction even if animals possess eligibility [for knowledge], given that their exclusion from eligibility or the observation of such [exclusion] would be contradictory? Anticipating this doubt, he says "niṣedha... (regarding the prohibition), stating that the first point is not the case.
The word "of them" (teṣām) is also connected here;
it should be joined with "in the case of eligibility" (adhikāre) and so forth.
Therefore, in the absence of prohibitions, the possession of specific cognition and so on is itself the determinant for eligibility.
It is indicated that this is not the case alone, lest there be a deviation (vyabhicāra) in the instance of a Śūdra and so forth.
He states "na dvitīyaḥ" (not the second [alternative]) and says: "For they are seen... (dṛśyante hi).
The word "as" (*iti*) implies "by virtue of being entitled to the Vedas.
The particle "hi" indicates well-known tradition from the *Mahābhārata* and other sources.
For this very reason, it is stated in the *Mahābhārata*:
Thus addressed by his brothers, Jaritāri, with palms joined in reverence, offered praise to Vibhāvasu; hear that, O lord of men.

By such statements, it is established that among the birds known as Jaritāri, Sārisṛkka, Stambamitra, and Droṇa, Jaritāri— the eldest— being entreated by his brothers to release them, praised Agni with the *Āgneya-sūkta* beginning with "O Agni, this singer [praises you]" (*Ṛgveda* 10.142.1), and thereby saved his brothers from being consumed by fire during the burning of the Khāṇḍava forest.
Alternatively, the particle *hi* is used here in the sense of "because."
In this context, the reading "jaritāryādayaḥ" is appropriate,
and not the short-vowel reading "jaritaryādayaḥ," because the latter contradicts the *Mahābhārata*.
It should be understood that this is because it contradicts the *Tattvapradīpa*.

By the phrase "for they are seen," the probans (*upādhi*) of "humanity" is refuted in the inference favored by the proponent (the Siddhāntin), which is: "The gods are qualified for Vedic knowledge, because, while being free from prohibitions, they possess specific intellect and other faculties, like such-and-such mortals."
Because [the reason] does not pervade the probandum in the case of Jaritāru and others—such as Sārisṛkka and so forth—who are included by the word "and so on" (ādi)—the aphorism states: Oṃ.
If it is argued that there is a contradiction regarding action, we say no, because we observe the attainment of various [results].
It has been stated that "above that" [refers to] humans becoming gods and so forth.

If it is argued that there is a contradiction regarding ritual acts dedicated to the deities—on the grounds that if humans, while remaining human, become gods and so forth, they would lack the status of a deity prior to that transformation—[the author] reads the Sūtra which resolves this by challenging the notion of their having a beginning (sāditva) for the sake of establishing the eligibility of gods for Vedic knowledge, and first explains the portion concerning the objection: "There is a contradiction."
"Only humans" means that living beings who are destined for the state of gods and so forth were previously humans on earth for some time, and only then do they become gods and so forth;
the meaning of the word "only" (eva) is that this does not happen without the state of being human.
Thus it has been said.
Regarding the phrase "it has been said here," the ellipsis is "that is incorrect.

To the question "Why?", he explains the portion beginning with "contradiction" (virodha), which aims to state the refutation of that position, along with its reasoning: "In that case, if... and so forth.
The passage beginning with "yadi" and ending with "bhavanti" is a restatement of the meaning of the preceding sentence, intended to demonstrate its logical necessity (*apādakatva*).
In this context, the indeclinable "tatra" has the sense of "then" (*tarhi*) and should be construed after the word "bhavanti.
Alternatively, the passage ending with "manuṣyā eva devādayo bhavanti" is a restatement of the meaning of the preceding sentence, intended to demonstrate its logical necessity.
In this context, the indeclinable *tatra* means "then" (*tarhi*) and is to be construed after the word *bhavanti*.

Alternatively, in order to dispel the doubt regarding non-difference that might arise from the statement "human beings themselves become gods and so forth," he explains his own words beginning with "human beings themselves" by saying "therein" (*tatra*).
Alternatively, there is grammatical coreferentiality (*sāmānādhikaraṇya*) between "there" (*tatra*) and "rites dedicated to the deities" (*devatoddiṣṭakarmani*).
In this view, since the word "if" (*yadi*) is heard, the word "then" (*tarhi*) is understood;
and after the word "occur" (*bhavanti*), the phrase "it has been stated" (*ity uktam*) exists.
In both cases, the word "etc. (*ādi*) includes Upadevas and others.
The term "object" (*karman*) also implies "sound" (*śabda*).
Thus, if it is said that those who were previously human beings later become gods and so forth, [then this is the case].
In that case, regarding the phrase "prior to that" (*tatpūrvam*):

prior to them, that is, prior to their attainment of the state of gods and so forth, while they are in the stage of being a means of accomplishment (*sādhakatvāvasthāyām*), because of the "non-existence of the deity" (*devatābhāvāt*)—
that is, because the deity does not exist— at which action it was stated that the status of a god and so forth is to be accomplished?
The construction is as follows: "there," that is, in that very "rite dedicated to a deity"—
a rite performed with reference to a deity in a previous kalpa— and in the "word denoting the deity," there is "contradiction," meaning the futility of those two.
The sense is that [the objection arises] because of the absence of a thing to be designated (*uddeśya*) and the absence of a thing to be expressed (*vācya*).
This is not so, because we observe the comprehension of multiple words denoting deities; as it is said:
"Those great ones attain the heavenly world."
"Wherein the ancient Sādhyas, the gods, abide. // 27 //
He explains the portion of the refutation with the words: "No."
And this [verse] recurs. The construction, however, is as follows: there is no contradiction regarding the object [of the action]; why?
because the state of being a deity did not exist previously.

The sense is that, because their stream is beginningless, even though these particular gods may not have existed previously, other deities did exist. Nor is there a lack of evidence for this; therefore, in order to dispel the misconception that the word *pratipatti* means "knowledge"—which would imply the aforementioned multiplicity [of cognitions]—he explains it by first demonstrating its connection [to its object], saying:
"of many."

In the Śruti passage, "of them" (*teṣāṃ kāmaḥ*), [the word] "of many" (*anekānām*) means that it is observed that, in groups of one by one, infinite humans who are fit for divinity and so forth attain the state of various preceding deities through knowledge and ritual action.
If it is argued that what was stated in the passage "above this" (anenaitadupari)—namely, that the finitude (*sāditva*) of the gods is untenable—is incorrect;

and that if that were so, then regarding the action by which the status of being a god and so forth is to be accomplished, there would be a contradiction in both that action and the word [denoting it], resulting in its futility because the state of being a deity would not have existed prior to it—[we reply]: No.
Since there was no state of being a deity previously, how is that so? Even though these particular deities did not exist previously, other deities did exist; nor is there a lack of evidence for this.

The meaning of the sūtra is stated as follows: "Because the attainment [of the goal] by many is observed"; that is, because it is stated in the passage "they indeed go to the heavenly world" (*te ha nākam*) that many qualified persons attain each preceding stage.
In the Śruti, in the preceding passage, "By means of sacrifice the gods sacrificed to the Sacrifice;
those were the first dharmas," the gods under discussion are referred to by the pronoun "those" (tāni).
The word *ha* signifies "furthermore" or "well-known.
Thus, those who are "non-gods"—
that is, humans capable of attaining divinity— by means of "sacrifice," which consists of knowledge and action;
They "sacrificed" to Viṣṇu; that is, they worshipped him.
Then, having attained the state of the gods through that action preceded by knowledge, [they attained] the "first" [worlds].

The "first" ones mean the primary; they were the "laws" (dharmas), the sustainers of the world. The "greatnesses" (mahimānaḥ) means the great-souled ones, or those whose nature consists of the quality of greatness.

Then those gods, subsequently at the conclusion of their respective offices, [attained] the "nāka"; "ka" means happiness, while "aka" is that which is other than it, namely suffering; that which is not so (na-aka) is "nāka."

By means of the two negative particles (*nañ*), the state of being "consisting of perfect bliss" is obtained. They "attain" (*sacante*) liberation that is of such a nature; here the present tense (*laṭ*) is used in the sense of the imperfect (*laṅ*).
The forms *laṅvā* and the absence of *etva* and *āḍa* are Vedic (*chāndasa*).
"Where" means in liberation; "in former times" means those liberated in a previous kalpa; "the Sādhyas."
The plural number is used in the sense of "and others.
For the upright ones are indeed the chief Brahmins, as well as Suparṇa and Śeṣa;
Sarasvatī, Suparṇī, Vāruṇī, and those named Sādhyas.
Thus, the meaning of the Vedic scripture is that the deities beginning with the Sādhyas exist.

Furthermore, among the Vasus, Rudras, Ādityas, Maruts, and Sādhyas, since the Vasus come first, one should have said in the commentary "the deities beginning with the Vasus" (vasvādi-devāḥ) rather than "beginning with the Sādhyas" (sādhyādi).

Therefore, it should not be argued that the *Tattvapradīpa* states: "The gods, such as Vasu and others, are either to be accomplished (*sādhya*) in the future, or they are already established or liberated";
for this would involve a primary transgression of the sequence of those denoted by the term "to be accomplished."
This is because the *Tattvapradīpa* proceeds in accordance with the sequence of the *Chāndogya-śruti*.
Nor should it be argued that, if explained in this manner, the citation of this passage in the *Puruṣārthādhikaraṇa* as referring to deities who have attained their status would be inappropriate;

for those who, having attained the state [of the Self], became the sustainers of the world—those gods performed the sacrifice with the sacrifice, and they indeed [attained] *nāka*, the excellence of the state of liberation.

This is because the meaning of the Vedic text "sacante" is intended to convey a different sense, which is logically consistent with that [interpretation], and because, in accordance with that, the grammatical derivation in its commentary is also justified. Sūtra—Oṃ.
If it is argued that [the world] is sound, it is not so, because it originates from this [Brahman], as established by both perception and inference.

Because of such Vedic texts as "O Virūpa, with eternal speech" (Ṛgveda 8.64.6), there is no certainty regarding the authorship [of the Vedas], and because the primary means of knowledge depends upon eternity;

and as for that which was stated [in the previous section] regarding the possession of beginning and end for the sake of establishing the eligibility of the gods, that has been refuted by the two verses beginning with "upari" and "aneka".
Having raised that objection and then resolving it by reciting the sūtra, he first explains the portion concerning the objection, beginning with the word "sound" (śabda).

The phrase "there is no contradiction because multiple paths are observed" and so forth is to be supplied [to the previous argument]. If this [phrase] is to be supplied here as well, then the construction is as follows:

if it is argued that there is no contradiction regarding ritual action because we observe that many [persons] attain the state of a deity through successive prior liberations, [then the response follows].
In that case, there would be a contradiction known as invalidity regarding that very word—the Veda—designated by the term "vision" (darśana).
Why? Because the gods are impermanent;
for it has been stated [in the verse beginning with] "aneka... that the gods are impermanent and finite.

Now, one might ask: "Even if the gods are impermanent, why does that entail the lack of authority (*aprāmāṇya*) of the Vedas? To this he says: "Of those uttered by them" (*taduditānām*). This is a qualification containing a reason (*hetugarbha-viśeṣaṇa*).
By this, the reason—"because they denote impermanent gods"—is indicated.
Now, one might object: "Even if the gods are impermanent, it does not follow that the Veda which denotes them lacks authority by way of being devoid of a denotable object;
for, like the gods, the Veda which denotes them is also impermanent, and thus there is never a time when it is devoid of a denotable object. To this, it is said: "Because the Veda is eternal."
To the question "Why is the Veda eternal itself?", it is said: "By speech."
The phrase "from scripture" (śruteḥ) is connected with the statement "because this Veda is eternal.
This [term] is indicative of knowledge (*jñāna*).
By the word "etcetera" (*ādi*), [the qualities] "eternal" and "non-eternal" are included.
The Pauṣyāyaṇa-śruti is cited,
beginning with the passage: "The Śruti is indeed eternal."

Now, it might be argued: "The Veda is not eternal, nor is there a contradiction with the Śruti, because the Śruti has a figurative meaning, in that its sense is 'eternity' in the form of existing for a very long time"; to this as well, he says:
If that were the case, because the Veda would be non-eternal, there would be the contradiction known as a lack of authority (*aprāmāṇya*).

Now, one might object that even if the Veda is non-eternal, its authority is possible on the basis of being rooted in a reliable person (*āpta*); to this he says: "because of the uncertainty regarding reliability" (*āptyaniścayāt*).
The word "of the author of the Veda" is to be supplied [to the end of the previous sentence].
Thus, the meaning is that since there is no proof for the author's omniscience and so forth, there is no certainty regarding the author of the Veda possessing such qualities as omniscience.
Alternatively, even if there were certainty regarding the author's status as an authoritative person (*āpta*), [the argument continues...]
Nevertheless, he states that there is no certainty regarding the Veda being rooted in that [author], saying: "because of the lack of certainty regarding its authoritativeness" (*āptyaniścayāt*).
The word "of the Veda" (*vedasya*) is drawn over from the previous context;
thus, the meaning is: because there is no certainty regarding the Veda’s being based on an authoritative source, in the form of its having been composed by a trustworthy person (*āpta*).

Therefore, since there is no means of knowledge (*māna*) to ascertain its authoritativeness or its basis in such an authority, it would follow that if the Veda were non-eternal, it would lack validity; hence, the intention is that one must not claim that the scriptural statement of its eternity has a figurative meaning.
The eternity of the Veda is established not only by scripture, but also by the inference of elimination (pariśeṣānumāna); thus he says: "By eternity... and so forth.
The logical connection (*anvaya*) is as follows: because the root authority (*mūlapramāṇa*) depends upon eternity, the eternity of the Veda is understood.

This is the underlying point: for the sake of establishing its validity, if the Veda were composed by a reliable person (*āpta*), there must be a root authority [for that person], since it is a rule that anything of human origin necessarily depends upon a root authority.

Otherwise, because of a lack of confidence [in other means of knowledge], that which teaches that sacrifices and the like are means to merit must be rooted in the Veda; for since perception and inference are impossible [in this case], it must by process of elimination be stated to be a verbal testimony (vākya) alone.
Furthermore, if one accepts its impermanence and searches for its source, an infinite regress would result; therefore, its very eternity must be asserted.
Consequently, it is better to simply accept the eternity of the Veda itself.
"Because it is established by scripture," and because the self-evident authority of the Veda is well-known due to its eternity, whereas the gods mentioned therein are non-eternal.

Now, one might object: "Just as the impossibility of validity due to the lack of certainty regarding the author's reliability (*āpta*) serves as a subverting argument against the non-eternality of the Vedas, so too, even if they were eternal, there would be an impossibility of validity because they would not be produced by the quality consisting in being spoken by a reliable person; thus the subverting argument is equal on both sides. To this, he says: "Intrinsic" (*svataḥ*).
The term "of the Veda" (vedasya) is understood to carry over [from the previous context]. And thus,
"of the Veda" means of the validity (*prāmāṇya*)— in the form of the correspondence with reality (*yāthārthya*) residing in the knowledge produced by the Veda— "by itself alone" (*svata eva*).

The meaning is that [the means of knowledge] is established "from the very cause of the cognition in general," that is, because it is logically justified and known through valid cognition (*pramita*).
Alternatively, it refers to the intrinsic validity (*svata eva*) of the instrumentality of the Veda, which consists in its being the cause of true knowledge regarding the objects contained within it.

The meaning is that [the Veda] is established as having the nature of a capacity to produce true knowledge, which is non-different from the innate capacity to serve as the instrument of knowledge (*jñānakaraṇatva*).
This connects with the phrase "because this Veda also has the possibility of being eternal.

Thus, since the eternity of the Veda is established, if the deities who are its denotata were non-eternal, it would follow that the Veda lacks authority due to the deficiency of its denotata; such is the intended sense.
If it is argued that there is no contradiction in the case of sound because there is no necessity for another [sound] to exist, [we reply:

"But surely, just as in a past kalpa, when one deity has ceased to exist, there is no contradiction based on the absence of the intended object in a ritual because another deity may come into existence, so too here, even upon the destruction of one deity, another deity can arise; therefore, the contradiction known as *vācyahīnatva* (deficiency of the denotable) does not apply. To this, he says: "And because there is no necessity for another to exist."
The word "again" (*punaḥ*) has the sense of immediate succession, meaning "immediately after the destruction of the preceding kalpa," or it has the sense of "in the subsequent kalpa.
"The existence of another" (*anyabhāvaḥ*) means the arising of something else.
The meaning is that there is no authoritative evidence for its restriction [to a specific deity].
The intention is that there is a disparity because there *is* authoritative evidence regarding the stream of past deities.

By this, it is stated that since the contradiction regarding the non-existence of a deity at a later time applies equally to ritual action (*karman*) as well, the word "word" (*śabda*) in the Sūtra should be understood as an indicator (*upalakṣaṇa*) for ritual action too.
Nor does this entail the drawing down of the term "contradiction" (*virodha*) here as well, for that would contradict the *Ṭīkā*;

for it is stated in the commentary on the sūtra "tadupari" that the particle "api" is drawn down [from the previous sūtra], and its meaning is that the contradiction regarding the absence of a deity at a later time applies not only to the word but also to the ritual action itself. Thus one must explain it.

This is because [the opponent] does not accept the meaning that the word *ākarṣaṇa* (attraction) serves as the connective term (*anvaya*)— not only for the word *virodha* (contradiction) in the preceding sūtra, but also for this sūtra— as would be required by the interpretation of the *Ṭīkā* regarding the "attraction of the two words *api* and *virodha*.
Alternatively, let it be a *dvandva* (copulative compound).

Nevertheless, there is no inconsistency, because it is not accepted that the particle *api* has the sense of a conjunction of actions (*karmasamuccaya*), since its meaning is accepted as "even though" (*apeḥ svarūpanityatvābhāve 'pītyarthābhyupagamena*).
For this very reason, the *Ṭīkā* states: "even though the gods lack eternity of essential nature."
In this context, there is one *ca* (and) for the conjunction of scripture and inference which establish permanence;
another for the conjunction of the sublation of impermanence and the absence of that [sublation] in the case of permanence;
and yet another for the conjunction of the non-existence of the restriction [that impermanence must be otherwise] and the absence of impermanence—such is the distinction.
"O Virūpa, urge forth with an eternal voice a beautiful hymn of praise for that bull who shines toward the sky" (Ṛgveda 8.64.6).
The meaning of this Ṛg and Yajus mantra has been explained in the commentary on the section concerning "Difference in Nature" (*vilakṣaṇatvādhikaraṇa*).

In this regard, although a contradiction appears—since it is stated in the *Viṣṇutattvanirṇaya-ṭīkā* that "O Virūpa" is an address to one's own self, while elsewhere it is stated to be an address to the sage named Virūpa—there is nonetheless no contradiction, because its meaning is accepted as being an address by the sage Virūpa to his own inner controller (antaryāmin). For it is said in the *Tattvapradīpa*: "The prayer 'Impel me' is directed toward the inner controller of the sage Virūpa."

Even in the view that the vocative is directed toward Virūpa with him as its agent, there is no contradiction, because the meaning of the *Ṭīkā* is accepted as being a call addressed to one's own self, which is to say, one's own individual soul (*jīva*).
Under this view, there will be another interpretation as stated in the *Tattvapradīpa*.

Nor should it be argued that this contradicts the *Nyāyaratnāvalī*, Padmanābhatīrtha’s commentary on the *Viṣṇutattvanirṇaya*, where it is stated: "This is said by Dharma to the sage Virūpa. [This is because that statement refers to a different context.]
First, because it is possible that the mantra was seen by Virūpa immediately after it was seen by Yama, there is no contradiction in the possibility of him addressing himself at that time;
and thus, "O Virūpa, to that showerer (*vṛṣṇe*) who has light (*dyauḥ*) on all sides, [that is,] *abhidyuḥ*."
Or, "to Vṛṣṇe" means "to the one who rains," or "to the exceedingly capable one.

According to the *Tattvapradīpa*, "vṛṣan" means "the most excellent"; thus, it is the dative singular of that word, "vṛṣṇe. [The word] "anūnam" refers to that Blessed Lord (bhagavat), having Him as the object.
"Surely, with the eternal"—
that is, with the word characterized by the Veda which is without beginning or end—
"inspire a beautiful hymn," that is, a splendid praise.
"Prompt me" means "act.
No; for as it is said: "The Creator fashioned the sun and moon according to their prior order" (Mahānārāyaṇa Upaniṣad 5.7).
Just as there is a fixed law regarding time, so too is there a fixed law regarding the gods and other such factors.
Therefore, this universe will never become anything other than what it is.
From such [statements], and precisely because their origin is restricted to those great beings by means of verbal testimony, as well as through direct perception;
he explains the portion concerning the refutation: "No."
There is indeed a contradiction;
and thus the meaning is that there is no contradiction in the Veda consisting of invalidity caused by a deficiency in its denotable object (*vācya*).

To the question "Why?", he explains the reason—"because of their origin" (*prabhavāt*)—by first demonstrating its connection and by interpreting it as referring to the rule of origin through a continuous stream: "Because of the rule regarding their origin" (*teṣāṃ prabhavaniyamāt*).
‘Of them’: of those deities denoted by the Vedas; ‘of the origin’: of their arising through a continuous stream; ‘by necessity’: meaning that they arise with certainty in every kalpa.

And thus, although the gods lack eternity in their individual forms (*svarūpa*), they possess eternity in the form of a continuous stream (*pravāha*); therefore, the meaning is that there is no invalidity of the Veda which denotes them. Now, [an objection is raised]: "The reason (*hetu*) is unestablished due to a lack of evidence. To this, he restates the word *ataḥ* (therefore) and explains it with emphasis: "Precisely for this reason, from the word itself.
If one asks what that word is, it is precisely that very word regarding which the contradiction was suspected.
With the intention that [the lineage] does not come from another who is not of the same nature, he provides an illustration with the words beginning "Sūrya," etc.;
the phrase "even in this kalpa" is to be supplied as the ellipsis.
To the objection that there would be an absence of a progenitor, he says: "For this very reason."
The meaning is that [the source] is from Viṣṇu alone— the element (dhātu) denoted by the syllable *a* and mentioned in the Śruti— and not from any other.
In this view, there is another interpretation of the phrase "from that word" (*ataśśabdāt*).
But surely, because of its connection with the *laṅ* suffix in the word " akalpayat," this scriptural passage refers only to the past;
therefore, it does not establish a rule regarding the origin of the gods. To this he says: "For this very reason.
And thus, just as the Creator fashioned the sun and the moon in the previous kalpa, so too in this kalpa—in this manner, at every kalpa.

The sense is as follows: since the existence of what is called "procreation" for the gods in all kalpas is established by direct Vedic statement (*śruti*), there is no room for the aforementioned objection; for this is established not only by the word "just as" (*yathā eva*)—which, being present in the mind, implies that no ellipsis (*adhyāhāra*) is required—but also by another clear Vedic text (*spaṣṭa-śruty-antara*).

Now, one might object that a statement in the Veda can also occur through metaphorical usage (*upacāra*), and thus that text alone cannot determine the certainty of the rule regarding the origin of the gods; therefore, he explains the portion beginning with "directly perceived" (*pratyakṣa*) by saying "of the great ones" (*mahatām*).
The meaning is "of those who know the past and the future.
This also connects with the phrase "because of the fixed order of their arising.

Now, one might object that since the perception of another is not [one's own] direct perception, there can be no certainty regarding it; therefore, he says: "from the direct perception of the great ones."
Just as the various characteristic signs of the seasons appear in their recurring cycle according to the season,
so too do these same phenomena reappear at the beginnings of the Yugas.
The meaning is: "from the direct statement" (*pratyakṣāt*)— that is, from the perceptible words— of the "great ones," namely the teachers of the *Mahābhārata*.

In this view, the grammatical connection is: "from non-perceptual" means "from certain perception. This is also because of the inference of others that "just as it is now, so too will the gods be hereafter. // 28 //

Now, one might object that because non-yogins lack confidence in scripture and perception, they cannot have certainty regarding the origin of the gods; therefore, [the author] explains the portion concerning inference with the words "just as" (*yathā*).

The meaning is that just as there are gods at the present time, so too will there be gods in future times—this is known through inference by others who are not yogins, distinct from the great ones (the sages).
This also connects with the phrase "from the necessity of their origin" (*prabhava-niyamāt*).

The word "ca" (and) serves to restrict the origin [of the world] and to conjoin the three means of valid cognition known as verbal testimony, perception, and inference, as well as to conjoin other arguments that will be stated later.
As for the form of the inference: the subsequent period of time was possessed of a creator, because it is not a period of dissolution, just like the present period of time.
By this [argument]: if, for the sake of establishing the authority of the gods, their state of having a beginning and an end is admitted,
then in that case, regarding the "Word" (śabda) in the preceding Sūtra, by whose force was the beginninglessness of the succession of preceding deities stated?

If it is argued that, because the Veda is established as eternal in such scriptural passages as "By the eternal word, O Virūpa," there would be a contradiction—namely, the lack of authority characterized by the absence of a subject to be addressed—in both the ritual action and in subsequent kalpas; [the answer is] no. Why?
Because of "origination" (prabhava): since the gods' origination is necessarily regulated in all kalpas, their eternal existence is logically established.
This means that they are eternal by way of their continuous flow;
nor is there an absence of a cause for their arising,
because they originate from Viṣṇu alone.
Nor is there a lack of proof; for [the word] "as" is heard from the word under discussion, namely "dhātā yathāpūrvam" (Mahānārāyaṇa Upaniṣad 5.7). Thus, [it means] "as before."
And because of this clear scriptural statement;
likewise, for the great yogis who know the past and future times, [it is known] "through direct perception," as in the passage: "Just as in the seasons..."

Thus, from the statement of direct perception (*pratyakṣa*)—that is, from the perception of the great ones which apprehends the necessity of the origin of gods in past and future times—and likewise from the inference of others who are not yogis regarding those same [great ones], the meaning of the Sūtra is stated to be that their existence is established.

As for the meaning of the scriptural passage "just as" (*yathaiva*): just as at the end of a previous Yuga or at the end of a Kalpa there is the production of another Yuga or Kalpa, such is the necessity of origin in time.
Likewise, there is a fixed rule regarding the gods, demi-gods, and others, that at the end of each preceding kalpa they must again assume other forms. As it has been said:

"For he, the most worshipful one, creates, protects, and destroys the various Viśvasṛjs, Vibhus, Śambhus, Purandaras, Sūryas, and others; and by his wisdom, he leads those who bow before him to his own state."
Thus [it is said]. The word "in every kalpa" is to be understood as the ellipsis.

Therefore, just as in a previous kalpa, so too in a subsequent kalpa, because of the very rule governing the production of all things similar to those of the previous kalpa, this entire universe arises from Viṣṇu "from somewhere" (kvāpi).
At no time will there ever be anything "unprecedented"— that is, dissimilar to what has preceded it and devoid of the power of the deity— but rather,
it will always be endowed with its very existence.
Alternatively, the meaning is: "this"—the universe consisting of sentient and insentient beings—will not be otherwise than it is now; rather, through name and form, it will remain exactly as it is.
However, in the *Tattvapradīpa*, this scripture is cited under the heading: "Just as there is a restriction of time."
Thus it is recited in reverse order.
Sūtra: Oṃ.
And for this very reason, there is permanence.
For this very reason, and precisely because sound is eternal, the eternity of the succession of the gods is logical. // 29 //
Having recited the sūtra that establishes the eternity of the stream of deities through another argument, he explains it with the words: "For this very reason."
The phrase "for this very reason" is a restatement (anuvāda). Its explanation is: "because of the eternity of the word," that is, because of the eternity of the Veda.

By the use of the particle *eva*, it is indicated that no further reasoning need be sought regarding the eternity of the succession of gods; rather, since the opponent has already stated the eternity of the Veda along with its proofs, this [eternity of the gods] is established precisely from that, as it would otherwise be untenable.
The phrase "precisely because of its eternality" is an elliptical indication (*upalakṣaṇa*);
it should be understood as an explanation of the word "therefore" (*ataḥ*) meaning "precisely because there is no lack of validity, since the means of valid cognition has been established.
Otherwise, the proponent of the prima facie view (*pūrvapakṣin*) might argue for an alternative explanation based on the lack of validity regarding the flow of the gods.
The phrase "and it is logical" (*yuktam iti*) is a statement from the remainder of the Sūtra.
"Logical" (*yuktam*) means established by reasoning known as the impossibility otherwise (*anyathānupapatti*) of the eternity of the Veda.

As for the word "and" (*ca*), since the other reasonings to be combined have already been shown by the words "from verbal testimony, perception, and inference," it is explained by implication as having the purpose of combining those.
For this very reason, the word "ca" (and) was joined in the commentary on the preceding sūtra;
here too, by the word "ca" in the commentary, an alternative explanation is provided based on the eternity of the very nature of the deity denoted by that [word].
For this very reason, it says: "The sun and the moon" (Mahānārāyaṇa Upaniṣad 5.7).

From the very scriptural passage cited beginning with "yathaiva," as well as from the numerous passages concerning dissolution such as "this world he enters at the time of death" (Nṛsiṃhapūrvatāpanīya Upaniṣad 2.5) and "that into which they enter when they depart" (Taittirīya Upaniṣad 3.1), it is understood that the gods, beginning with the Sun, are subject to origination and destruction.

Therefore, since their eternity in the sense of an intrinsic nature is untenable, their eternity must necessarily exist only in the form of a continuous stream; thus, the entire meaning stated in the commentary [the Ṭīkā] has been summarized. Sūtra: Oṃ.
And because name and form are the same, there is no contradiction even in the case of returning, on account of both scripture and tradition.
Because the past and future gods possess identical names and forms, there is no contradiction even if those who have attained their station do not return after liberation.
Now, it may be argued that the authority of the Veda cannot be established even on the basis of the eternal continuity (*pravāha-nityatva*) of the gods.
For instance: did the gods who were liberated in the previous kalpa return again in the subsequent kalpa, or were they others?
Not the first, because liberation is characterized by non-return.
Not the second [alternative];

for if that were the case, even in the absence of a contradiction based on the impermanence of the gods who constitute the substratum (*dharmin*), a contradiction would still arise due to the diversity of attributes such as name and form (*nāmarūpa*);
moreover, because the Veda, which is the expressive word, remains uniform across every kalpa without any variation in its recensional readings.
Otherwise, there would be a contradiction with their eternity;
furthermore, since the deities to be addressed possess various names and forms, the author sets forth and explains the aphorism—beginning with "samāna" (equal)—in order to dispel this doubt.
Here, the term "past" (atīta) refers to what is prior;
the term "future" (anāgata) refers to what is other than that, namely the future and the present.
This [expression] provides both the locus (dharmin) and its counter-correlate (pratiyogin).
"Name" refers to Indra and so forth; "form" refers to the configuration.
Following the [wording of the] Sūtra, the word "and" (ca) should also be supplied here.
The meaning of that [sūtra] is "and because they possess common properties and karma";
the phrase "even in their own words" is the ellipsis.
The statement "even upon liberation and non-return" is for the purpose of indicating the reason for the contradiction suspected by the proponent of the prima facie view (pūrvapakṣin).
The word *api* recurs in the sense of "even though" (*yadyapi*) and "nevertheless" (*tathāpi*).
The word *śabda* exists [in the compound]. Thus, the construction is as follows: "of those who have not attained the stages" (*aprāptapadānām*).
Because the ancient gods have attained liberation— that is, because they have achieved release— there is no contradiction even if they do not return to their own stations,
even if they are no longer present there, and even if others remain in those places.
Therefore, there is no contradiction—known as a lack of authority—in the Veda, even though it is a single type of word expressive of those [deities].

Why? Because even the deities who have passed away or are yet to come possess "identical names and forms" (*samānanāmarūpatva*); that is to say, they are so described because their names and forms are identical—that is, of one and the same kind.
Their state is *tattva*; [the phrase] "from that" refers to this.

However, in the *Candrikā*, based on the *Tattvapradīpa* and others, it interprets the *Sūtra* and the *Bhāṣya* by making a division at the word "āvṛttau" (in the case of returning), and taking "muktyāvṛttau" in the *Bhāṣya* as a single compound. Thus, it explains it either as:

"even though there is a return from liberation in a sequence where, upon one person attaining the state (*pada*), another is liberated from that state, and then yet another attains the state," or alternatively: "even though there is a return from liberation."

The phrase "even upon the repetition of their respective words" (*svasvapadasyāvṛttau api*) has been explained through two modes not mentioned in the *Ṭīkā*, as indicated by the particle *vā* and the observation of the passage:
"'as before' (*yathāpūrvam*)" (Mahānārāyaṇa Upaniṣad 5.7).

Now, since there is no evidence for the identity of name and form among all the gods, the reason [adduced] is unestablished; therefore, he explains the portion beginning with "as is seen" as follows: "Just as..."
The meaning is as stated in the Śruti: "As the Creator [ordained] of old. "Speech, without beginning or end, eternal, was emitted by the Self-existent One."
The names of the sages and the visions found within the Vedas.
In the beginning, that Great Lord fashioned [the world] from the words of the Veda alone.
And because of this traditional teaching (smṛti). // 30 //

But surely, this scriptural passage could also be intended merely to establish a rule for the conceptualization of their respective individual forms; thus, the certainty of the identity of names and forms is not established by it.

Furthermore, even if the stream of deities were eternal, or if they possessed identical names and forms, the authority of the eternal Veda would not be established on the basis of denoting them, because the very possibility of such denotation is untenable.
For it is not possible for the non-human (apauruṣeya) Veda to function with the deliberation, "This deity was spoken of by me up until this point;

from here on, I shall speak of him"; therefore, the portion [of the objection] beginning with "smṛteḥ" (from memory) is established. With this intention, he shows that [portion] by saying "anādi" (beginningless).
To prevent the statement regarding eternality from being merely figurative, it is said to be "without beginning or end";
therefore, there is no tautology.
For this very reason, it is stated in the *Tattvapradīpa*: "It is eternal by virtue of being without beginning or end."
However, it was stated that this is not [the case] merely by virtue of being without end;
rather, it should also be understood as being due to their existence over a vast period of time.
The words "spoken in the Vedas" are to be supplied immediately after the mention of the Vedas.
The word "nirmame" (he created) is to be repeated; "tathā" (likewise) is the ellipsis;
and by that, the word "eva" (indeed/only) is also connected.
And thus, "in the beginning"— at the time of creation— by "the Self-born," the independent Maheśvara, Viṣṇu, [she was declared] "beginningless and endless, eternal."

It is eternal precisely because it is empty of beginning and end; it is not eternal merely by way of metaphorical designation, nor simply through its long duration, nor merely through its lack of cessation.
That which is "spoken"—meaning the form of the Veda—is "uttered," that is, articulated.
‘From those words of the Veda’;
that is, from those very words contained within the Veda,
and not from others.
He, Maheśvara Viṣṇu, "fashioned the names" of the "sages," that is, the gods beginning with Brahmā;
he assigned those very words to them, making it known at the beginning of every kalpa that this word has power (denotative capacity) for this object.

The meaning of the *smṛti* is as follows: "And those"—namely, the *dṛṣṭayaḥ*, which are forms (*rūpāṇi*) seen as described in the Vedas by the sages and gods—"and those" [beings], he created in that very same way, namely, by means of similarity to the forms belonging to the previous *kalpa*.
The word "and" (*ca*) is used in the sense of conjunction (*samuccaye*).
The connection is with the phrase "because of the similarity in form between these two, namely seeing and remembering.
This also serves as an indicator for traditional scripture (āgama);
thus, the meaning is that there is no lack of proof (asiddhi).

By this [it is shown]: even though the ancient gods do not return to their own positions after liberation, and although others different from them do return there, why would there be a contradiction—known as a lack of authority—in the single word that denotes them? Because both the ancients and those others possess "identical names and forms" (*samānanāmarūpatva*) and possess the qualities and duties appropriate to those [names and forms].
Nor is there a failure of the reason (*hetvasiddhi*),
because of the scriptural statement: "Because it is seen," and "As before," [it is] "without beginning or end."
Thus, the meaning of the sūtra, "iti smṛteśca," has been stated.

Here, in the *Tattvapradīpa*, having raised the objection that at the time of dissolution (pralaya) the Veda would lack authority because it would be devoid of a subject matter due to the absence of any deity whatsoever, a resolution is intended: that this is possible because its subject matter is the Lord alone.
Consequently, there is no contradiction or lack of authority arising from the Veda being devoid of a subject matter at any time.
Why? Because Viṣṇu, the primary referent of the word, exists at all times.
Why is this so?
From the word "for this very reason," it is understood that the Lord (Īśa), who is the author of the origin, dissolution, and so forth of those gods, also exists eternally.
And this is evident to the great ones.
Why? "Precisely for this reason";
[it is said that he] "strives for the Supreme Person."
This is understood from the very Vedic scripture beginning with "The poets weave" (Mahānārāyaṇa Upaniṣad 1.3), as well as from inference regarding other [periods].
For instance, just as the gods exist in their present state, so too did they exist at other times; this is known through such inference.

Thus, "for this very reason" means that because sound is eternal, the speaker is also eternal. Likewise, because Viṣṇu possesses identical names and forms [in all incarnations], while others lack this, there is "no contradiction."
There is no contradiction in its being expressible by all words.
Those forms which have names that are "samāna"—meaning similar—are so described; he who possesses such forms is so described, and [the reason follows] from the state of being that.
For those whose forms are other than Viṣṇu’s, there can be no identity of name and form,
due to the absence of the grounds for the application of words;
nor is there a lack of evidence in this regard.

This is because of the scriptural statement, "as before" (*yathāpūrvam*). According to the Śruti, just as previously [the Lord] possessed full knowledge, was entirely independent, and was established in all names and forms, even so did that Creator fashion the sun and the other [worlds].

Therefore, it is established that even prior to the arrangement of the sun and other celestial bodies, there is no contradiction with the authority of the Word (śabda) regarding the dissolution (pralaya).
Having this very point in mind, the commentary (ṭīkā) presents the answer to an objection beginning with the words "And not... (na ca).
And the response, "and because [the scripture] has the past as its object," has also been stated.
Sūtra: Oṃ.
Jaimini [holds that] there is no qualification for those who have entered the state of a forest hermit, because of the impossibility [of performing sacrifices] with honey and other such substances.

Because [the fruits] such as those mentioned in the passage beginning with "Becoming one of the Vasus" (Chāndogya Upaniṣad 3.6.2) are results to be attained, Jaimini considers that the gods who have already attained their respective stations have no qualification for the Madhu-vidyā and other such meditations. // 31 //
But is it not the case that the eligibility for Vedic knowledge is not appropriate for the gods?
For Vedic knowledge is of two kinds: that which has liberation as its fruit and that which has other fruits.
Those with fruits other than liberation are also of two kinds.
This is due to the distinction between the knowledge of Brahman and ritual action.
Among these, the first is, for example, the Madhu-vidyā;
the second is, for example, the Agniṣṭoma-vidyā.

In this regard, it is first of all not tenable that the gods have the qualification for the two kinds of knowledge which have liberation and other fruits as their results; for among the various fruits—liberation and others—that are to be accomplished by those knowledges, some are already attained [by the gods], while others are unattainable, and thus they lack the desire [for them]. Thus, setting forth the sūtra that raises an objection based on the view of Jaimini, he explains it with the words: "In the case of the Madhu-vidyā and so forth... (madhvādiṣu).
By the phrase "the first and so forth," the statement of the learned is intended;
likewise, there is the Vājasaneyaka statement: "Having become a god, one goes to the gods" (Bṛhadāraṇyaka Upaniṣad 6.1.2).
Likewise, there is the statement from another Śruti text, "He attains vigor," and the passage within the second Madhuvidyā: "Having become one of the Rudras" (Chāndogya Upaniṣad 3.7.2).
And such [terms] as these are included.
Because of being a fruit attained and because of being a fruit not attained, there is a distinction in both ways;
this [distinction] applies to both cases.
The phrase "of the words *vasu* and so forth" is the ellipsis [to be supplied].
In that context, by the word "and so forth" (*ādi*), the words *deva*, *rudra*, and others are included.
Alternatively, the term "of the words" (*padānām*) from the expression "of those who have attained the words" (*prāptapadānām*) is mentally separated and connected here as the subject (*dharmin*).
The term *prāptapadānām* is both a *bahuvrīhi* and a *karmadhāraya*;
among these, the former functions as a qualifying attribute containing a causal implication.
The second [word] is connected with both [locations].
"Of the gods" (*devānām*) is either a word supplied (*adhyāhṛta*) in the sūtra or obtained from the context (*prakaraṇa*).
The word *madhu* refers to the first and second *amṛta*-vidyās taught beginning with the passage "Not honey" (*na madhu*).

Here, by the word "etc. (*ādi*), the ritual and meditative sciences (*karma-vidyā*) that have the status of the Vasus and so forth as their fruit, as well as the sciences of speech and so forth mentioned in the Vājasaneyaka, are included.
And this must be repeated;
the reason from the Sūtra, "because it is impossible," should be applied here as well. Its explicit statement is omitted because its mention is achieved simply by stating the proof for it.

Alternatively, since it has already been stated that [the fruit] is impossible because those who have attained [a certain stage] do not obtain a fruit that was not previously attained, the phrase "because of impossibility" should not be added here.

If this is the case, the construction of the commentary (*bhāṣya*) is as follows: In the *Madhu-vidyā* and other meditations, having introduced the passage, "The sun, indeed, is the honey of the gods," it is recorded: "He, knowing this very nectar, becoming one of the Vasus themselves, being satisfied by seeing this very nectar through Agni as his mouth... [and so forth].

In such statements as "of the words," meaning the words *vasu* and so forth; "because they are fruits to be attained," meaning because it is heard that they are fruits to be attained through the meditations (*upāsanā*) taught in the Madhu-vidyā and other sections; and "and of the words already attained."
Because it is "impossible" for the Vasus and other deities to have attained their respective positions—
and thus impossible for them to desire it— for the deities,
since there is no fruit yet to be attained by those gods who have already reached their stations.
Or [it means] "because they have results that are not to be sought.

Jaimini considers that there is no lack of qualification—that is, there is qualification—for those such as Rudra and the other deities like the Vasus in the Madhu-vidyā and other such meditations, because the states of Rudra and so forth, which are the fruits of the second vidyā and the immortal vidyā (amṛta-vidyā), are "results not to be attained" (*aprāpya-phalatvāt*)—meaning they are results unfit to be attained—and thus there is no possibility of seeking them even for those [deities]. Therefore, there is no absence of qualification for them in these meditations on honey and the like.

By the mention of Jaimini— that is, because this is the view of Jaimini himself, who is the most authoritative— it is indicated as another logical reason that they (the gods) have no qualification [for Vedic study].
By this [reference], the passages beginning with "Madhu etc."—
namely, "That sun, indeed, is the honey of the gods"— [are to be understood].

Regarding the lack of qualification of the gods in the Madhu-vidyā and other such meditations, Jaimini considers that there is no such lack of qualification; for that reason, "because of impossibility," he—the most authoritative teacher—considers that since among the fruits described in those vidyās some have already been attained by them while others are unattainable, the desire for them is impossible for them. Thus thinks Jaimini.
Thus the meaning of the Sūtra has been stated.
For in the Chāndogya, by the passage "That indeed is the Sun," the state of being honey (madhutva) of Viṣṇu, as the Sun, is declared through his nature as supreme bliss; then [it says] "He this..."

By these and other such passages, [it is shown that] among the five forms known as Vāsudeva, Saṅkarṣaṇa, Pradyumna, Aniruddha, and Nārāyaṇa— which are denoted by the five terms beginning with "first nectar" (prathamāmṛta) and reside within the eastern, southern, western, northern, and upper rays of the solar orb of the Lord designated as "Honey" (madhu)— there are gods residing in those respective directions, such as the Vasus, Rudras, Ādityas, Maruts, and Sādhyas, who are described as the five groups of upright-natured beings suitable for those respective stations.

It is said that when worship is performed sequentially through the mouths of Agni and the others—namely Agni, Vāyu, Indra, Soma, Viriñca, and Pradhāna—one attains the status of the Vasus and other classes of deities by means of the grace of [Brahman] generated through the direct realization (aparokṣajñāna) of Him; this applies to those situated among the respective groups.
And so it is stated: "He who..."
The qualified person "knows" this nectar—
the form called Vāsudeva—
in the manner thus described.
"And having become one of the Vasus";
