that is, having become the lord of the place and time to be enjoyed by the Vasus, "with fire as his mouth," meaning primarily through that [fire] or by its instruction.
"Having seen"— that is, having directly realized— "this very nectar," which is called Vāsudeva, "one is satisfied."
The meaning is that he becomes liberated.
Thus, "he who"—the qualified aspirant fit for divinity—who meditates upon Brahman under the names of speech, breath, sight, hearing, mind, and heart, attains divinity;

having become divine, he attains union (*sāyujya*) with his own superior deities, and then, together with the four-faced Brahmā, he approaches the gods, who are specific forms of the Lord residing in Śvetadvīpa.
The meaning of another Vedic passage is that this qualified person "approaches nourishment"— that is, food— and thus attains it as he desires.
Sūtra—Oṃ.
And because of its existence in the luminous realm.
And because omniscience is included within luminosity;
for just as all things are included within the light of the sun, so too are all objects included within the knowledge of that [omniscience].
And because the knowledges are eternally established. // 32 //

Now, one might object: "Granted that the gods may lack the qualification for those forms of knowledge whose fruits are other than liberation, nevertheless, they will possess the qualification for those knowledges aimed at liberation, such as: 'Brahman is truth, consciousness, and infinite' (Taittirīya Upaniṣad 2.1.1)."
Having read the sūtra which dispels the doubt that "desire for [liberation] is possible there," he explains it as follows: "In the case of the luminaries... (jyotiṣi).
"Jyotiṣī" is a restatement of the words of the sūtra;
its explanation is "omniscience" (sarvajñatva).
Although it should have been explained as "in knowledge" (jñāne), [it is stated thus].
Nevertheless, because a cognition not specified by its object cannot be determined,

and because in a cognition having some particular object, no entity whatsoever is established as being that object, it has been explained that "omniscience" (sarvajñatva) is [the term used] to indicate that [cognition].
By this, it is indicated that the word "of things" (*vastūnām*)— which indicates the inclusion and the relationship [between the knower and the known]— must be supplied within the Sūtra.

The particle *ca* signifies conjunction (*samuccaye*). The connection with the preceding [verse] is as follows: because this reason is impossible, one considers there to be no qualification for the Madhu-vidyā and so forth, by way of the recurring word "reason" (*hetu*).
By the word "and so forth" (*ādi*) in the phrase "in the Madhu-vidyā and so forth," the knowledges for the sake of liberation (*mokṣārthavidyā*) are also to be understood.
And the word *jyotis* (light) is to be repeated as "two lights" (*jyotiṣī iva jyotiṣī*).
It has been indicated that the locative case is appropriate in the sense of "in the intellect of Caitraratha," as in the expression "the meaning of the scripture.
To the question, "How is there the inclusion of objects within knowledge? he explains it in its own terms by saying "the Sun," because [objects] exist within omniscience.

Just as all things are included within the light of the sun, so too, because all things are "included" (*antarbhāva*)— meaning they become objects (*viṣayībhūta*)— within the knowledge of that [deity] performed by the deity under discussion;
he clarifies this intention with the word "eternal" (*nitya*).

The meaning is that for the gods, because of their "omniscience"— that is, because of the fact that all knowledge to be accomplished through the sciences of Brahmanic rituals is "eternally established," meaning it is invariably attained.
Alternatively,
the meaning is: "because of the constant and regular accomplishment"— that is, the attainment— of the "sciences," namely the sciences that are the means to knowledge.
The sense is that [the Vedas] were seen by the gods;
or alternatively, because the "Vidyās"—
meaning the knowledges that serve as the means for attaining liberation and other fruits, and the meanings taught therein— are eternally established.
The meaning is that [the gods] know them by necessity.
And thus, the intention is that it is not possible for the gods to have a desire for knowledge to be accomplished through both types of learning (*vidyā*).
The construction of these two words ending in the fifth case (*pañcamyanta*) is as before.
Nor should it be asked how the word "ca" (and) occurs here, given that this reason serves to establish the impossibility of the [desire for liberation] mentioned in the previous sūtra;

for while previously the impossibility was intended from the perspective of the result (*phala*), whereas here it is intended from the perspective of the means (*sādhana*), even though this reason establishes the second type of impossibility, the word "ca" is justified because it establishes the general category of impossibility.

Although in the Bhāṣya, the sūtra "In the case of the light" (*jyotiṣi*) appears to be intended for the purpose of pointing out defects by way of establishing [the opponent's position] regarding both alternatives— whether [gods] have the qualification for knowledge aimed at results other than liberation, or for knowledge aimed at the result of liberation;

In the *Ṭīkā*, however, it is stated that even with respect to the knowledge for the sake of liberation (*mokṣārthavidyā*), the gods have no entitlement; for although they possess a desire for the fruit [of liberation], they lack a desire for the knowledge consisting of the meditation on the means to that [fruit],
and because knowledge has the nature of being for the sake of realization (*jñāna*).
And because knowledge has already been attained—this was explained as being intended solely to state the defect in the second position alone.
Thus, there is a contradiction.

Nevertheless, regarding the ancient position that there is no entitlement to the knowledges (vidyās) whose fruits are other than liberation, it is not only the case that there is no entitlement to those specific knowledges because the gods lack desire for the fruits such as the status of a Vasu—which are the fruits of the Madhu-vidyā—since those have already been attained; [the same applies to other cases].
[Objection: There is a fault.

[Response: However, since there is an absence of desire even for the knowledge that is the means to achieve results such as the status of a Vasu, there is an absence of qualification; thus, because the *Ṭīkā* states that another supporting argument has been presented regarding this fault of impossibility, there is no contradiction.
For this very reason, the presence of the word "ca" (and) is not unjustified.
This is because that [explanation] is tenable when intended as the first alternative (*pakṣa*).
Furthermore, the *Sattarkadīpāvalī* proceeds with the intention of the first alternative, stating that this is established by another reason (*hetu*).
Alternatively, the word "and" (*ca*) signifies the conjunction of two kinds of knowledge (*vidyā*).
By this [statement], Jaimini does not consider there to be a lack of qualification for the Madhu-vidyā and others merely for the sake of fruits other than liberation;

rather, by the word "etc. (ādi) or by the word "repeated" (āvṛtta) referring to the light (jyotis), he includes even the knowledge for the sake of liberation, namely, "Truth, Knowledge... (Taittirīya Upaniṣad 2.1).
Why? Because, "as in light"—
that is, as in the light of the sun—
there is an absence of all things as objects within the "light," which is the knowledge of the deity regarding all objects.
Because the knowledge that is the means to liberation has already been established;
for this very reason, there is no [desire] for liberation, since that too is almost as good as established and thus desire for it is impossible.

Jaimini considers that the gods, such as Vasu and others, lack qualification for the Madhu-vidyā and other such meditations not only because they have no desire for the fruits [of those rites], but also because, "in the light"— that is, even regarding the knowledge which is the means to achieve the status of Vasu and so forth— they cannot possibly possess a desire for it.

Whence is that [knowledge]? It is because it exists "in the light" (*jyotiṣi*), meaning it exists within the knowledge of the gods; or rather, the meaning of the sūtra is stated to be that since all things are included as its objects, the knowledge of the means and the fruit [of action] is already established.
Sūtra—Oṃ.
But Bādarāyaṇa holds that there is indeed [an intermediate state], for it exists; om. 33.

Bādarāyaṇa maintains that even for the gods who have attained their respective stations, there is eligibility for the honey-liquor and other such offerings, because of the existence of specific fruits [of action].
For there is indeed a distinction in the manifestation [of power].
Thus, since the gods have already obtained fruits suitable for purposes other than liberation, and since it is impossible to obtain what is unsuitable, [there is no further need] even for liberation.

Since they have effectively attained the status of knowers of Brahman, they lack any desire for further goals; thus, having been established by Jaimini that they have no eligibility for any of the meditative sciences (*vidyās*), the author now reads and explains the sūtra which re-establishes their eligibility: "The existence... (*bhāvam*).

By the phrase "due to the existence of a specific fruit" (*phalaviśeṣabhāvāt*), the recurrence (*anuvṛtti*) of the term "from the preceding state" (*pūrvasmād bhāvāt*) in the sūtra is indicated. Regarding the term "of those who have attained the stages" (*prāptapadānām*): a "stage" (*pada*) is so called because it is reached (*padyate*); it refers simply to the fruit that has been attained.
By the word "api," a specific meaning is also intended; the particle "tu" has the sense of "api";
and since "api" is said to mean "even though" (yadyapi) as well as "nevertheless" (tathāpi), this is what is expressed here.
The phrase "of the gods" (*devānām*) is a supplementary statement (*śeṣokti*) from the Sūtra.
The phrase "in the honey[-meditations] and so forth" (*madhvādiṣu*) is a restatement of the word that recurs [from the previous context].
Here, by the word "and so forth" (*ādi*), all Vedic rites and knowledges (*brahmakarmavidyā*) intended for the fruits of liberation and everything other than that are included.
"Adhikāram" means the state of being an authority;
by this, the meaning of the word "bhāvam" has been explained.
The phrase "it is thought" (*manyate*) is an elliptical statement.
Since the verb "exists" (*asti*) requires a subject, he indicates that subject as "a particular manifestation of light" (*prakāśaviśeṣa*);
the meaning is "an excellence of cognition" (*jñānātiśaya*).
The word "hi" (for) has the sense of "because.
Thus, the construction is as follows: the venerable Bādarāyaṇa, however, maintains that there is eligibility for the gods in all the vidyās, such as the Madhu-vidyā and others;
nor is it a fault to claim a lack of desire [for these] on the grounds that they have already attained their fruits.

Although the gods have attained their stations and, by virtue of being knowers of Brahman, have achieved liberation and other fruits that are otherwise unattainable and unsuitable for them, nevertheless, even for those gods who have attained their stations, there exists a distinction of fruit through the performance of the meditations (*upāsanā*) and rituals prescribed in the *Madhu-vidyā* and other such scriptural passages; and because there is a presence of excellence in the fruit of liberation— which cannot be accomplished by mere knowledge alone— there is the possibility of their desiring perfection (*siddhi*).

Nor should it be argued that, although there may be a desire for the fruit because its excellence is established, there can be no desire for the inquiry into knowledge (*vidyā*) because the means to that knowledge are eternally established, and the inquiry into knowledge is for the sake of [attaining] knowledge;
for since others than the Blessed Lord lack unqualified omniscience, there is a "distinction in illumination" (*prakāśaviśeṣaḥ*) through the inquiry into knowledge.
"A specific cognition exists," meaning it is possible;
by this, the application of the sūtra is shown.
In this context, the term "Bādarāyaṇa" is used for the sake of honor.
As long as there is service toward the supreme reality, so long does a particular excellence of happiness arise;
and because such manifestation is impossible except through Hari, the Supreme One.
And by virtue of their power, they also perform the worship of the gods.
"Everything is ordained eternally, as well as all rites such as sacrifices," so it is stated in the Skanda Purāṇa.

Now, one might raise the objection: "How is it known that by performing the meditations and rites prescribed in each respective Vidyā, there arises for the gods not only the fruits specified in those Vidyās but also other fruits and specific manifestations? To dispel this doubt, [the author] cites a Smṛti text indicated by the word *hi* (for) regarding the aforementioned point.
He demonstrates this with the words "as far as."
The word "is performed" (*kriyate*) is to be supplied as the ellipsis.
The suffix *tal* is used in its own sense (*svārthe*),
or because one intends to express the non-difference between the state (*bhāva*) and that which possesses the state (*bhavitṛ*).
The word "siddhyati" (is accomplished) is to be understood as the ellipsis.
The particle "ca" (and) serves to aggregate the reasons;
alternatively, the first "ca" is connected with the phrase "of the manifestation."
And this [term] is a collective of results,
and it is also a collective of impossibilities; the word "because of possibility" (sambhavāt) is understood to recur [in each case].

And likewise, regarding that subject described as "in the supreme reality" (*pare tattve*)— that is, in the nature of the Supreme Self— as in the passage beginning "This indeed is the Āditya" (*asau vā ādityaḥ*, Chāndogya Upaniṣad 3.1.1), [there is the mention] of "the gods."
By the gods, Vasu and the others, [it was said]: "As much as";
"as much as is excessive";
"this is service."
Thus it has been said: "To that extent," the worship consisting of hearing and so forth is performed;

"to that extent," there is for them an "excess of specific happiness"—an excellence in the happiness of heaven, liberation, and so on—which is accomplished by mere knowledge according to each individual's capacity.
Therefore, "beyond that," there is none other than the one independent Hari, because for others "illumination is impossible," meaning they lack unqualified omniscience.
Precisely because the manifestation that is to be accomplished through the investigation of knowledge is possible,
and precisely because the desire [for it] is possible, for those gods— due to their "endowment with capacity," that is,
due to the possibility of capacity and also the possibility of learning— even though they have already attained their station, [the scripture is intended for] "those gods."
By the gods, "all worship"—
meaning all worship taught in the various sciences as well as all rituals such as sacrifices— is "enjoined" as "constant," that is, as a matter of obligatory rule.
The construction is: "it is understood in the Śrutis as something to be performed.
The particle *ca* is used in the sense of conjunction (*samuccaya*).
In the reading *aprakāśasya*, the meaning is "of one who lacks non-figurative omniscience."
In that case, the word "ca" (and) includes "prakāśa" (manifestation).
Since "sambhavāt" (because of the possibility) is already established, it has the dual meaning of "sattvāt" (because of existence).
In both readings, the word "anyeṣām" (of others) is to be supplied as the remainder.
The word "eka" (one) has the sense of restriction and serves to exclude even Viriñca from being excluded; this is the remainder of the sentence, as it is stated in the Skanda Purāṇa.
Therefore, because there is a difference in the results, there is indeed a difference in the manifestation; thus, these two [arguments] are not unestablished—this is the completion of the statement.
Jaimini’s opinion concerns merely the lack of entitlement to the aforementioned results; therefore, there is no contradiction with his view.
Granted that this may be so, and that there is a defeat of the reasoning stated as "due to impossibility" (*asambhavāt*);

nevertheless, if one accepts the eligibility (*adhikāra*) of the gods, there would be a contradiction with the view of Jaimini, who is considered most authoritative. To this, he says: "It has been stated" (*ukteti*).
And it has been stated that "that result" (*tat-phalam*) is a compound analyzed as *tat* (that) and *uktam phalam yasya* (that which has its result stated).

Thus, this qualification—which is for the sake of the results stated for each respective Vidyā and for the sake of attaining the knowledge previously mentioned as having those results—is merely the absence [of such results]; this is the meaning of "Jaimini’s opinion," i.e., what is intended by Jaimini.

By the word *mātra* (only), the absence of any qualification for other results is excluded. To the question "What follows if this is so?", he says "Therefore" (*ataḥ*). The meaning is that there is no contradiction between these two, because what was stated by Jaimini has been accepted by the author of the Sūtras, and what was stated by the author of the Sūtras has not been refuted by Jaimini.

"Only regarding that which has been conceived as a single part by the omniscient Kṛṣṇa, may the sages speak after having accepted it; thus their doctrine is not contradicted. So it is said in the Brāhma [Purāṇa]. (33)
Thus ends the section concerning the deities (Devatādhikaraṇa). 8.

Now, one might ask: "Why should we not simply assume a contradiction between these two views by postulating a difference in their respective objects? To this, he says: "Of the omniscient one... [and so forth].
The word *tu* has the sense of specification;
the particle *eva* is displaced in its order [of construction].
And thus, because they are "sages" (*munayaḥ*).

Jaimini and others, having accepted only a portion of what was contemplated— that is, only a single part of the intended meaning or a single part of his doctrine— of Kṛṣṇa Dvaipāyana, who is the unqualifiedly omniscient, would speak only that and nothing else.
Therefore, the meaning is that "their view"— the view of those Kṛṣṇamunis— is not mutually contradictory;
the word "stated" is to be supplied after the word "brahmic."
Therefore, the intended meaning is that one must simply postulate a difference in the objects [of cognition], not a contradiction between philosophical systems. // 8 //
Thus concludes the section concerning the deities.
9. The Section Concerning Those Other Than Śūdras.

When it is stated that "the qualification belongs to humans," since there is no distinction made, one might argue that even a Śūdra has the qualification, based on the statement by Pautrāyaṇa: "I, O Śūdra, am Hāretvā" (Chāndogya Upaniṣad 4.2.3).
In this section, the qualification for the Śūdra—who is other than the three [upper] castes—to study the Brahmavidyā taught in the Vedas is refuted.
Since this is an incidental discussion, it is not necessary to seek its connection with the chapter and so forth.
He indicates the connection with the scripture and the subject matter, etc., by the words "manuṣya" (human being).
This is a locative of occasion (*nimitta-saptamī*);
or rather, it means "because there is no distinction regarding the state of being human," which is mentioned here for the sake of the present context.
It is not only for the twice-born (*dvijāti*).
But the word "also" (api) implies that this applies even to the Śūdra;
thus, it follows that the Śūdra also possesses the qualification for Vedic knowledge.
Why? Because "the qualification belongs to human beings."
Since this [text] has stated that human beings possess the qualification [for Vedic study],

and since there is no distinction— meaning an absence of difference— between a Śūdra and the twice-born regarding their shared status as humans, which is mentioned as being applicable to that qualification; [therefore, the Śūdra is entitled].

But is it not the case that being human (*manuṣyatva*) is not what is required for eligibility for Vedic knowledge, but rather the possession of a distinguished intellect and so forth? To this he says: "because there is no distinction" (*aviśeṣāt*). Even though a Śūdra may possess a distinguished intellect and so forth, there is "no distinction" [between him] and others [in that regard].
The meaning is "because there is no distinction.

Having thus stated the argument known as "lack of distinction," he states the observation of an indicative mark (*liṅga*)— namely, "because of the mention of Pautrāyaṇa"— to show that there is no entitlement [for a Śūdra] due to the non-observation of a Śūdra's entitlement to Vedic knowledge.
The meaning is that this is because we see the mention in the *Chāndogya* of Pautrāyaṇa’s study of the Vedic Saṃvarga-vidyā.

Now, one might ask: "How is it known that the person named Pautrāyaṇa was indeed a Śūdra? To this, he states the evidence for it: "‘O Śūdra, [drive] the horse-chariot! This refers to the mention of Pautrāyaṇa.
The meaning is: "simply because of Raikva’s address directed toward Pautrāyaṇa.

To the objection—"Even in the absence of [formal] qualification, why could it not be that Pautrāyaṇa investigated the Vedic knowledge?"—the author says further: "because of what was said by Pautrāyaṇa.
The meaning is: because the sage Raikva, being free from desire, taught the Saṃvarga-vidyā to Pautrāyaṇa.

Alternatively, the construction may be: "Because instruction from a sage is impossible for one who lacks qualification, and because the qualification of Pautrāyaṇa is stated in the Śruti by implication. Following the word "qualification" (*adhikāra*), the phrase "therefore there is a contradiction" (*ato virodhaḥ*) is to be supplied.
The word "of that" (tasya) connects with the phrase "has been stated" (uktaḥ).

Because this [objection] raises a challenge regarding the contradiction with scriptural authority (*śruti*) and other means of valid cognition concerning the meaning already stated by means of the aforementioned reasoning, its connection with the preceding section is one of objection (*ākṣepikī saṅgati*).
The subject matter (*viṣaya*) is known as the qualification for the study of Vedic knowledge (*vedavidyādhikāra*).
And thus the prima facie argument (*pūrvapakṣa*) is shown with its supporting logic.
For in the *Chāndogya Upaniṣad*, in the fourth chapter, in the section on the "Absorber" (*saṃvarga*), there is this narrative: A king named Pautrāyaṇa was lying on the roof of his palace at night;
at that time, swans were flying over the palace.
As they were falling upward and conversing with one another, two of them were leading the way. There, one said to the other:
"What is this? O Pautrāyaṇīya, do not approach that splendor!"
"In connection with him, his splendor might burn you.
Thus addressed, the other swan (Jānaśruti), by means of the interrogative word "whom" (*kam*), showed disregard for the king and praised the sage Raikva alone.
Hearing this, the king, his mind deeply distressed, rose from his bed and quickly summoned his charioteer, commanding him to search for Raikva.
Having first returned, saying, "I did not find Raikva," while searching for him here and there,

he was again commanded by the king to seek him out after the latter had described his characteristics. Having searched once more and beheld Raikva in a certain place, he returned to the king and said, "I found Raikva," reporting exactly what had occurred.
Then, having determined the location of the sage Raikva by means of his own charioteer’s words, the king—desiring to know the truth from him—took a teacher’s fee and went into his presence.
Thereupon, seeing Raikva standing beneath a cart at the gate, he addressed him, presented the fee, and said, "Teach me the knowledge.
Then Raikva, who was far beyond the ordinary world, rejected that Pautrāyaṇa.

What [is the meaning]? It is "ahaha āre tvā śūdre" and so forth. Here, *āre* is a vocative; when *hāra* and *itva* are treated as separate words, the visarga is elided and the *guṇa* substitution occurs, resulting in *hāretva*.

And likewise, O Śūdra, "hāretvā" means a chariot—specifically a vehicle called *kaṇṭhamālā* (neck-garland)—or, according to the *Tattvapradīpa*, a cart; the meaning is: "May that be yours together with the cows. In the alternative view where *hāretvānaḥ* is treated as a single word, either the dual ending must undergo the substitution of the singular ending, or the substitution of the vowel *ā*.
And in each case, there is a connection with the verb "let it be.
Therefore, he says: Sūtra—Oṃ.
For it is indicated by the fact that Śuka heard of that disregard and then rushed toward him.
This Pautrāyaṇa was not a Śūdra; rather, "Śūdra-ness" consists simply in running away out of grief (*śucā'dravaṇam*).
He introduces the sūtra that establishes this conclusion with the words: "Therefore... (*ata iti*).
Since the argument regarding the mention of non-distinction will be refuted in the *Śravaṇa-sūtra*,

[the author] shows the resultant meaning of the sūtra— which is intended to demonstrate that the observation of marks cited by the opponent can be explained otherwise— by stating "no," thereby raising the requirement for a sense compatible with the positive concomitance (*anvaya*) of the phrase "because of its tending toward that" (*tad-ādravaṇāt*).
‘Asau’ (this one): Pautrāyaṇa, having been addressed by Raikva, [was told] ‘not a Śūdra’;
the meaning is that he was not a Śūdra by birth, but rather a Kṣatriya.

In that case, how is it appropriate for him to be addressed as "Śūdra," given the absence of conventional usage? With the intention that it is due to etymological derivation (*yoga*) alone, he explains the portion of the Sūtra—"on account of running toward him" (*tad-ādravaṇāt*)—which indicates the ground for the application of that word, taking it to be restrictive: "By grief" (*śucā*).
"Grief" (*śucā*) means sorrow; "the state of being a Śūdra" (*śūdratvam*) consists simply in his rapid running toward Raikva or the *kṣattṛ*.
The meaning is that "śūdra" is the cause for the address,
not the birth-status (jāti).
By this, it is indicated that the phrase *tadādravaṇāt* in the Sūtra is connected with the word *śūdratvam*, which is supplied (*adhyāhṛta*) and conveys the sense of being addressed as "śūdra."

And thus, since there is no impossibility of addressing [him], this is not an indicative mark (liṅga) for the eligibility of a Śūdra to the Vedic sciences; therefore, the connection is with the negation (nañ), such that "there is no eligibility for a Śūdra to the Vedic sciences.
By the word "eva" (indeed), it is shown that this word "Śūdra" is derived etymologically as "one who runs away out of grief" (śucā-adravaṇāt śūdraḥ), and not from the rule "śucer daśca."

Thus, by means of the *uṇādi* sūtra, with the addition of the suffix *ra*, the lengthening of the root vowel, and the substitution of *da* for the letter *ca*, the form *ruḍha* is established; this is what is meant.

By the word *pautrāyaṇa*, the meaning of the pronoun *idam* (this), which refers to something present in the mind, is indicated; by the word *śuci*, the meaning of the second *tat* in the sūtra mentioned previously is shown; and by the suffix *tva*, the meaning of the ablative case expressing the cause (*nimitta*) is demonstrated.
The author of the Sūtras refers to him as "Śuka" because he is eternally omniscient;
and in the Bhāṣya, the use of the remote demonstrative "asau" (he) in accordance with the Śruti is appropriate, as in the passage:
"Kam varam enam etad santam... (Chāndogya Upaniṣad 4.1.3).
Because of the hearing of this [charge of] disrespect;

as an answer to the question "From what cause does his grief arise?", he explains the portion of the Sūtra beginning with "śugasya tadanādaraśravaṇāt" (his grief is from hearing that disrespect) with the words "kam varam" etc.
The word division is *kaṃ u are*. "Are"—O Haṃsa, with reference to whom did you say this: "the virtuous" (*santam*), meaning one who is faultless, and "Sayugvān"?
The meaning is "Raikva with the cart" (sa-śakaṭam). The particle *u* has the sense of censure (*nindā*).
The meaning is that this is inappropriate to say to this king; Raikva alone is worthy to speak thus.
"Etatsantam" (this being).
The meaning is "you have spoken of one who is censurable"; this is stated in the *Tattvapradīpa*:
"'etatsantam'—here [the word] 'santam' [is used]. Or [it may be read as]: "'atra santam'."
"Because of hearing such disrespect" means that "disrespect" (anādara) is censure.
Thus, the meaning is: because of hearing a statement made by a swan (*haṃsa*) indicating such disrespect, or a statement from himself expressing his own lack of respect.
Immediately after "from hearing," the word "having attained" (prāptayā) is to be supplied;
this is to be construed with the word "purity" (śuci).
For it is indicated [in scripture] thus: "As he was indeed rising, he said to the charioteer" (Chāndogya Upaniṣad 4.1.5). // 34 //
But surely, it is known that grief arises even for a king who has merely heard of disrespect;
yet that certainty does not arise from direct perception.
This is because the mental state of another, in the form of hearing about disrespect, is not directly perceived, and therefore the arising of grief from that is also not directly perceived.
Nor can there be an inference of the effect from the cause,
because the cause lacks an invariable concomitance (avinābhāva) with the effect; therefore, he explains the remainder of the sūtra, "For it is indicated," beginning with the word "saha" (together).
The word "hā" expresses wonder.
That Pautrāyaṇa, who was disrespectful toward what he had heard, while "rising up"— that is,
even as he was getting up from his bed— [addressed] the "steward."
The meaning of the Śruti is that [Raikva] spoke to the charioteer for the purpose of searching for Raikva.
This is indicated by the phrase "iti sūcyate hi" (for it is thus indicated).

By the fact that the mind of Raikva was occupied with something else—which is known through the otherwise inexplicable nature of the sentence's meaning—the cause of that state, namely his grief (*śuk*), is "indicated."
The meaning is that it is known.
The sense is that although there is no necessary concomitance of the cause with the effect, there is necessarily the concomitance of the effect with the cause.
This connects with the preceding [verse]: because of hearing this disregard for him, she simply ran away due to the grief she had incurred.
Furthermore, the sage Raikva’s thorough knowledge of the cause for not running away due to grief is possible because of his omniscience.
As it is stated in the *Chāndogyopaniṣad-bhāṣya*: "King Pautrāyaṇa was addressed as 'Śūdra' by the sage because of his grief."
"Having obtained the knowledge of the vital breath from him, he attained the supreme Dharma. Thus [it is said].

‘Śokāt’: the meaning is "because of not running away due to grief. Alternatively, this form is derived from the root ‘at-’ (meaning "to go continuously") preceded by the prefix ‘āṅ’ and having ‘śoka’ as its upapada, with the suffix ‘kvip’; in that case, the word ‘yataḥ’ (from which) is to be supplied.
If it is asked: "Since the meaning is already complete by the words *taddravaṇāt* (because of melting that), for what purpose is the prefix *āṅ* elided [to form *ādravaṇāt*]?"—the answer is: No.

Although one ought to say *śūdret* in the Śruti, the long vowel in the form of the letter *ū* heard as *śūdreta* is intended to make explicit its meaning, so as to indicate an excess of grief (*śoka*).
Nor should it be asked: "Why does the Śruti say *śūdreta* when one ought to say *śūgdreta*?"
For it is established that in the Śruti passage, "He is Rudra because he causes [the world] to weep (rudraṇāt)," the letter *ga* is used as a substitute for the letter *da*;
therefore, it is stated in the *Tattvapradīpa* that "the third [letter] of the third [group] is used in the sense of excellence."
And because it is appropriate [to explain] it as in the Smṛti: "it causes pain to melt away";
by this, [the name is derived] from "flowing toward" (ādravaṇa) due to grief (śucā).
Raikva’s designation as a *śūdra* and his being addressed as "O *śūdra*" were due solely to the circumstance of his rapid departure from him, and not because of a lower caste;
furthermore, grief (*śuka*) and sorrow (*śoka*) arose in him upon hearing that disregard.
The word "tat" (that) is a reference to what has been stated in the Śruti.
The genitive case signifies the relationship between the action and its agent.
Thus, it means "because of hearing [the scripture] speak of disregard for that."
The meaning is "from hearing the disrespect shown by the swan.
According to the *Tattvapradīpa*, the meaning is "from hearing one's own disrespect from that swan.
Some maintain that this is a compound formed by the elision of the middle term (*madhyamapadalopī samāsa*).

Now, one might ask: how is it known that grief arises even from disrespect toward what has been heard, given that the experience of suffering denoted by the word "grief" in another's mind is not perceptible? To this, it is said: "For it is indicated."
The word "hi" means "because.

Since the meaning of the sentence as a whole would otherwise be untenable, the cause—namely, the grief of this person—is "indicated," that is, known, by its effect, which is called "the state of having a distracted mind" (due to that grief).

Therefore, the address "O Śūdra" is not a *liṅga* (indicative mark) for the eligibility of a Śūdra to the Veda; the sense is that the Śūdra's eligibility for Vedic knowledge does not follow from the force of this [passage]. Thus, the meaning of the Sūtra has been stated.
Sūtra—Oṃ.
And because his status as a Kṣatriya is understood from a subsequent indicative mark concerning Caitraratha.
Furthermore, because of the indicative mark (*liṅga*) consisting of the mention of a "chariot drawn by mules" (*aśvatarī-ratha*), it is understood that Pautrāyaṇa was a Kṣatriya.
Now, one might ask: why is this word "Śūdra" accepted here as being etymological (*yaugika*)?
Why should it not be taken in its conventional sense alone? For between etymological derivation (*yoga*) and conventional usage (*rūḍhi*), the latter is more powerful.

Thus, setting forth and explaining the Sūtra which dispels the doubt that the qualification for Vedic knowledge might be established for a Śūdra by the very example of Pautrāyaṇa, [the author] says: "In the state of being a Kṣatriya... etc.
Here, the word "uttaratra" (later on) from the Sūtra should be connected with what precedes "ayam";
the word "śrutena" (by what is heard) is to be supplied as the ellipsis.
And likewise, because of Pautrāyaṇa’s approaching Raikva later on—
specifically after that [instruction] was imparted later on—
or else, because of being addressed by the word "Śūdra" later on, as in: "This is the chariot with mules."
The meaning is "having heard thus.
To dispel the suspicion that the chariot being given by Pautrāyaṇa might belong to someone else, the word *caitrarathena* is used in the Sūtra as a term emphasizing the state (*bhāvapradhāna*).
Otherwise, he would have simply said *citrarathena*.

In this context, "Caitraratha" is analyzed as "this belongs to Citraratha," where *citra* means "variegated" and *ratha* means "chariot. Intending this grammatical analysis (*vigraha*) and demonstrating the meaning of the suffix (*pratyaya*), he explains it as "by way of connection with Citraratha," which means "by way of a natural connection with Citraratha.
Here, the chariot alone is the indicative mark (*liṅga*).

The use of the specific word "charioteer" (rathin) is for the purpose of stating his true nature; or else, that word is intended to suggest his status as a Kṣatriya by means of his connection with an extraordinary chariot;
or again, when his status as a Kṣatriya is already certain simply by virtue of being a charioteer.
The word "that" (tat) is used for the purpose of indicating that [the chariot] is even more exceptionally variegated at that time;
for although in the passage "this is a chariot drawn by mules," only the "variegated chariot" (citraratha) is heard, its connection to him is not explicitly stated there.

Nevertheless, because in the preceding sentence—“*hāretvā tavaiva*”—the connection of the chariot with the meaning of the word *itvā* is understood through the genitive case, and since that connection with the chariot is established by direct scriptural statement (*śruti*), what was said is correct.

However, the explanation that “*citraratha*” means “one whose chariot is variegated,” and thus “by him who possesses that state of being the Citraratha” (*caitrarathya*), is incorrect; for it requires the assumption of a secondary suffix (*aṇ*) in the sense of an abstract state (*bhāva*), and it contradicts both the scripture and the commentary.
Nor should it be argued that the mere mention of the connection with Caitraratha does not dispel the suspicion of it belonging to someone else;

for when its belonging to him is established by itself and there is no subverting evidence, it is possible that this very belonging is inherent, and thus it is improper to assume it is merely occasional (*naimittika*).
As it is said: "In the absence of ownership, there can be no acquisition of wealth."
Because this is established by such principles [of interpretation],

he explains the ablative case in "liṅgāt" (from the indicative mark) by means of a transposition in order to achieve grammatical coreferentiality (*sāmānādhikaraṇya*) with "rathena" (by means of the chariot)— that is, he interprets it as "liṅganā" (by the indicative mark).
The word "pautrāyaṇasya" (of Pautrāyaṇa) is an explanation of the meaning of the term "asya" (of him), which is understood from the context.

The phrase "because of the understanding of his being a Kṣatriya" connects with the preceding [statement] to mean that his status as a Śūdra arises precisely from his not fleeing out of grief, and not through conventional usage (*rūḍhi*).
The word "and" (*ca*) is connected with "and by means of an indicative mark" (*liṅgena*).
By this, [the term] "one who gives much" (*bahudāyī*) [is explained].
The indicative mark (liṅga) mentioned in the supplementary portion of the passage beginning with "ityādi" is here combined [with other means of proof].
The word "ca" (and) is used either to indicate the superior strength of the indicative mark due to its being posterior to direct statement (śruti) and its multiplicity;
likewise, in the Sūtra as well, the word "ca" is placed out of its logical order and serves the same purpose.

The sense is this: even though conventional usage (*rūḍhi*) is generally more powerful, in this case, because there is a subverting factor in the form of several scriptural marks (*liṅga*) heard here, it is proper to accept the word *śūdra* as having a derivative meaning (*yogavṛtti*).
As stated in the *Tattvapradīpa*: "Those born from a female donkey by a male horse are called *aśvataryas*."
"In mules born from she-asses and horses are 'asvataryah'"; thus it is stated in the *Vyāsatīrthīya*.
The meaning is that a chariot yoked with such [mules], an *aśvatarī-ratha*, exists for you as a sacrificial fee (*dakṣiṇā*).
This is the statement of Pautrāyaṇa addressed to Raikva:
"The chariot yoked with mules is called *citra* (the variegated)," according to the Brāhmaṇa.

Now, since the word *aśvatarī-ratha* (chariot of mares) is used in the Śruti, and it ought to be used exactly the same way in the Sūtra as well, why did the author of the Sūtra [use a different term]?

Anticipating the objection that the word *citraratha* might be used [in a different sense], he states the definition there with the intention that there is no contradiction because the meaning of both terms is identical: "A chariot (*ratha*)."
The word *tu* (but/however) has the sense of distinction (*viśeṇa*) or restriction (*avadhāraṇa*).
It is connected with the phrase "yoked specifically with a mule" (*aśvatarīyukta eva*).
Here, the mention of "chariot" (*ratha*) is merely a statement of the actual object (*vāstava-viśeṣokti*).

However, even "chariot-ness" (*rathatva*) cannot be included within the category of what is possible [to be denoted by the word]; thus, it should be understood that there is no inconsistency between the *Śruti* and the *Sūtra*, because it is stated in the *Brāhma* [Upapurāṇa]: "Where the Veda is the chariot, there the Veda is not; where there is no chariot, there the Veda is not. And so, according to the *Upaskāra*, the connection is as follows: since the word "chariot" is employed in the *Sūtra* for the sake of producing a cognition whose qualifier is "chariot-ness," its usage is not purposeless. Therefore, there is no discrepancy between the *Śruti* and the *Sūtra*.
Where the Veda is the chariot, there the Veda is not; where there is no chariot, there the Veda is not.
Thus it is stated in the Brahmavaivarta [Purāṇa], verse 35.

Thus, the Kṣatriya status of Pautrāyaṇa has been established directly by means of his possession of a natural chariot. Anticipating the objection that "if he possesses a natural chariot, why should he not be of a lower caste?"—that is, the lack of logical necessity—it is replied: "Not so; for even a chariot acquired adventitiously is impossible without the Veda, and according to the principle to be stated later—that 'the Veda [is the cause] of refinement' (saṃskāra)—it is impossible for a Śūdra."

With the intention that the absence of Śūdra-status in Pautrāyaṇa is established by means of inferring the Veda from the chariot, [the author], in order to avoid the suspicion of deviation (*vyabhicāra*) in the inference of the Veda from the chariot, demonstrates the pervasion (*vyāpti*) of both [the Veda and the non-Śūdra status] through scripture (*āgama*) in the verse beginning with "yatra.
The word "tatra" means "in that very place."
Therefore, just as in the case of "where there is fire, there is smoke," the Veda attains the status of a pervader (*vyāpaka*).
For this very reason, in the portion demonstrating the negative concomitance (*vyatireka*), the phrase "not in the Veda" is stated first to indicate the absence of the Veda.
This is because, in the case of *smṛti*, the word "chariot" (*ratha*) is intended to signify chariots in general, encompassing both adventitious and inherent types.
Or, the statement "where there is Veda" is made with the intention of equal pervasion (samavyāpti).

For this very reason, the *Ṭīkā* states: "Because the chariot is invariably concomitant with the Veda," and having thus stated that the chariot is the pervaded (vyāpya), it says: "The state of being a charioteer exists merely in relation to being Vedic."
By this, its pervasiveness (*vyāpakatva*) has been stated.

In reality, however, there is no inconsistency in the formulation: "Wherever there is a chariot, there is Vedic knowledge. And thus, since the certainty of pervasion (*vyāpti*) is established by this, there is no suspicion of deviation (*vyabhicāra*). Consequently, through the inference of Vedic knowledge based on the mere presence of such a chariot, the absence of Śūdra-hood is ascertained; therefore, Pautrāyaṇa does not belong to a lower caste outside the [three] Vedas.
The sense is that this is to be suspected.
By this, the objection of the opponent— that since the Śūdra also accepts the Vedāṅgas, it is not proper to prove the absence of Śūdra-hood on that basis—
is refuted, because that point will be rejected in the subsequent sūtra.

Nor should it be argued: "Even if his status as a Vedic practitioner is determined by his being a charioteer—a role common to Brāhmaṇas and others—and even if his non-Śūdra status is established thereby, how can his specific status as a Kṣatriya be determined?
For, by stating that the mere quality of being a charioteer is pervaded by Vedic practice, the Smṛti intends that natural charioteership is also pervaded by the specific Vedic status of a Kṣatriya.
Since this [natural charioteership] is absent in Brāhmaṇas and others who possess a chariot only occasionally, its presence establishes his status as a Kṣatriya directly.

Nor should it be argued that there is a deviation (vyabhicāra) in this case because the status of being a charioteer for a Śūdra is perceived through the necessity of accounting otherwise for his being a warrior— as established by the rule "and not fleeing from battle is [the duty] of a Śūdra"—
for since being a warrior can be accounted for as a foot soldier, it does not necessitate the status of being a charioteer.

The ellipsis (*iti śeṣaḥ*) is that it is understood that, by supplying the words "because it is stated in the *Brahmavaivarta*," there is a connection with the phrase "he is not a Śūdra. By this [is meant]: either from the word "approaching" (*ādravaṇāt*), or from the vocative address, or from the subsequent passage:
"This is a chariot drawn by mules" (*Chāndogya Upaniṣad* 4.2.2).

Because of the scriptural statement, "By the [mention of] Caitraratha through an indicative mark," and because his Kṣatriya status is understood from the indicative mark of his natural chariot and from indicative marks such as his being a great giver; therefore,
it is precisely due to this subverting factor— that he ran toward him— that his Śūdra status [is established].
But he is not a Śūdra by birth;
likewise, because of his knowledge of the chariot and his certainty regarding the Vedas, it is stated that he is not a Śūdra—this is the meaning of the Sūtra. Om. Sū. 3.1.25.
Because of the grasping at formative forces and because of the expression of their non-existence.
"One should initiate a Brahmin at eight years of age and teach him [the Veda]," because this refers to a purificatory rite (saṃskāra) for the purpose of study;
as for what was stated regarding the understanding that Pautrāyaṇa was a Kṣatriya based on the indicative mark (liṅga) of his being a charioteer—
"It is not the case that the Śūdra’s entitlement to the Vedas is established by that sign.
This is not correct, because even a Śūdra can be a charioteer (*rathin*).
Nor should it be argued that since a chariot is pervaded by the Veda, and since a Śūdra lacks [the Veda], he must also lack a chariot.

Anticipating the objection that even a Śūdra might be entitled to the study of the Vedas because [the author] accepts that they are eligible for Vedic rites, he presents the sūtra as a rebuttal: "On account of the purificatory rites... (saṃskāra-).
In this regard, the Vedic scripture states: "One should initiate a Brāhmaṇa at eight years of age;
one should teach him.
Thus, it is specifically for the Brāhmaṇa that there is a requirement for initiation (upanayana) prior to study.

In order to dispel the doubt that this does not apply to others, he explains the portion [of the sūtra] beginning with "because of the reference to the purificatory rite" (*saṃskāraparāmarśāt*), starting with the words "eight-year-old. The phrase "having stated the initiation" (*upanayanam uktvā*) is to be supplied after the words "he should initiate" (*upanayīta*).
The meaning is: "him"—that is, the initiated boy—"the self," desiring to perform the role of a teacher (*ācāryakaraṇakāmaḥ*), "should teach" (*adhyāpayīta*).
After the word "iti," the word "thus" (iti) is understood as the ellipsis in the Śruti.
With the intention that "reference (parāmarśa) is the statement for another purpose," he explains the term *parāmarśa* as "for the sake of study."
The meaning is "by virtue of being an auxiliary to study.

The intention is that the statement regarding teaching also has as its purport the injunction for study for the sake of a livelihood, in accordance with the Vedic revelation: "One's own Veda is to be studied" (Taittirīya Āraṇyaka 2.15.1).
‘Because of the reference to the saṃskāra’; the meaning is: because of the mention of the saṃskāra known as initiation (upanayana) alone;
the words “by that word” are to be supplied [to complete the sense].
The meaning of the word *mātra* (only) is that this does not, however, refer to the "touching of a Brāhmaṇa.
Thus, the intention is that there is no room for the aforementioned doubt.
Some, however, say that the word "Brāhmaṇa" occurring in the Vedic text here refers to members of the three higher castes who are fit for the contemplation of Brahman (*brahmāṇana*).
That [objection] is to be considered, because it is not consistent with the resolution of the doubt.

Why is it so conceived? Because even in the *Smṛti*, the study of the *Āraṇyaka* portion of the Veda is prescribed only for one who possesses the second birth known as initiation (*upanayana*). With this intention, it is stated in the Sūtra and the Bhāṣya: "The entire Veda..."
The word "ca" (and) has been employed for the purpose of aggregating the Smṛti texts, [the sense of which is]: "It must be mastered along with its secret doctrines by the twice-born";
this [word "ca"] connects with the phrase "by means of reflection" (*parāmarśāt*).

The phrase "because of the subsequent reflection" implies that it is understood that study depends upon the sacramental rites (*saṃskāra*); furthermore, this is because the Paiṅgi Śruti declares the absence of such rites for a Śūdra: "For a Śūdra there is no fire, no sacrifice, no ritual action, no sacramental rite, and no vows."

Granted that study requires the sacrament of initiation (*upanayana*), nevertheless, the absence of Vedic study for the *śūdra* is not established; for it might be argued that a sacrament is possible even for a *śūdra*. It is in response to this that [the Sūtra] states: "Because of the declaration of its absence."
Thus he explains this fragment of the Sūtra: "Not fire."
"From expression, from naming"—
in this [context], there is supplied in the Sūtra [the phrase]: "A Śūdra has no entitlement to the Vedas, nor does he possess the status of a charioteer, which is invariably concomitant with that."
Thus is the positive concomitance with the probandum.
"Fire" refers to both that prescribed by the Śruti and that prescribed by the Smṛti.
"Sacrifice" refers to the Agnihotra and other such rites.
Or "rite" (*kriyā*) refers to sacrifices to the gods, ancestors, and so forth; or it refers to rituals such as the twilight worship (*sandhyā-vandana*),
or the subsequent funeral rites (*uttara-kriyā*).
"Saṃskāras" refers to the initiatory rites such as the upanayana;
"vratas" refers to ascetic observances such as the kṛcchra and cāndrāyaṇa.
But for excellent women, it is not like that of Śūdras, because we observe their eligibility [for such rites] in passages such as, "O most base one, do not wrong my co-wife."

Now, if it follows that women of the highest class (uttama-strī) are likewise ineligible for the Vedas due to the absence of sacramental rites (saṃskāra), then the same would apply to them as well. If they were granted eligibility despite the absence of such rites, then the same would accrue to the Śūdra as well. To this, he says: "The word *tu* (but) indicates a distinction characterized by being a seer of the Vedas."
"By the absence of formative forces (saṃskāra), there is absence"— this is drawn in; "of the governing topic (adhikāra)" is the ellipsis.
The analysis of the compound is "the women of the highest [castes]," or it is a *karmadhāraya*.

And thus, just like a *śūdra*, it must be stated that for excellent women such as Śacī, Yamī, and Urvaśī, there is an absence of entitlement to Vedic knowledge due to the absence of sacramental rites (*saṃskāra*).
Why? Because in such Vidyās as "Drive away my rival" (Mantra-praśna 1.16), their qualification [for those rites] is seen through their being the perceivers thereof; this is the construction.
Here, by taking the phrase "sapatnīm" as a pratīka, [it refers to the mantra]: "Drive away my rival; make my husband mine alone."
The entire sentence, "I am the superior; may I rise above those who are superior," is taken as this statement of Śacī.
"O Blessed One, drive away my co-wife— another woman who has taken my husband's hand— and cast her aside;
[grant] my husband to me alone."
Make [your mind] attached to me alone.
"Utterābhyaḥ" means from women who are superior in beauty, or those who are more excellent than I am. "Uttarā" [is used here].

The meaning of the Vedic text is: being preeminent, she "crosses over" (uttaret); being truly the most beloved, she "crosses over" (uttare); that is, she crosses over the suffering caused by rival wives.

By the word "etcetera" (*ādipadena*), there is the inclusion of such [hymns] as seen by Devamātṛkā, Yamī, Paulomī, and others, beginning with: "Soma has risen for some upon the mountain; yonder sun has risen" (*Ṛgveda* 10.159.1).
However, non-existence due to the absence of formative factors (saṃskāra) is [non-existence] in a general sense.
In that case, there would be a deviation [from the rule] regarding excellent women due to the absence of mental impressions (*saṃskāra*); therefore, he says: "mental impressions... and so forth.
There is an absence of qualification for the Vedas;
the word "but" (tu) indicates a specific distinction within the general nature of the previously stated principle;
the words "it has been said" are to be supplied as the ellipsis.

And thus, that absence of qualification for the Vedas mentioned in the Sūtra on the ground of the absence of *saṃskāra* (sacramental rites) is intended according to the "general" (*sāmānyena*)— that is, by way of a general rule (*sāmānyanyāya*) which includes exceptions (*sāpavāda*),
and not by way of an exceptionless rule (*nirapavāda*).

The meaning is that, therefore, there is no deviation (vyabhicāra) regarding the scope of the exception (apavāda). By the statement concerning "being a general category" (sāmānyatva), the counter-example of the Śūdra is refuted.

Thus, although the universal pervasion (sāmānyavyāpti)—that "due to the absence of sacraments (saṃskāra), there is an absence of entitlement to the Vedas"—is sublated by the exception known as the observation of the entitlement to knowledge (vidyādhikāra) in the case of Śacī and others, there is no sublation of that [pervasion] even in the case of the Śūdra and so forth.
The meaning here is that, within the context of eligibility for Vedic knowledge, there is no specific proof, authoritative text, or exception [to the contrary].
Furthermore, they do undergo refinement (saṃskāra), according to the Smṛti: "For women, the very rite of giving away in marriage is equivalent to the initiation ceremony (upanayana). // 36 //

Thus, it has been stated that even though women lack the initiation ceremony (*upanayana*), they possess the entitlement to the Vedas because an exception is possible due to the general nature of the aforementioned pervasion (*vyāpti*).
Now, he states that there is indeed such entitlement because a substitute for that [initiation] exists, even in the absence of the rite called *upanayana*: "And there is" (*asti ca*).
The word "and" (*ca*) serves to aggregate the grounds for entitlement.
To the question, "From where does this [distinction] regarding those women arise? he says: "Of women.
The word "of men" is to be supplied as the ellipsis.
And thus, just as initiation (*upanayana*) is a sacrament (*saṃskāra*) for men, [so too is it for women].

Likewise, the meaning of the Smṛti of Vyāsa is that for women, "the very act of giving" (pradānakarma)— that is, the rite of marriage itself— is the purificatory sacrament (saṃskāra). The word "of the Smṛti" (smṛteḥ) is to be construed with the word "for them" (tāsām).
The word "iti" implies "it is known.

Thus, the sense is that there is no deviation (vyabhicāra) because, in the case of the highest-ranking women, the absence of the general qualification (*saṃskārasāmānya*)—which was made the reason here and is common to both actual injunctions and substitutes—is absent.
Nor should it be argued that if the mere presence of *saṃskāra* were the cause for eligibility for the Vedas, then the same would apply even to the lowest-ranking women.
This is because it is accepted that [the eligibility for Vedic study] is conditioned precisely by that [lack of prohibition] accompanied by the absence of a prohibition.

Now, one might object: "In this way, since women of the highest class possess eligibility precisely because they are endowed with the sacraments (*saṃskāra*), it can be argued that there is no violation of the stated principle; so why accept the absence of sacraments in them and state that the aforementioned principle has an exception? To this we reply: No.
Because [the eligibility for knowledge] includes even animals and others who are devoid of the capacity for giving and so forth;
for even they are seen to possess the qualification for knowledge, as evidenced by such passages as "O Agni, this singer... (Ṛgveda 10.142.1), which constitutes an exception to the general rule.

By this [statement], because the word "that" (*tat*) in the phrase "one should teach him" (*tam adhyāpayīta*) refers back only to the previously mentioned sacrament known as initiation (*upanayana*), and because the Smṛti declares that "the Veda is [to be studied] in its entirety," and because the Śruti states that there is no fire for this Śūdra due to the mention of the absence of such sacraments, [he is not entitled].
Thus, it is stated that he has the qualification for the Vedas; this is the meaning of the Sūtra. Om.
And because activity proceeds when there is the determination of the absence of that [object].

This is because, by means of Satyakāma’s truthful statement, "I do not know, sir, what my lineage is" (Chāndogya Upaniṣad 4.4.4), it was determined that he was not a Śūdra; furthermore, because Hāridrumata proceeded to initiate him into the sacred rites, saying, "A non-Brāhmaṇa would not be able to speak thus" (Chāndogya Upaniṣad 4.4.5). // 37 //
Is it not the case that the statement regarding the Śūdra’s lack of entitlement to Vedic knowledge due to the absence of sacramental rites (saṃskāra) is untenable?
For, since there is no prohibition such as "one should not initiate a Śūdra," it is possible for him to undergo those rites as well.

Regarding the Vedic text, "There is neither fire nor sacrifice," it is stated that the Śūdra lacks the purificatory rites (saṃskāra), but it is not prohibited by saying that [the rites] are not to be performed; therefore, there is no contradiction with that [other scriptural authority]. Anticipating this objection, he recites and explains the Sūtra beginning with "tadabhāve... (in the absence of that).
‘By means of truthful speech’ (*iti satyavacanena*) means by means of speech and mind being of one form, that is to say, by means of the straightforwardness (*ārjava*) indicated thereby;
[this refers to] ‘one whose desire is truth’ (*satyakāmasya*).
This refers to the seer named after that [Satyakāma], and it is connected both previously and subsequently.

By the words "by means of truthful speech, of Satyakāma," and so forth, it is stated that the word *tat* (that) in the Sūtra is analyzed; being distributed across multiple case-endings, it recurs as it is mentally distinguished.
And the phrase "in the determination of the absence of Śūdra-hood" is connected with the words "this is not a Brāhmaṇa.
The particle *ca* (and) is used in the sense of emphasis (*avadhāraṇe*).
Since the Śruti text conveys the intention that all who are merely non-Brāhmaṇas are ineligible for initiation, following that [text], he does not say "the absence of Brāhmaṇa-hood," but rather...

By explaining the term "absence of Śūdra-hood" (*śūdratvābhāva*) as the absence of that [Śūdra-status], it is stated that in the Vedic text the word *brāhmaṇa* refers to members of the three higher castes who are capable of performing *brahmāṇana* (reverence for Brahman). This sentence establishes the determination of the absence of Śūdra-hood either by way of a reductio ad absurdum (*tarka*) against the contrary case—stating that if this non-Brāhmaṇa were a Śūdra, then he would not be fit to speak this truthful statement or straightforward speech, which is a statement where there is no discrepancy between mind and speech—or by way of stating a negative concomitance (*vyatireka-vyāpti*), namely: "He who is a non-Brāhmaṇa is one who is incapable of speaking thus, being devoid of truthful speech. Thus, it serves as a means of determining the absence of Śūdra-hood.
The offspring of Haridrumata is Hāridrumata Gautama;
[the phrase] "of his activity" connects with the supplied word "there is no absence of that for him."

Thus, the application of the great statement (*mahāvākya*) here is as follows: when Satyakāma’s non-śūdra status has been determined through his truthful declaration— "I do not know this"— through the knowledge of negative concomitance (*vyatirekavyāpti*) that "one who is not a brāhmaṇa is not capable of speaking thus," and through the subverting argument (*bādhakatarka*), it is precisely by inferring that [status] for him that the initiation rite (*upanayana-saṃskāra*) was performed for that Satyakāma by Hāridrumata.

Because Gautama’s [rule] regarding "non-engagement" has already been applied, there is no absence of that [engagement] for a Śūdra; thus, there is no prohibition against his sacramental rites (*saṃskāra*).
The particle *ca* is used in the sense of a conjunction of reasons.
By this [statement], the word *tat* in the Sūtra is taken both as a separate word with its case-ending elided and as a compound, by way of *tantra* (a single term serving multiple functions).
The word *ca* (and) is used in the sense of restriction (*avadhāraṇe*) and is to be construed in a different order:
not only is there an absence of sacraments for the Śūdra on account of mere Vedic revelation (*śruti*), [but also because of other reasons].

But there is also the word "and" (ca) in the sense of a conjunction, [indicating] "and because of the indicative mark that makes known the prohibition of mental impressions" (saṃskāraniṣedhajñāpakaliṅgāt).
The word "not" (na) is present;
it is to be supplied with the phrase "in the absence of that" (tadabhāve).

And likewise, "of him," that is, of Satyakāma; "by that," namely by truthful speech—meaning straightforwardness (*ārjava*), which is the non-contrariety of the actions of mind, speech, and body, and which is itself truthfulness; [he was purified] by that such speech, that is, by the uprightness made known thereby.

Having presented the negative concomitance (*vyatirekavyāpti*) and the subverting argument (*bādhakatarka*)—namely, "A non-Brahmin is not entitled to speak thus"—and having ascertained the absence of that [Brahminhood] through the determination of the absence of Śūdra-hood, Gautama proceeded with that initiation rite for him, saying, "Bring fuel, my dear; I shall initiate you" (Chāndogya Upaniṣad 4.4.5).
Since his engagement in that initiation rite is observed, there is no absence of that rite for a Śūdra, nor is there an absence of a prohibition against it.

The meaning of the Sūtra is stated as follows: if there were no prohibition against the initiation (*upanayana*) of a Śūdra, how could this [text] proceed only upon the determination of its absence? Thus, it is understood that the intention is that a prohibition exists.
For in the *Chāndogya*, there is this narrative: a sage named Satyakāma approached his mother, who was called Jabālā, and spoke to her.

"Why? [Satyakāma asked. "I intend to approach a teacher for the purpose of Vedic study; since study there depends upon the sacrament of initiation (*upanayana*), they would not teach me without that initiation.
Furthermore, they would not perform the initiation without [knowing] one's lineage and so forth; therefore, I ask: what is my lineage?
Having been addressed thus, Jabālā said to her son Satyakāma: "My dear child, as for the question of what your lineage is, I do not know."
Thus addressed, Satyakāma approached Gautama and said: "What is it? [He replied: "O Blessed One, I have come to you for the sake of the life of a student.
Being thus addressed, Gautama said: "O gentle one, what is your lineage?"
He said, "In that same way.
Thus addressed, Satyakāma replied again to Gautama: "I do not know this, sir.
"Sir," meaning venerable Gautama, "I do not know" this which ought to be known: what my lineage (gotra) is.
The meaning is "I do not know.
Thus, having understood Satyakāma’s straightforwardness through his truthful speech, [the teacher] spoke to him again,
beginning with "This is not so," and so forth.
In this context, the word *brāhmaṇa* refers to members of the three [higher] castes who are fit for the veneration of Brahman (*brahmāṇana*).

This is because, in a Smṛti text which serves as an exposition of the Śruti passage, "Straightforwardness is manifest in a Brāhmaṇa; a Śūdra is characterized by lack of straightforwardness," the Śūdra is mentioned as the counter-correlative (*pratiyogin*) to the Brāhmaṇa.
And likewise, this "speech endowed with straightforwardness" refers to one who is "not a Brāhmaṇa"— that is,
a Śūdra other than the three [upper] castes— and who is "unable to speak."
"In every way, it is not fit to say [that]; it is not appropriate.
Therefore, since you are speaking thus, you are indeed a Brāhmaṇa;
so, my dear, bring fuel, for I shall initiate you."
Sūtra — Oṃ.
Because of the prohibition against hearing, studying, and understanding [the Veda], and because of the Smṛti.
‘Upon hearing [the teaching], his ears are to be filled with tin and lac;
upon reciting it, his tongue is to be cut off;
and upon grasping its meaning, his heart is to be torn asunder.’
Because of the prohibition [stated in] Gautama-dharma-sūtra 12.4–7.

One might object: according to the reasoning already stated, since there is no distinction [between castes], the eligibility of even a Śūdra would be established on the grounds that he possesses specific intelligence and other such qualities.

Anticipating the objection that otherwise even the attainment of qualification for the deities and so forth would not be possible, he presents and explains the Sūtra beginning with "śravaṇa": "In the Sūtra, by following the Śruti [which says] 'in the determination of the meaning' (arthāvadhāraṇe), the word 'artha' refers to the determination of that [meaning]."

And likewise, the meaning is that in the Vedic text "In hearing [the Veda], [a Śūdra is forbidden] by means of tin and lead," the hearing, study, and comprehension of the meaning of the Veda are prohibited for a Śūdra.
This connects with the predicate "he does not lack that," which is supplied from the context.
The meaning of that [statement] is the absence of a prohibition against study.

Thus, since it is accepted that the possession of specific intelligence and so forth—provided there is no prohibition—is the very factor that entitles one to the Veda, and since that [possession of intelligence] is absent in a Śūdra, it follows that his salutation of the gods cannot be cited as grounds for his entitlement to the Veda;
this is the intended sense.
The meaning of the Śruti is that when a Śūdra listens to the Veda, his ear-cavities must be filled with molten tin and lac by the king’s officers.
The remainder is easy to understand.
There is no fire-sacrifice for the Śūdra, nor likewise the study [of the Veda]; how much less so [the performance of sacrifices]?
However, service alone is prescribed for the three castes.

And because of the Smṛti. To remove the doubt as to whether this Śruti passage might not refer to those outside the [four] castes—since the Śruti does not explicitly state "when hearing is performed by a Śūdra"—the Sūtra says "and because of the Smṛti.
He cites that Smṛti: "Not... [iti].
Just as for a Śūdra—
by whom fire must never be consecrated and even the fivefold sacrifice must not be performed—
so too how could there be study? From nowhere at all.
Then he asks what means for achieving the next world must be practiced by him, using the word "tu" (but) to introduce the question. He provides the answer with the word "kevalā" (alone);
the meaning is "without wages."

"Trivarṇa" means those who are both three and castes; the meaning is "of those [three], namely the Brāhmaṇas, Kṣatriyas, and Vaiśyas. The connection is that "service" (śuśrūṣā) indeed means "attending upon" (paricaryā).

It is prescribed; the phrase "as something to be performed" is to be understood as the ellipsis. Regarding the expression "from the Smṛti," the connection is with the supplied words "there is no absence [of study]," because it is understood from that Smṛti that the prohibition of study applies specifically to the Śūdra.
And thus, by the force of clear recollection, the intention is that even the Śruti has as its subject matter only the Śūdras.
However, in the case of Vidura and others, there is some distinction because they had already attained knowledge. // 38 //
Thus concludes the section concerning those who are not Śūdras (Apaśūdrādhikaraṇa). // 9 //
Now, if it is objected that since the determination of the meaning of the Vedas and so forth is prohibited for a Śūdra, how is it that Vidura and others possessed such knowledge of Vedic matters?
Likewise, if those devoid of sacramental rites (*saṃskāra*) have no entitlement to the Vedas, how did the Kṣatriya Karṇa, who was devoid of sacramental rites, master all the *Śrutis*?
Nor should it be argued that he was an exception to this rule.

Since those for whom the initiation (*upanayana*) was not prescribed—namely, women of the highest class, animals, and so forth—are the objects of the exception regarding prohibited study, and since Śūdras, who are prohibited from such study, are not included among them, [the author] says:
"of Vidura and others. By the word "others," Dharmavyādha and the like are included.
The word "tu" (but) has the sense of specification.
He states that very point: "because they possess arisen knowledge.
Those for whom there is immediate (*aparokṣa*) knowledge—arisen through a lineage [of teachers] from having studied the Vedas in another birth—are so described; their state is "that-ness" (*tattva*).
Therefore, the meaning is that "there is someone"— that is, there exists among them a specific quality (*viśeṣa*) that is uncommon and distinguished from other Śūdras and so forth;
the word "since" (*yataḥ*) is to be supplied [at the beginning of the sentence].

Therefore, the meaning is that these [words] are not the objects of prohibitions such as "not non-fire," but rather they are the objects of exceptions; thus, one should not suspect that other Śūdras have the right to study the Veda on the grounds of that [logical] counter-argument.

The meaning of the Sūtra, however, is as follows: because of the Vedic revelation prohibiting a Śūdra from hearing [the Veda]— namely, "with tin and lac" (referring to the ears)— and because of the Smṛti clearly prohibiting the study of the Veda for a Śūdra alone— namely, "no fire, no sacrifice"— it is not the case that there is an absence of that [prohibition], i.e., an absence of the prohibition against the study of the Veda, for him.
Thus concludes the section concerning those other than Śūdras (Apaśūdrādhikaraṇa). // 9 //
// 10. The Section on Trembling //
"Whatever there is in this entire world, it quivers, having issued forth from the vital breath;
it is a great terror, a raised thunderbolt. Those who know this become immortal. (Kaṭha Upaniṣad 2.3.2) Thus, liberation is heard to result from the knowledge of the raised thunderbolt.
In this section, the name "Vajra" is employed.
He indicates the connection with the scriptures and the subject matter, etc., by the words "yad idam" (that which is this).
In this regard, the previously stated view that for the three twice-born classes (traivarṇika), knowledge of Brahman derived from the Veda bestows liberation is incorrect;

for, according to the scriptural passage "This which... (*yad idam*), liberation is heard to result from the knowledge of the raised thunderbolt (*udyatavajra*), as established by construing the text through grammatical supplementation (*vākyopaskāra*).

By this, the connection (saṅgati) of this [section] as an "objection-based" (ākṣepikī) one is stated; for in the previous section (*pūrvādhikaraṇa*), it was intended that for the three social classes (*traivarṇika*), knowledge of Brahman derived from the Veda grants liberation. However, in the section on the "consisting of bliss" (*ānandamaya-adhikaraṇa*), by the phrase "not the other" (*anetaraḥ*), it was asserted that Viṣṇu alone is the object of that knowledge which generates liberation. Since that [assertion] is now challenged [by the opponent] as applying to someone other than Viṣṇu, the objection-based connection is thereby explained.
It is indicated that the word "thunderbolt" (*vajra*) is the subject matter (*viṣaya*).

Based on the conventional usage (*rūḍhi*) of the term "vajra" for a thunderbolt, as well as the force of the indicative mark (*liṅga*) of being "upraised" found in the Smṛti passage beginning with "those whose staff-like arms upraise weapons," and in the Śruti passage "Indra upraised the vajra," this prima facie argument (*pūrvapakṣa*)— supported by reasoning— is indicated: that this vajra is indeed Indra’s weapon.
In the Vedic text, the word "prāṇe" ends in the locative case;
the word "sthitam" (situated) is to be understood as the ellipsis.

Alternatively, by treating "prāṇe" as having a causal locative sense (*nimitta-saptamī*) or by changing the case ending (*vibhakti-vipariṇāma*), it may also be connected with the word "nissṛtam" (issued forth) through repetition (*āvṛtti*).
The word "yat" (that which) is either repeated or supplied by ellipsis;
since "yat" is heard, "tat" (that) is understood. Thus, according to the established conclusion (siddhānta), this is the meaning of the scriptural text: "whatever [it may be]."

Whatever is seen or heard—all this world—is situated in Hari, who is denoted by the word "Prāṇa" on account of the act of breathing; it has issued forth from Prāṇa and is born from Him. This entire world "moves from whence," meaning it acts through His impulsion; and because of His greatness and worshipfulness, He is "Mahat."
It terrifies, thus it is *bhayam* (fear); it is "terrifying" (*bhayaṅkaram*) for the wicked.

It is "raised up" (*udyatam*), meaning endowed with all effort; for "being raised up" (*udyatatvam*) means "possessing effort," since the root *yam-* preceded by the prefix *ud-* has that as its meaning.
Thus it is stated in the *Candrikā*.
This is the form of the word *yatī* with the prefix *pra-*; furthermore, some maintain that the syllable *ut-* denotes excellence (*utkarṣa*).

"Vajra" is that which is denoted by that word because of the avoidance of faults or the avoidance of what is unpleasant; those who "know this"— who know it through direct perception— they are "immortal."
"They become liberated. Alternatively, the word *prāṇa* is in the nominative case; thus, *prāṇa* refers to the chief vital breath (*mukhyaprāṇa*).
The meaning is: "Those who know this thunderbolt—from which this seen world and all else that is heard have issued forth, and from which the entire universe moves."
Alternatively— there is a repetition of the word "yat" (which), wherein the first instance functions as a qualifier of the world,
the second refers to the principal vital breath (mukhyaprāṇa),
and the third refers to the thunderbolt (vajra).
The word "sa" (he) is understood; it is syntactically connected with the nominative term "prāṇa. Thus, that from which the entire world has emerged is the primary vital breath (mukhyaprāṇa).
The meaning is that those who know that *vajra* which moves;

in this regard, the distinction is as follows: in the first explanation, the chief vital breath (*mukhyaprāṇa*) is shown to be impelled by the Lord because it is included within the universe; in the second, through its similarity to the universe;
but in the third, the distinction is that the chief vital breath itself is directly impelled by the Lord, whereas the universe is impelled by the chief vital breath.
The proponent (pūrvapakṣin), however, maintains that the rainbow itself is what is expressed by the word "vajra";
he considers that its state of being raised—that is, its status as the object of the act of raising—is the indicative mark (liṅga) belonging to that very thing.
Therefore he said:
Sū-oṃ.
Because of trembling.
Because of the statement "it moves," which refers to trembling, it is the Blessed Lord himself who holds the raised thunderbolt.
Introducing the aphorism that establishes this conclusion, he explains it with the words "Therefore... (ataḥ).
"From the statement regarding trembling" (*kampanavacanāt*);
this means from the statement that [the Self] is the mover of the entire world, which takes the form of that [phrase].
Alternatively, it means from the statement regarding the trembling of the principal vital breath (*mukhyaprāṇa*), namely the declaration that it "trembles" (*ejati*).
By the phrase "on account of the statement," it is meant that the word "trembling" (kampana) refers to that statement.

Nor should it be argued that, by accepting a syntactical split (*vākyabheda*) in the Vedic text, the quality of causing trembling is not predicated of the thunderbolt (*vajra*); for since the quality of being terrifying—which is the cause of trembling—is explicitly stated in reference to the thunderbolt, a syntactical split is untenable.

In the *Udyatavajra* Sūtra, there is a supplementary statement: following the word "that" (*tat*) which is carried over from the *Samanvaya* Sūtra, and in accordance with either the term "vajra" as the subject or the term "vital breath" (*prāṇa*), the explanation "the Blessed One" (*bhagavān*) is provided.
This is restrictive;
by it, the meaning of the word "but" (*tu*) is demonstrated.
Although it would have been sufficient to state merely that "Vajra is indeed the Blessed One," the qualification "raised" (*udyata*) was nonetheless included as an epithet of Vajra.

Nevertheless, this was stated in order to demonstrate that the logical mark (*liṅga*) of being "raised" cited by the opponent— namely, the sense of being "raised" in the form of possessing effort— is not without scope [and thus does not constitute a definitive proof].
"For who indeed could breathe, who could live, if this bliss did not exist in the ether?"— so says the Śruti. (Taittirīya Upaniṣad 2.7)

Now, one might object: "Since the prima facie view (pūrvapakṣa) was established by both direct scriptural statement (śruti) and indicative mark (liṅga), how can the conclusion be reached by the indicative mark alone?

To this, with the intention that it is precisely because the indicative mark is otherwise impossible (niravakāśatva), he demonstrates through scripture that the indicative mark—namely, being the general mover of the universe, which is mentioned in the context of the *vajra* according to the first and second explanations of the word *śruti*, and which is common to both Prāṇa and others—is impossible elsewhere than in Viṣṇu, by asking: "Who indeed..."?
