The word *hi* is used in the sense of a reason (*hetau*), meaning "since" or "because," or as a particle of well-known fact (*prasiddhau*).
The word "exists" (*asti*) is to be supplied [as the verb].
The remainder of the sentence is: "Therefore, one should not suspect that the indicative mark (*liṅga*) has scope elsewhere."
And [it says]: "The life-breath of the life-breath, and the eye of the eye" (Bṛhadāraṇyaka Upaniṣad 6.4.18).

Since, in general, the state of being the impeller of all movement in the entire universe resides in Viṣṇu alone, what then need be said regarding the fact that the mark (liṅga) of being the impeller of the life-breath—the mover of the entire universe—found in the Vajra [hymn], resides in Viṣṇu alone according to the third method of interpretation of the Śruti?
With the intention that the state of being the mover of the world is impossible in any other way, he shows the scriptural authority for this with the words "of the prāṇa.
The word "ca" (and) has the sense of "because" (yasmāt),
or it serves to connect with the preceding scripture.
The word "scripture" (śruti) is to be supplied [from the context].
The remainder of the sentence indicates that the aforementioned indicative mark (liṅga) has no other scope of application.

Alternatively, the indicative mark intended by the phrase "on account of trembling" (kampanāt)—namely, the fact of being the initiator of the world and the cause of vital activity—is [to be understood as follows].
To avoid the failure to establish that [the Self] is devoted to Viṣṇu, he cites scripture as authority therein:

"of the prāṇa" (prāṇasya) means of the chief vital breath which is the cause of all movement; "the prāṇa" (prāṇam) means that which bestows the state of being prāṇa, characterized by the excellence of causing movement; "and" (uta).

Likewise, the meaning of the Vājasaneyi Śruti is: "Those who know the Supreme Self as the 'eye of the eye'— that is, as that which bestows the nature of being an eye (cakṣuṣṭva) by virtue of being the instrument of vision— they have 'perceived' (nicikyuḥ) Brahman, or rather, they shall attain it."
Even all the activities of the wind belong to the Blessed Lord Hari;
how much more so those of the rest of the world, whose activity is the wind itself?

Thus it is stated in the Skanda Purāṇa. Furthermore, even in the first commentary on the Śruti, [the author] cites a Smṛti passage which proceeds by taking as its reason the fact that the movement of the vital breaths is directed by [the Supreme], in order to clarify the principle of *kaimutya* (a fortiori): "Of the wind... and so forth.
Furthermore, even the "winds" (nabhasvataḥ), who impel the world, have all their movements originate from Lord Hari, who is full of qualities such as knowledge.
In that case, what need is there to mention that the movement of the rest of the world—other than the wind—is produced by Hari?
Why is this so? Because the meaning of the statement is that the movement of that world does not arise from the wind (nabhasvat).
The word "in the Skanda [Purāṇa]" is to be understood as having been stated immediately after [the previous sentence].
Therefore, the sense is that there is no scope for the [inferential] mark (liṅga) elsewhere.

Because he moves about [as a wheel], he is called the Wheel; because he shatters [obstacles], he is called the Thunderbolt (vajra). Since he is the very embodiment of all limbs, he himself is Hari, bearing the name of the Weapon.
Thus it is stated in the Brahmavaivarta [Purāṇa]. // 39 //
Thus concludes the section on trembling (Kampanādhikaraṇa), number ten.

Now, one might object: even if the mark (*liṅga*) of being the wielder of the raised [thunderbolt] has scope in Viṣṇu, since the scriptural mention (*śruti*) of the thunderbolt is without scope and is stronger by its very nature, how can it be determined that the thunderbolt is indeed Viṣṇu based on the mark of being the impeller of all activity—even though that mark is itself without scope?

To this, with the intention of showing that the "lack of scope" for the scriptural mention of the thunderbolt—favored by the proponent of the prima facie view—is actually unestablished, [the author addresses] even that scriptural mention of the thunderbolt...
He indicates the scope [of the term] with respect to Viṣṇu by means of a traditional authority (smṛti), stating: "The wheel.
"This" Blessed One is called "the wheel" because of his "wandering"—that is, because he causes the individual soul (jīva) to wander within saṃsāra.
As it is stated in the *Tattvapradīpa*: "It is called a *cakra* because it causes one to move about (*caṅkrāmayati*).
Likewise, [it is so called] "because of being avoided" (*varjanāt*);
that is, it is avoided by the Daityas from afar.
It is not brought face-to-face;
it is called "vajra" because it is to be avoided by the wicked according to the method of the *Sattarkadīpāvalī*, or because it avoids all faults.
The meaning is that this is a *khaḍga* because of its "cutting" (*khaṇḍana*), that is, the severing of defective limbs, and because of its "subduing" (*damana*).
By the word "this" (*eva*), its non-difference from that [sword] is excluded.
To the questions "What follows from that? and "And what is this?", he says: "As a weapon" (*heti*).

Thus, Hari is "himself" (svayam), meaning directly and without relation to anything else; he is "named after his weapons" (hetināmā), which means he possesses those names which are the primary designations for all his weapons, such as the discus and so forth.
By the general term "the weapon" (*hetīti*) in the Bhāṣya, it is implied that the word "vajra" is indicative of other [weapons] as well;
the words "stated immediately after [the mention of] the Brahmavaivarta" are to be supplied as the ellipsis.
Thus, the sense is that there is no contradiction with the Śruti either.
By the statement "He is called by the name Heti," it is indicated that there is also a conventional usage (*rūḍhi*) among the learned for words such as *vajra* and so forth to refer to Viṣṇu.

Consequently, the objection that [the etymological derivation] is impossible because the conventional meaning (*rūḍhi*) weakens the stated etymological connection (*yoga*)— namely, that he is so called because he "avoids" (*varjana*) [sin]— is refuted.

Nor should it be argued that this contradicts the statement in the *Kāṭhakabhāṣya* regarding the word "vajra" being applied metaphorically (*gauṇa*) to Viṣṇu, as in the phrase "and [it is] like a thunderbolt, causing fear.
This is because the intent of that passage there is simply to establish that the sentence can somehow be made to refer to Brahman;
for since its reference to Brahman is established even through metaphorical usage, there is no intention to restrict it to a literal sense.

In this context, however, because the etymological (*yoga*) and conventional (*rūḍhi*) meanings alone have been stated with the intended purpose of establishing the primary sense promised in the *Samanvaya-sūtra*, the meaning of the sūtra is clear.
Thus ends the section on "Trembling" (Kampanādhikaraṇa). // 10 //
11. The Section on Light (Jyotir-adhikaraṇa)
The light placed within the heart is called the Supreme Self (*paramātman*).
Regarding this, it is said: "This person consisting of consciousness (*vijñānamaya*), who is the light within the heart among the vital breaths" (Bṛhadāraṇyaka Upaniṣad 6.3.7);
and here [it is further stated]: "He wanders through both worlds" (Bṛhadāraṇyaka Upaniṣad 6.3.7).
From this statement, it is understood that [the object] is the individual soul (jīva).
In this section, the term "light" (jyotis), which is well-known in both senses, is harmonized [with the context].
He demonstrates the connection with the Śruti and so forth, as well as the subject matter and other factors, by saying: "In the heart."
The meaning is that in the *Jyotirnaya* [section], it is stated that the light deposited and placed within the heart—that which is denoted by the word "that" (tat)—is the Supreme Self.
To the question "What follows from this?", he says: "Therein," meaning in the context of the subject matter concerning light.
The word "iti" is followed by the ellipsis "is heard.
To the question "What follows from that?", he says: "atra" (here).
This means "in this sentence."
The term "light" (jyotis) heard [in the text] is to be supplied here as well.
Thus, it is understood that the light mentioned here is none other than the individual soul (jīva), whose nature is knowledge, and who is denoted by the word "that" (tat).
Why? Because [the text states]: "Being identical [to them], he moves between both worlds."

The construction is: "because of such statements," meaning because of the supplementary passages (*vākyaśeṣa*) that declare the marks of the individual soul (*jīva*), such as [the passage beginning with] "Thus it is said.

By this, through the refutation of the light mentioned in the Vājasaneyaka statement "The light within the heart," the previously mentioned [light] is also refuted; thus, its "refutative connection" (*ākṣepikī saṅgatiḥ*) is stated.

The subject matter is the light mentioned in the Vājasaneyaka, and the prima facie argument—that this light is indeed the individual soul (jīva)—has been indicated. For in the Vājasaneyaka, it is asked of this person: "What is his light? (kiṃjyotiḥ)?

When Janaka asked, "What is the means for the knowledge of the individual soul? What is the means for its knowledge?", Yājñavalkya replied with the words, "'The light of the sun, O Emperor,' he said" (Bṛhadāraṇyaka Upaniṣad 6.3.2).
By this, he stated, "O Emperor"—meaning King Janaka, the sovereign of the whole earth—"this person has the sun as his means for knowledge."

In this manner, through a series of questions and answers, having explained that during the waking state—among the sun, the moon, fire, and speech—the subsequent light takes over upon the setting of each preceding one for the living being (*jīva*), [the text] then asks again regarding deep sleep and dreaming, when the four [lights] beginning with the sun have set: "What is the light of this person? (Bṛhadāraṇyaka Upaniṣad 6.3.2).

Thus questioned by Janaka, Yājñavalkya stated, "The Self alone is his light," thereby declaring that the Jīva's nature is that of the self-luminous light of the Supreme Self; then, being asked again—"Which is the Self?"—referring to that Self described as light, he replied, "This which... [Bṛhadāraṇyaka Upaniṣad 6.3.7], in order to specify what that Self is and of what nature it is.
By this, it is stated that he gives the answer: "The Supreme Self is distinct from the individual soul, the body, the senses, and so forth.
He who is "consisting of consciousness" (*avijñānamaya*) is full of consciousness; [he is] "among the vital breaths" (*prāṇeṣu*).

Existing as the internal controller within the senses and within the heart, He is the "Light," the "Person" who illumines the intellect and other faculties of the individual soul, and is complete in the six divine attributes.
The meaning is "this very Self.
He describes its greatness with the word "he":
"He" refers to the Self, the Supreme Self, who is "equal."

The meaning is that, being changeless and always of one form, [the Self] moves along with each individual soul, taking up "both worlds"— namely, the earthly world and the heavenly world, or waking and deep sleep.
But the proponent of the prima facie view (pūrvapakṣin) [argues as follows]:

The term "ātman" and the term "saḥ" (he) refer to the individual soul (jīva); furthermore, it is intended that even its wandering through both worlds is dependent upon karma, and one considers that characteristic mark (liṅga) to belong to that very [soul] by virtue of karma.
Therefore, it is said:
Sūtra—Oṃ.
Because of the sight of light.
"Viṣṇu alone is light, Viṣṇu alone is the Self, Viṣṇu alone is Brahman, Viṣṇu alone is strength, Viṣṇu alone is glory, and Viṣṇu alone is bliss"—
thus it is seen in the Caturvedaśikhā.
Light is indeed Viṣṇu.
Introducing the sūtra that establishes this conclusion, he explains it by first citing the scriptural passage mentioned under the heading "darśana": "Therefore...
Viṣṇu alone is light... Viṣṇu alone is bliss."
Because it is seen in the *Caturvedaśikhā* with the words "thus," and because it has been stated that Viṣṇu alone is primarily denoted by the word "light" (*jyotis*),
therefore Viṣṇu alone is the referent of that term.
The meaning is "not the individual soul" (jīva).
By the phrase "Viṣṇu alone," the meaning of the word "that" (tat), which is understood from the context, has been stated.
The meaning of the scriptural passage (śruti), however, is clear.
The distinction, however, is this: *bala* is the giver of strength;
as it is said in the *Bhāgavata*: "He indeed is the strength of the strong and of others."
In the *Tattvapradīpa*, it is stated that Viṣṇu alone is glory (*yaśas*), based on the scriptural text: "His name is great glory" (*Mahānārāyaṇopaniṣad* 1.10).
The entire passage is cited here to demonstrate that, just like the word *brahman* and others, the word *jyotis* (light) also refers exclusively to Viṣṇu.
For this very reason, the restrictive particle *eva* appears in the Śruti:
"Mounted by the conscious self (*prājña-ātman*), he goes forth emitting [sound]" (Bṛhadāraṇyaka Upaniṣad 6.3.35).
From this statement, it follows that even for him, there is indeed movement through the worlds. // 40 //
Thus concludes the section on Light (Jyotir-adhikaraṇa), number eleven.

If it is argued that if Viṣṇu is the light, then there would be a contradiction with the scriptural indications regarding the departure [of the soul] from both worlds, he dispels even this doubt by means of the scriptural passage indicated by the word "darśana" (vision) in the Sūtra: "By the conscious one... (prājñena).
"From this statement"—
that is, from the sentence of the Vājasaneyi Śruti— "of him too";
the meaning is that even for the Supreme Self (paramātman), there is indeed movement through the worlds.
The word "also" (api) implies that this applies not only to the individual soul (jīva).
The word "only" (eva) in the phrase "not its absence" means precisely that.
Thus, the meaning is that since the indicative mark (liṅga) has another scope, there is no contradiction with it.
The embodied self, the individual soul (jīva), at the time of death,
is "mounted" (*anvārūḍha*) by the "wise one" (*prājña*)— the wise one being one who knows thoroughly and completely (*pra-āsamantāt jña*), or else by that Supreme Self (*paramātman*).

According to the statement in the *Bṛhadbhāṣya* that "the Blessed One, having mounted Jīva as his vehicle, goes," the meaning of the *Vājasaneyi-śruti* is that [Jīva], serving as His vehicle, "emits" (*utsarjat*)— that is,
casting off the previous body— and "goes" (*yāti*)— that is, proceeds— to another body and another world.
The meaning of the sūtra, however, is clear.
Thus ends the section on Light (Jyotir-adhikaraṇa). // 11 //
// 12. The Section on Space //
The status of Viṣṇu as the support of all has been stated; and that [is confirmed] by the passage: "Space, indeed, is the bringer-forth of name and form" (Chāndogya Upaniṣad 8.14.1).
In this passage, space (*ākāśa*) is understood;
for there is an instruction based on what is well-known (*prasiddha*). And that which is well-known as space must be accepted [as the referent].
In this case, the name "ether" (ākāśa), which is not well-known in either sense, is harmonized with Brahman.
He demonstrates the connection with scripture and so forth, as well as the subject matter and other factors, by stating: "the state of being the support of all.
The phrase "in the section concerning heaven, earth, and so forth" (dyubhvādyadhikaraṇa) is to be supplied as the remainder.
To the question "What follows from that?", he says: "And that" (*tacceti*).
The word "and" (*ca*) is used for emphasis.
"In this" (*ityatra*) means in the statement of the Chandogas (the Sāmavedins) of such a form.

By this, through the statement that the word "ether" (*ākāśa*) here refers to something other than Viṣṇu, it is implied that the previously mentioned status of being the support of all things also resides in another; thus, its "suggestive connection" (*ākṣepikī saṅgatiḥ*) is stated. Furthermore, the subject matter—the ether named in the Chāndogya Śruti—is indicated.
He demonstrates the prima facie view (*pūrvapakṣa*) along with its reasoning: "vainām iti."
The word "sa" (he/it) is to be supplied [as the subject].
The particle "ca" is used for emphasis.
Thus, the "space" mentioned in the Chāndogya Upaniṣad must be accepted as the well-known, witness-attested *avyākṛtākāśa* (undifferentiated space).

Why? Because it is taught that this [space] possesses well-known status, as indicated by the two particles *vai* and *nāma* accompanying the word "ether" (*ākāśa*); the meaning is that this has already been stated.

However, some—relying on the reading of the *Ṭīkā* intended by the author of the *Candrikā*, which states: "'In the *Sattarkadīpāvalī*, the elemental ether (*bhūtākāśa*) alone should be accepted as what is well-known; for even space (*avakāśa*) possesses name and form'"—[hold a different view].

They say that because the *Sudhā* states that "the ground for the application of the term 'space' (ākāśa) is the quality of providing room (avakāśatva), which is unlimited in the [gross] element," it is the gross element itself— denoted by the word "space"— that constitutes the subject of the prima facie view (*pūrvapakṣa*).
In the Śruti, the two particles "vai" and "nāma" signify well-knownness.
"Name" refers to the manifold of expressive words; by the term "form," only the manifold of objects subsumed within primordial matter (prakṛti) is meant.
And thus, Ākāśa is the "evolver" of both name and form—that is, of the two manifolds of word and object.

The meaning is: "the one who carries across" (nirvoḍhā), the substratum (āśraya), and the agent (kartṛ). "'Those' (te)" refers to name-and-form (nāmarūpa) as they are presented here as that which is to be carried across. "'Between'" (antarā) means by way of distinction.
"'That which'" (yat) means that which exists as distinct from the manifold of name-and-form (nāmarūpa-prapañca).

Alternatively, by the word "that" (tat), both the denotable object—comprising the manifold of forms such as blue—and the denoting name are grasped. Thus, "between those two" (te antarā) means without them;
that is to say, devoid of them.

The meaning is that Brahman is that which exists in its entirety, expressible by names yet devoid of a material form (*prākṛtarūpa*). Alternatively, it means that which exists "between" (*antarā*) those things possessing name and form, as a distinct entity.
As it is stated in the *Tattvapradīpa*: "That which is neither name nor form—that is Brahman.
Therefore, it is said:
Sūtra—Oṃ.
Space [is not non-existent], because it is designated as being a different entity and so forth.
"Whatever is between them, that is Brahman" (Chāndogya Upaniṣad 8.14.1).
Because of such designations as being "other than the two," the ether is indeed Hari.
Introducing and explaining the sūtra which establishes this conclusion, [the author] says: "Therefore... (ataḥ).
Thus, [the expression] "because of the designation as 'a different object' (arthāntara) and so forth" is used;
in both the Sūtra and the Bhāṣya, the word *artha* is employed to indicate the meaning of a word (*padārtha*),
while the word *antara* is used in accordance with the Vedic revelation (*śruti*).
The word "by those two" is to be supplied as the remainder [of the sentence].

And thus, "another object" (*arthāntara*) means an object different from those two, namely name and form; or, an "other object" (*arthāntara*) is an object distinct from them. Its state (*tattva*) is the fact of being so.
This consists either in being distinct from the manifold of name and form (*nāmarūpa-prapañca*), or in being devoid of the name and form belonging to primordial nature (*prakṛti*).

The meaning is that it is because of the designation of a different object (arthāntara) consisting in the absence of name and form (*nāmarūpa*). By the word "etc. (*ādi*), the state of being Brahman (*brahmatva*) is included.

Alternatively, since the absence of name and form themselves, independently [of anything else], establish the state of the ether as Brahman, the term "different object" refers to the absence of form, and by the word "etc.," the absence of name is also included.
And thus, the meaning is that it is because of the reasoning regarding the difference in nature (*arthāntaratva*) and so forth.
This "ether" (*ākāśa*) heard in the *Chāndogya* is that which is denoted by the word "that.
He states the meaning of the word "that" (*tat*), which follows from the *Samanvaya-sūtra*, as "Hari alone."
By this [statement]—this space is indeed Hari.
Why? Because of its designation as being distinct from other things; for in the passage "That which is within them," there is stated a unique meaning characterized by the absence of name and form.
Thus, the meaning of the sūtra, "And because of the mention of Brahmanhood," has been stated.
For that very [Brahman] possesses such characteristics, according to scriptural passages such as "without color" and "from which words turn back" (Taittirīya Upaniṣad 2.4).

One might ask: how can Viṣṇu be ascertained from the mention of "space" (ākāśa), given that such a term possesses characteristics like name-and-form (nāmarūpa)? With the intention of showing that [Viṣṇu] is established therein, [the author] cites an Atharvaṇa Śruti as the authority for this:
"avarṇam" means devoid of natural colors such as white and so forth, or else distinct from them.
Alternatively, "avarṇam" means "not to be described" (na varṇyam), or "not consisting of color" (na api varṇātmakam).
This is the meaning of the scriptural passage: "from which. From *yataḥ*, i.e., from Brahman, *vācaḥ*—names—*nivartante*—turn back.
This should be explained as being intended to state that [the Self] is nameless;
by the word "etcetera," such scriptural passages as "without sound, without touch, without form" (Kaṭha Upaniṣad 1.3.15) are included.

The connection is to be understood by supplying the words: "From such scriptural passages as these, it is known that having this form and so forth is the definition—that is, the unique attribute—of that Viṣṇu.
For this reason (hi), there is no fallacy of the mark being unestablished due to a difference in substratum; this is the intended meaning.
By the restrictive particle *eva* in the phrase "of that alone" (*tasyaiva*), even the suspicion of deviation (*vyabhicāra*) is dispelled.
Although the scriptural passage "from which" (*yataḥ*), which teaches that [Brahman] is nameless, should have been cited first, [the passage] "that which is between them" (*te yad antarā*)...
Thus, because the very absence of name was stated first,
there is no scriptural statement regarding form such as "without color" (*avarṇa*).

Nevertheless, since the name as the signifier is subordinate to the signified, and because the signified alone is primary, it is not a fault that the scriptural statement regarding the absence of form within the expansion of the signified was cited first.
As stated in the *Brāhma*: "He is nameless because he is not well-known; he is formless because he is devoid of the elements. (41)
Thus ends the section concerning space (ākāśādhikaraṇa). 12.

Now, an objection might be raised: "Is it not the case that Hari's being devoid of name and form is untenable, since he is denotable by all words and possesses forms such as the golden-hued one? Otherwise, there would arise a contradiction with what was stated [in the Brahma Sūtras]: 'Because of the seeing [of Him] as such' and 'Because of the presentation of form'? To this, he says: "Anāma" (without name).

"He" refers to Hari. Because he is "unestablished"—that is, because he is not cognized in his entirety by anything other than himself, such as sound and so forth—for that reason, he is called "nameless.
Nor should it be argued that this contradicts the two particles (*nipāta*) which indicate the well-known status of that which is denoted by the word "ether" (*ākāśa*).

This is because the well-known meaning [of "space"] is understood through its status as a particle (nipāta), and thus— according to the view of the opponent— it lacks connection with the subject (uddeśya) "space" due to its connection with the predicate (vidheya) "the state of being the sustainer" (nirvoḍhṛtva).
Furthermore, although the state of being the sustainer is not well-known in common worldly usage, it is nonetheless established by such scriptural passages as "The One alone sustained [the worlds]."
And because that [form] is not established, as indicated by the phrase "since it is not prohibited";
and because of the "exclusion of the elements" (*bhūtavarjanāt*),
meaning that he is "formless" (*arūpa*) due to being devoid of a material body or lacking such a form.
Since this has been stated in the *Brāhma* [section], there is no contradiction with what was previously mentioned; thus is the connection with the supplied words.
This concludes the section on Space (Ākāśādhikaraṇa). // 12 //
// 13. The Section on Deep Sleep (Suṣupti-adhikaraṇa) //

The state of non-attachment of the Supreme Self has been stated; and that is understood from the passage concerning the witness of dreams and so forth: "Whatever he sees there, he does not follow after it, for this person is unattached" (Bṛhadāraṇyaka Upaniṣad 6.3.15).
In this section, the mark of being the seer of dreams and so forth is shown to be consistent with Brahman.
He indicates the connection with scripture and the subject matter, etc., by the words "the state of being unattached" (*asaṅgatvam*).
In the passage from the section on the Imperishable (*akṣara*), it is stated: "without smell, without taste."
The meaning is that the state of non-attachment of the Supreme Self is thus declared in the Vājasaneyi passage.
To the question "What follows from that?", he says: "And that" (*tacceti*).
The particle *ca* is used for emphasis (*avadhāraṇe*).
The phrase "iti" means "in such a statement from the Vājasaneyi [Upaniṣad].

By this, through the refutation that the state of being a dreamer and so forth resides in something other [than the Self], the previously mentioned non-attachment (asaṅgatva) is also shown to reside in something else; thus, according to the method of the *Akṣara-adhikaraṇa*, its "refutative connection" (*ākṣepikī saṅgati*) is indicated.
The object designated as the "seer of dreams and so forth" has also been indicated;
and that [seer] is the individual soul (jīva), because of its well-known status.
To the question "What follows from this?", he states the prima facie position (pūrvapakṣa) along with its reasoning, beginning with the words "And that... (sa ca).
The word "eva" is used for emphasis;
"he" would be none other than the individual soul (jīva), the seer of dreams and so forth.
The meaning is: why? Because in the world, the agency of seeing is well-known to belong to the individual soul (*jīva*) alone.

In the established doctrine (*siddhānta*), by the word "he" (*saḥ*) in the Śruti passage—"He, having rejoiced and wandered about in this state of profound serenity (*samprasāda*), and having seen both the auspicious and the inauspicious, returns again according to the rule, according to his origin, for the sake of dream-sleep itself"—the pronoun refers to that very [jīva].
In the preceding passage (Bṛhadāraṇyaka Upaniṣad 6.3.15), the Supreme Self under discussion is referred to;
the word "vai" (indeed) indicates well-knownness.
The term *samprasāda* refers to deep sleep (*supti*), because in it the living self (*jīva*) becomes perfectly serene (*samyak prasīdati*).
And thus, that Supreme Self, having "enjoyed" (*ratvā*) in the state of *samprasāda*, that is, in deep sleep—
Having performed [their respective functions], having seen— and not experienced— the merit and demerit residing within the living being,

and having "traversed" (sañcaritvā) according to the principle that "one must proceed to another state by following the rule" (pratinyāyam), or rather, "according to each respective karma," they go "to their respective wombs" (pratiyoni).
In every body, or rather in all bodies according to their respective origins and following each particular path,
[the vital breath] "rushes again" (*punar ādravati*) solely for the sake of the individual soul's attainment of sleep (*svāpnāyaiva*).
It comes to the region of the throat.
That Supreme Self, whatever undesirable thing He perceives there in the state of dreaming, by that—
He is "unfollowed" by— the untouched by— the suffering that is the fruit of the evil committed therein; the reason for this is "non-attachment."
The meaning is: because this person is "unattached"— that is,
established as being devoid of contact with the fruits of the sins committed by that [body]—
therefore [it is so].

The proponent of the prima facie view (pūrvapakṣin), however, taking the word "that" (tat) in its literal sense to refer to the individual soul (jīva), explains the entire passage as being centered on the soul;
therefore, he says:
Sūtra—Oṃ.
On account of the difference between deep sleep and departure.

"Embraced by the intelligent Self (prājña-ātman), he knows nothing external nor internal" (Bṛhadāraṇyaka Upaniṣad 6.3.21); "Mounted by the intelligent Self, he goes forth emitting [sounds]" (Bṛhadāraṇyaka Upaniṣad 6.3.35). Because of these designations of difference, it is not the individual soul (jīva), but rather the Supreme [Self] alone that is unattached (asaṅga).
Introducing the aphorism that establishes the final conclusion, he explains it with the words "ataḥ" (therefore).
The word "vakti" (he says) means he provides a resolution.
The phrase "the state of being the seer of dreams and so forth belongs to him alone" is also to be connected here.

Therefore, for the sake of understanding the subject and the predicate in the Sūtra, it is indicated that there is a transformation (*vipariṇāma*) of the word *tat*—which had been repeated and then followed—as required by the context.
Furthermore, although the gender of the term to be connected has already been grasped by the word *tat*, it is specified by its own original term (*svaśabda*) for the sake of clear comprehension.
Immediately after the word *iti*, the Sūtra-word *suṣuptau* should be joined.
The word "because of designation" (*vyapadeśāt*) is a term supplied from the preceding [sūtra] by means of the intellect;
furthermore, the word "non-attachment" (*asaṅga*) is supplied in the sūtra to indicate a reason.

By the phrase "the individual soul is the Supreme," it is stated that the terms *suṣupti* (deep sleep) and *utkrānti* (departure), though indicative of that specific context, also refer to the individual soul and the Supreme Self.

If that were the case, the word *suṣupti* would be derived from the root with the suffix *ktin* in the sense of the agent (*kartari*), and the word *utkrānti* would mean "one who causes [the self] to depart from the body. In that case, the construction would be as follows: the state of being the seer of dreams and so forth must belong to that Supreme Self alone, not to the individual soul (*jīva*).
Why? Because it is heard in scripture that He is unattached (*asaṅga*).
Nor should it be asked, "How can this Viṣṇu be [the subject] even when there is a scriptural statement regarding the dreamer's state of non-attachment?
For this non-attached one is the Supreme Self alone, being superior due to not being bound by karma, and not the individual soul (jīva).
Thus, since the indicative mark (liṅga) has no other possible application, its lack of probative force (aprayojakatva) is not to be suspected; this is the intended meaning.
Nor should it be argued that even with respect to the individual soul (*jīva*), the statement of its being unattached (*asaṅga*) is possible by way of its difference from the Lord (*īśvara*);

for in the two sets of passages concerning deep sleep and departure—beginning with "by the conscious one" (*prājñena*)—there is a designation of the difference between the individual soul, who is the witness of dreams and so forth, and the Lord, who is unattached. By citing the scriptural passage beginning with "by the conscious one," the word "deep sleep" (*suṣupti*) in the Sūtra is intended to include liberation (*mokṣa*) as well.
By this, the doubt that "this distinction is merely conventional" is also dispelled;
furthermore, it is thereby stated that the section [of the text] is indicated by the terms "deep sleep" (suṣupti) and "departure" (utkrānti).
And the term "departure" denotes death, which consists of the soul's (jīva) exiting from the body.
In the Śruti, the word *prājña* ends in the suffix *aṇ* used in its own sense (*svārthika*). Thus, "enveloped" means surrounded by the *prājña*, that is, the omniscient Supreme Self (*paramātman*).

The meaning of the first statement is that [the Self], being embraced [by the Supreme], whether sleeping or liberated, does not perceive anything whatsoever—whether external or internal—such as objects and the like.
The meaning of the second statement, however, was already set forth in the preceding section:
and the status of being the witness of dreams and so forth is appropriate for that [Self] alone, because it is omniscient. // 42 //
Thus concludes the section on deep sleep (Suṣupti-adhikaraṇa). // 13 //
Now, one might ask: "How can it be logical for one who is bodiless to have visions such as those in dreams? To this he says: "svapnādi" (dreams, etc.).
The word "ca" (and) is used in the sense of conjunction, or in the sense of "also."
By the word "etcetera" (ādipadena), the states pertaining to the individual soul (jīva) are included.
Thus, it is not only non-attachment that is appropriate for the Supreme Being alone because He is unbound by karma;
rather, the state of being the witness of dreams and so forth also belongs to Him alone.
It is more appropriately applicable to the Supreme Self than even to the individual soul (jīva). Therefore, that statement applies to Him alone and not to the individual soul.
Why? Because He alone is "all-knowing" (sarvajña).
The sense is that because there is knowledge of all objects as real, and because the reality of dream-objects and the state of the individual soul (jīva) will be explained later;
nor is the mark of bodilessness a subverting factor, since it is stated here that the very same one who has consciousness as His body is the seer of dreams and so forth.
Nor should it be said that there is an inconsistency with such passages as "having seen both merit and evil" (Bṛhadāraṇyaka Upaniṣad 6.3.15);

for the construction is as follows: since the status of being the seer of merit, evil, and so forth—comprised by the word "etcetera" (*ādi*) here—and other indicative marks are appropriate only for that [Self], therefore [it is He].
The details regarding rebirth there should be understood from the *Bṛhadbhāṣya*.
By this [sūtra], [the states of] deep sleep and departure [are addressed]:
"by the conscious one" (*prājñena*).
Thus, in the two sections concerning deep sleep and departure, because deep sleep is associated with the state of deep sleep, deep sleep is the individual soul (jīva);
and because departure is that which causes one to depart, departure is the Lord (īśvara). And so, there is a "distinction" between the individual soul and the Lord.
Because they are designated as distinct,
as has been stated, there is no non-difference between them;
therefore, it is not tenable to speak of the soul's lack of attachment even by way of its non-difference from the Lord.
However, that [dreaming] belongs to that very Lord alone;

for this reason, it is appropriate to say that the state of being the seer of dreams and so forth belongs to Him alone and not to the individual soul (jīva). Thus the meaning of the Sūtra has been stated. This concludes the section on deep sleep (suṣupti-adhikaraṇa). // 13 //
// 14. The Section on the Brahmins //
"‘This is the eternal greatness of the Brāhmaṇa’" (Bṛhadāraṇyaka Upaniṣad 6.4.22); thus, the eternal greatness of the Brāhmaṇa is also perceived,
and he is that Brāhmaṇa.
From the word "unborn" (*aja*) in the passage, "This indeed is that great unborn Self" (Bṛhadāraṇyaka Upaniṣad 6.4.24), it follows that [the one who attains the state beyond the gods] is Viriñca.
Furthermore, the attainment of the station by the gods through knowledge and action has been indicated by the sūtra *tadupary api*.
In this section, the name "Brāhmaṇa" is connected [to the title].
It indicates the connection with the Śruti and so forth, as well as the subject matter and other elements, by means of the words "eṣa" (this) and "iti" (thus).
The meaning is that this refers to the Ṛgvedic mantra cited in the *Vājasaneyaka*. The force of the word "api" (also) is to indicate that this applies not only to Viṣṇu, but to some Brāhmaṇa as well.

Furthermore, "this one" (*eṣaḥ*) refers to that eternal majesty which was intended in the *Janmādyadhikaraṇas* by the statement that Viṣṇu is the creator of the universe independently of anything else.
In this sentence, the fact that [the attributes] are perceived even in the case of a Brāhmaṇa is to be construed by supplying the words "yat" and "tat.

By this, since there is an implication of someone other than Viṣṇu—who possesses the aforementioned eternally majestic nature—the *ākṣepikī* (implicative) connection with the *janmādyadhikaraṇa* (the section beginning with "The origin, etc. is stated by way of its result.
Likewise, the subject matter known as the Brāhmaṇa is also indicated.

Alternatively, the sentence "of the gods" (devānām) should be understood as having been explained as being intended to restate what is established in the *Devatādhikaraṇa*; by that, one should see that its introductory connection (*ākṣepikī saṅgati*) has been stated.

For instance, by the sūtra "above that" (*tadupari*), it was stated that for the gods—namely Viriñca and the other immortals—the attainment of the eternal state, which is to be accomplished through knowledge and action, is not tenable.
Why? Because in the sentence "This [is He]," the eternal majesty of Viriñca, denoted by the word "Brāhmaṇa," is "perceived"; that is, it is set forth—such is the construction of the sentence.

The etymological derivation (*vyutpatti*) of *śrutau* is "that which is heard" or "understood through the Veda. The transposition of the long vowel [in *brahmaṇā*] indicates that Viṣṇu is understood through the Veda and is superior to the individual soul (*jīva*).
Thus, this aforementioned greatness of the Brahman, who is Viṣṇu, is eternal.

Why? Because this [text], "He is neither increased by action nor made smaller" (Bṛhadāraṇyaka Upaniṣad 6.4.22), means that he is not increased by auspicious action or by the pleasure that is its fruit, nor is he diminished by evil action or by the suffering that is its fruit; such is the meaning of the Śruti.
He presents the prima facie argument (pūrvapakṣa) with reasoning, beginning with the word "sa" (he). This refers to what is stated in the Vājasaneyi Śruti.
The particle "ca" (and) is used here for emphasis (avadhāraṇe).
"Virincha alone" is what is connected [to the context].
"From the word 'unborn' (aja)" means from the word 'unborn' heard in such preceding and following sentences.
The meaning of the scripture is that this very one is the Supreme Self, who is "great," which means immeasurable, and "unborn," meaning devoid of birth.
The proponent of the prima facie view (pūrvapakṣin), however, considers Viriñci to be the one denoted by the word "brāhmaṇaja.
But how could Viriñci be a brāhmaṇa?

For, according to the sūtra *tadupari* (2.3.14), it has been established that the gods attain their station through knowledge and ritual action; therefore, the state of being a brāhmaṇa—whose greatness is declared eternal in scripture—is impossible for Viriñci.

Because there is a rule that whatever has a beginning is impermanent, he says: "And of the gods. The word "and" (ca) is used for emphasis. After the word "iti," the word "sūtre" (in the Sūtra) is to be understood as the ellipsis.
And thus, in the Sūtra "and above that," the attainment of the state through knowledge and action is indicated and established as belonging only to the gods other than Viriñca,
but not to Viriñca himself.
The construction is as follows: because he, being of the nature of Īśvara, does not enter into the category of [ordinary] deities, it is indeed logical that Viriñca possesses eternal majesty;
therefore, he says—Sūtra: Oṃ.
From words such as "husband" (pati) and so forth.

From such scriptural passages as, "The sovereign of all, the lord of all... He, indeed, is this one who is 'not this, not this'" (Bṛhadāraṇyaka Upaniṣad 6.4.21), it follows that Viṣṇu alone possesses eternal majesty.
He introduces the aphorism that establishes the conclusion with the words "ataḥ" (therefore).

Fearing that there might be a contradiction with the Vājasaneyaka, since that text begins with a word expressing "sovereignty over all," he explains the aphorism in accordance with it by first citing a corresponding passage from another recensional branch (*śākhā*) as a means of resolving that objection,
beginning with the words "sarvasya" (of all).
"Of all": he who is superior in qualities to Brahmā, Rudra, and others, and who is the lord and protector of all, is thus the "Lord of All" (sarvādhipati).
"Of all": the meaning of the other scriptural passage is that he is the "Ruler of All" (sarvasyeśāna), as he is the impeller (anaḥ) of those who rule over the world, such as Brahmā and others.

The meaning of the term *sarvavaśin* (the controller of all), however, should be understood from the *Bṛhadbhāṣya*: "Because everything is under his control, Hari is therefore the controller of all (*sarvavaśī*).
The Vājasaneyi Śruti states: "He, indeed, is this one. Here, "he" (*saḥ*) refers to that which was designated by the word *prāṇa*, and "this one" (*eṣaḥ*) [refers to the same].
The term "Self" does not denote the Supreme Self;
nor does it denote [the Self] as something perceived.
It means "not like that which is heard," but rather distinct from both the seen and the heard; the word *vai* indicates what is well-known.

Why is this so? Because the complementary passage continues: "The Self is ungraspable, for it is not grasped; it is indestructible, for it is not destroyed; it is unattached, for it does not cling; it is unfettered, it does not tremble, and it is not injured... This very Self is ageless, undying, immortal, and fearless" (Bṛhadāraṇyaka Upaniṣad 2.4.24).
In this context, the passage beginning with "atrāgṛhya" and ending with "ātmanaḥ" provides, in its entirety, the reasons—such as being ungraspable—for the meaning already stated [by the word] "na.
On the other hand, the passage beginning with "na hi" indicates the reason for that [negation], namely, "because there is an absence of evidence (pramāṇa) regarding it.
Although it says "itina" in the *Bṛhadbhāṣya*...
Like the food of Rāmā,
not like that of Brahmā and others, nor like that of the bound.
It has been explained otherwise [in other contexts] that it is not like a pearl;
nevertheless, here it is explained in this way solely in accordance with the scriptural designation (*samākhyā-śruti*) "He who is unheard from this" (Ai. Ā. 3.2.4), so there is no fault.
Regarding the phrase "ityādi" (and so forth):
the meaning is "from those words heard in [the passage] beginning with 'ityādi' which denote universal sovereignty (*sarvādhipatya*) and so on.
By the word "ādi" (and so forth), there is an inclusion of words denoting universal mastery (*sarvavaśitva*) and other such qualities.

By this, it is stated that the word *sautrādi* not only includes words such as "Lord of All" (*sarveśāna*) mentioned in other recensions (*śākhā*), but also includes words such as "possessing all wonders" (*sarvavilakṣamatva*) and "all-controlling power" (*sarvavaśitva*) mentioned in the Vājasaneyi [Saṃhitā].

Having thus explained the reason (*hetu*), one should carry over the word *tat* from the *Samanvaya-sūtra* and, by modifying it, employ *tad* as the indicator of the subject (*uddeśya*) suitable for the connection (*anvaya*).
By supplying the word "eternal greatness" (*nityamahimā*), he explicitly shows the extracted proposition: "eternal greatness.
This [statement] takes the form of a declaration of the result (*phala*).
Regarding the phrase "from words," one should understand that while the reason is connected [to this], the probandum (*sādhya*)—namely "is Brahman"—is to be supplied as an ellipsis.
By this [scriptural passage]: "This Brahmin is indeed Viṣṇu himself, not Viriñca.
Why? Because of words such as 'Lord' (pati) and so forth."
From the words "all-sovereignty" and so forth heard here, it follows that he alone possesses eternal majesty; thus the meaning of the Sūtra is stated:
"And he is the Lord of immortality."
Regarding the passage, "That which grows by food" (Taittirīya Āraṇyaka 3.12), one might ask:

even though words expressive of universal sovereignty and so forth exist [elsewhere], how can there be a certainty that the Brāhmaṇa is Viṣṇu? To ward off the doubt that the reason is inconclusive (*aprayojakatva*), he first cites a scriptural text (*śruti*) concerning the fact that universal sovereignty resides in Viṣṇu alone, beginning with the word "uta."
And this [verse] is to be explained together with the preceding statement: "The Person alone is all this; whatever has been and whatever is to be."
As for its specific nature: that which is "past" (bhūtam), that which is "future" (bhavyam), and that which is "present"— all that is indeed the Puruṣa alone.
It is indeed dependent upon the Supreme Person.
Why? Because the Person is not merely the sovereign lord of all that is unliberated, but [it says], "the means to immortality."
Even for the collective [of the senses], he is the "Lord" (īśāna), meaning the sovereign;
for there is a scriptural statement that "the application of taddhita suffixes is manifold," and thus the suffix -tva is used in the sense of the collective.

In the *Tattvapradīpa*, however, another interpretation is stated: because of the designation of non-difference between the state (*bhāva*) and that which possesses the state (*bhavitṛ*), the suffix *-tva* is used in the sense of the state; thus, "of immortality" means "of liberation," and it is the "ruler" (*īśāna*) of that.
He states the reason for this with the word "yad" (that which);
here, the instrumental case is used in the sense of the accusative.
Thus, it is "yat."
The meaning is: because [the Self] "surpasses" (atirohati)— that is, excels over— "food," which is the mortal multitude of transmigrating beings, therefore [it is called so].
The sense is that if liberation were not dependent on [the Lord], it would be impossible for an omniscient and intelligent being to grant liberation to those in saṃsāra who are under His control.
As it is said: "The seven half-embryos of the world, the seed of Viṣṇu, abide according to His direction in the established order" (Ṛgveda 1.164.36);
and "He who is unheard from this" (Aitareya Āraṇyaka 3.2.4).
For those very words belong to that alone, according to such scriptural passages as these. // 43 //
Thus ends the section concerning the Brahmins. 14.
Thus ends the third quarter of the first chapter in the Brahmasūtra-bhāṣya composed by the venerable teacher Śrīmad Ānandatīrtha Bhagavatpāda. Om!
Now, regarding the fact that He is the impeller of all, as expressed by the word "all" in connection with every sound, he cites scripture— beginning with "Seven"—
which has been explained in the section on the Imperishable (Akṣara-naya).
Furthermore, even though He is distinct from everything seen and heard, as stated by "Not this, not this" (neti neti), he cites scripture beginning with "He" (saḥ).
This [verse] is also explained in every section [of the commentary].
By the phrase "and so forth" (*ityādi*), he indicates that other scriptural passages concerning "mastery over all things" (*sarvavaśitva*) and so on should likewise be cited.
The meaning of "of him alone" (*tasyaiva*) is "of Viṣṇu alone, and not of another."

‘For’ (hi); because these words, such as ‘sovereignty over all’ and so forth, are understood [to refer to Brahman], therefore one should not suspect that they are irrelevant—this is the remainder of the sentence.
Thus ends the section concerning the Brāhmaṇas (Brāhmaṇādhikaraṇa). // 14 //

Thus ends [the section] from the *Śrīmad-Brahmasūtra-Bhāṣya-Dīpikā* composed by the venerable ascetic Jagannātha, disciple of the venerable and worshipful Raghunāthatīrtha, the illustrious wandering mendicant preceptor who is independent in all philosophical systems.
The third quarter of the first chapter.
